  • Starts an enrollment: stores a fresh secret that does not count yet and returns it as an OTPHP\TOTP. getSecret() and getProvisioningUri() are the two shapes an authenticator takes it in. The label is the user's email and the issuer the pageName. Starting again replaces the secret and turns an active two factor off until the new one is confirmed, which is why the profile page refuses to start while two factor is on.

    $user->startTwoFactor(): TOTP

  • Turns two factor on when the code matches the stored secret. Returns false for a wrong code and for an account that already has two factor.

    $user->confirmTwoFactor(string $code): bool

  • Checks a code against the stored secret, one 30 second step either side of the current one. Returns false while the account has no secret.

    $user->verifyTwoFactorCode(string $code): bool

  • Returns whether two factor is on, and since when.

    $user->hasTwoFactor(): bool
$user->twoFactorConfirmedAt(): ?string

  • Turns two factor off and drops the secret.

    $user->disableTwoFactor(): void

docs.title: Login Tries
docs.text:
Failed logins are counted per account to rate-limit password guessing.

  • Returns false when the user has more failed tries than maxLoginTriesPerTimespan within the last maxLoginTriesTimespan. The event is logged as ACCOUNT_LOGIN_RATE_LIMITED. maxLoginTriesTimespan is a relative time string such as 3 minutes. When it is unset, the window start becomes 1970-01-01, so every recorded try of the account counts, however old. When maxLoginTriesPerTimespan is unset, it is null and the comparison only passes for zero tries, so the account is blocked as soon as a single try is recorded in the window.

    $user->checkLoginTries(): bool

  • Counts a failed login toward that limit.

    $user->recordLoginTry(): void

if(!$user->checkLoginTries()) {
    // blocked, notify the owner here if the application wants to
}

if(!$user->verifyPassword($password)) {
    $user->recordLoginTry();
}

The framework does not notify the owner of a blocked login, an application does that itself where it needs to.

docs.title: Role Assignment
docs.text:
Users can have multiple roles assigned or removed dynamically.

  • Adds one or more roles to the user and clears the user's cached fields. Adding a role the user already has inserts a duplicate row.

    $user->rolesAdd(Role ...$roles);

  • Removes one or more roles from the user (the assignment is set inactive) and clears the user's cached fields.

    $user->rolesRemove(Role ...$roles);

  • groupsAdd(Group ...$groups) and groupsRemove(Group ...$groups) do the same for groups and reject plain Role objects.

docs.title: User-Based Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions can be assigned directly to users in addition to role-based permissions.

  • Adds user-based permissions. Names are not deduplicated: an identical active row is inserted again.

    $user->permissionsAdd(string ...$permissionNames);

  • Removes user-based permissions.

    $user->permissionsRemove(string ...$permissionNames);

docs.title: Permission Checks
docs.text:
Permission checks always resolve the complete permission set. The permission methods (permissionsAdd, permissionsRemove, hasAccessAll, hasAccessAnyOf and the static buildPermissionVariants) come from the Permission trait that User, Role, Group and Organization share.

  • Checks whether the user has all specified permissions, wildcards included.

    $user->hasAccessAll(string ...$permissionNames): bool

    Without arguments it returns true, since no permission is missing.

  • Checks whether the user has at least one of the specified permissions, wildcards included.

    $user->hasAccessAnyOf(string ...$permissionNames): bool

    Without arguments it returns false, since no permission can match.

docs.title: Permission Retrieval and Refresh
docs.text:
• Returns only user-based permissions.

    $user->getUserPermissions(): array

  • Returns all effective permissions (user-based + role-based + group-based), cached on the instance until a permission, role or group is changed through these objects, after which the getters re-query on every call. The rows look like ["name" => "x.y"], while Role::getPermissions() returns plain strings. Only active role links, roles and permission rows count; z_user.active is not filtered.

    $user->getPermissions(): array

  • Reloads user-based permissions.

    $user->refreshPermissions();

  • Reloads all permissions including roles. Changes made outside these objects (admin forms, direct SQL) only show up after this or refresh().

    $user->refreshAllPermissions();

docs.title: User Data & Utility Methods
docs.text:
• Reloads the user data from the database and throws RuntimeException("Object no longer exists") when the row is gone or inactive. Call it after updateEmail(), updatePassword(), verify() and role or group changes, which clear the object's fields; reading a field like email() before throws Field 'email' does not exist.

    $user->refresh();

  • Returns the user’s email address.

    $user->email(): ?string

  • Returns the verification timestamp.

    $user->verified(): ?string

  • Returns the user ID.

    $user->id(): int

  • Returns the user's UUID.

    $user->uuid(): string

  • Returns the user's active roles without groups, cached on the instance.

    $user->getRoles(): array

  • Returns the user's active groups, cached on the instance.

    $user->getGroups(): array

  • Returns the organization the user belongs to, or null if none is assigned. The result is cached on the instance - including the null case - until clearFields() or a write operation invalidates it.

    $user->organization(): ?Organization

  • Returns whether the user belongs to the given organization. A removed organization has no members.

    $user->isMemberOf(Organization $organization): bool

  • Returns the cached data of the user as an array. This is the full z_user row, including the password hash and the salt column (null for natively hashed passwords), plus the internal cache keys permissions, user-permissions, roles, groups and organization. Never output it unfiltered, for example in a response or a log; read single values with getField() instead.

    $user->getAll(): array

  • Throws an InvalidArgumentException ("Instance no longer exists") once the object was nulled by remove(); every other method on it throws the same.

    $user->checkInstance(): void

docs.title: Role Object
docs.text: The Role object represents a named collection of permissions that can be assigned to users. A Group is a Role restricted to z_role.is_group = 1: it grants permissions the same way, has all methods below (returning only groups, so Role::byId() never finds a group id), and is accepted wherever a Role is type-hinted. Role and group names share one unique column.

docs.title: Role Retrieval
docs.text:
• Returns all roles assigned to a user, including those of its organization.

    Role::byUser(User $user): array

  • Returns the active roles an organization holds. Group::byOrganization(Organization $organization) does the same for groups.

    Role::byOrganization(Organization $organization): array

  • Returns the active role with that exact name or null.

    Role::byName(string $name): ?Role

  • Returns all roles that have all specified permissions, wildcards included. Without arguments it returns all active roles.

    Role::byAccessToAll(string ...$permissions): array

  • Returns all roles that have at least one of the specified permissions, wildcards included.

    Role::byAccessToAnyOf(string ...$permissions): array

  • Returns all roles.

    Role::all(): array

  • Returns a role by ID.

    Role::byId(int|string $id): ?Role

  • Returns all roles matching the given IDs.

    Role::byIds(int ...$ids): array

  • Returns a role by its UUID or null if not found.

    Role::byUuid(string $uuid): ?Role

  • Returns all roles matching the given UUIDs.

    Role::byUuids(string ...$uuids): array

docs.title: Role Creation and Loading
docs.text:
• Creates a new role and returns it.

    Role::add(string $roleName): Role;

  • Creates a role from a raw z_role row, which must contain the id key.

    $role = new Role(array $data);

docs.title: Updating and Removing Roles
docs.text:
• Updates the role name. All fields are cleared, so call $role->refresh() before reading the object again.

    $role->update(string $newName);

  • Soft deletes the role. The instance is nulled, so any further call on it throws InvalidArgumentException("Instance no longer exists"). Its permissions and user assignments stay but stop counting, and its name stays reserved.

    $role->remove();

docs.title: Role Data Access
docs.text:
• Returns the role's UUID.

    $role->uuid(): string

  • Returns the role name.

    $role->name(): string

  • Returns all active users assigned to the role, cached until $role->refresh().

    $role->getUsers(): array

docs.title: Role Permissions
docs.text:
• Returns all permissions assigned to the role.

    $role->getPermissions(): array

  • Reloads role permissions.

    $role->refreshPermissions();

  • Adds permissions to the role.

    $role->permissionsAdd(string ...$permissionNames);

  • Removes permissions from the role (soft delete).

    $role->permissionsRemove(string ...$permissionNames);

  • Replaces this role's permissions with the permissions of another role. The current permissions are removed and the source role's active permissions are copied over.

    $role->setPermissionsByRole(Role $role);

docs.title: Role Permission Checks
docs.text:
• Checks whether the role has all specified permissions, wildcards included.

    $role->hasAccessAll(string ...$permissionNames): bool

    Without arguments it returns true, since no permission is missing.

  • Checks whether the role has at least one of the specified permissions, wildcards included.

    $role->hasAccessAnyOf(string ...$permissionNames): bool

    Without arguments it returns false, since no permission can match.

docs.title: Refreshing Role Data
docs.text:
• Reloads the role data from the database.

    $role->refresh();

docs.title: Organization Object
docs.text: The Organization object represents a group of users. Users can belong to at most one organization. An organization has a name (not unique, may be null) and is soft-deletable (active) like the other authentication objects. Like a user, it can hold permissions, roles and groups, which all its members inherit.

docs.title: Organization Retrieval
docs.text:
• Returns the organization a user belongs to, or null if the user has none. This is a convenience pass-through to $user->organization().

    Organization::byUser(User $user): ?Organization

  • Returns all active organizations matching the given name. Names are not unique, so the result may contain zero, one, or multiple organizations.

    Organization::byName(string $name): array

  • Returns all organizations.

    Organization::all(): array

  • Returns an organization by its ID, or null if not found or inactive.

    Organization::byId(int|string $id): ?Organization

  • Returns all organizations matching the given IDs.

    Organization::byIds(int ...$ids): array

  • Returns an organization by its UUID, or null if not found or inactive.

    Organization::byUuid(string $uuid): ?Organization

  • Returns all organizations matching the given UUIDs.

    Organization::byUuids(string ...$uuids): array

  • Returns all active organizations that hold the role. Organization::byGroup(Group $group) does the same for groups.

    Organization::byRole(Role $role): array

  • Returns all active organizations that have all specified permissions, wildcards included, through their own permissions or their roles and groups.

    Organization::byAccessToAll(string ...$permissions): array

  • Returns all active organizations that have at least one of the specified permissions, wildcards included.

    Organization::byAccessToAnyOf(string ...$permissions): array

docs.title: Creating an Organization
docs.text:
• Creates a new organization with the given name (which may be null). When $createGroup is true, a permission Group named $groupName, by default "{$name}_Group", is created and linked to the organization (z_organization.groupId, NULL without a group). The linked group is then available via $organization->getGroup() and is used by User::updateOrganization() to sync group membership.

    Organization::add(?string $name, bool $createGroup = false, ?string $groupName = null): Organization

docs.title: Updating and Removing Organizations
docs.text:
• Updates the organization's name.

    $organization->updateName(string $name);

  • Soft deletes the organization (active = 0). Its active members are detached first (organizationId is set to NULL and the membership in the linked group is removed) and the linked group is deactivated, so $user->organization() returns null for them.

    $organization->remove();

docs.title: Organization Data Access
docs.text:
• Returns the organization's UUID.

    $organization->uuid(): string

  • Returns the organization's name.

    $organization->name(): string

  • Returns all active users assigned to this organization.

    $organization->getUsers(): array

  • Reloads the cached users list.

    $organization->refreshUsers();

  • Returns whether the given user belongs to this organization. The counterpart of $user->isMemberOf().

    $organization->hasMember(User $user): bool

  • Returns the permission Group linked to this organization, or null if none is linked. The result is cached on the instance until clearFields() or a write operation invalidates it.

    $organization->getGroup(): ?Group

  • Reloads the cached linked group.

    $organization->refreshGroup();

docs.title: Organization Roles and Groups
docs.text:
• Adds one or more roles to the organization. Adding a role it already has inserts a duplicate row.

    $organization->rolesAdd(Role ...$roles);

  • Removes one or more roles from the organization (the assignment is set inactive).

    $organization->rolesRemove(Role ...$roles);

  • groupsAdd(Group ...$groups) and groupsRemove(Group ...$groups) do the same for groups and reject plain Role objects.

  • Returns only the roles, respectively only the groups, the organization holds. Neither is cached.

    $organization->getRoles(): array
$organization->getGroups(): array

docs.title: Organization Permissions
docs.text:
Organization permissions are inherited by all its members.

  • Adds organization-based permissions. Names are not deduplicated: an identical active row is inserted again.

    $organization->permissionsAdd(string ...$permissionNames);

  • Removes organization-based permissions.

    $organization->permissionsRemove(string ...$permissionNames);

  • Checks whether the organization has all, respectively at least one, of the specified permissions, wildcards included, through its own permissions or its roles and groups.

    $organization->hasAccessAll(string ...$permissionNames): bool
$organization->hasAccessAnyOf(string ...$permissionNames): bool

  • Returns the names of all effective permissions (own + role-based + group-based), each once, as plain strings like Role::getPermissions().

    $organization->getPermissions(): array

  • Reloads the permissions.

    $organization->refreshPermissions();

docs.title: Session Object
docs.text: The Session object represents a login session (stored in z_logintoken) and provides methods for creation, retrieval, lifetime management, and invalidation. An api key is the same row with is_apikey set, represented by APIKey. The two are siblings, not parent and child: they get their behavior from the CanUseSession trait, so everything documented here applies to both. Type as Session|APIKey where either kind may turn up.

docs.title: Session Retrieval
docs.text:
• Returns a session by its token string, or null for an unknown or invalidated token; an expired session that was not yet invalidated is still returned. The row decides the class, so a token belonging to an api key returns an APIKey. This is the entry point of the authentication and therefore resolves both kinds, whichever class it is called on.

    Session::byToken(string $token): Session|APIKey|null

  • Returns all active logins of a user, expired ones not yet invalidated included, or an empty array. Api keys are listed by APIKey::byUser() instead.

    Session::byUser(User $user): array

  • Returns a login by its ID, or null if the ID belongs to an api key.

    Session::byId(int|string $id): ?Session

  • Returns all active logins matching the given IDs. Like all() and the UUID finders, it skips invalidated rows.

    Session::byIds(int ...$ids): array

  • Returns a login by its UUID, or null if the UUID belongs to an api key. This is the identifier to use when a session has to be addressed from outside the application - the token must not leave the client.

    Session::byUuid(string $uuid): ?Session

  • Returns all logins matching the given UUIDs.

    Session::byUuids(string ...$uuids): array

  • Returns all active logins.

    Session::all(): array

docs.title: Creating a Session
docs.text:
• Creates a new login session for a user. An optional $userExec can be passed to create an impersonation session where $user is the target user and $userExec is the acting. If omitted, both are set to $user. No cookie is sent; use $res->loginAs() for that. The optional $name labels the session, which is what a "your active sessions" list shows, and $reason records why it was created.

    Session::add(User $user, ?User $userExec = null, ?string $name = null, ?string $reason = null): Session

  • Names the session, or removes its name when null is passed.

    $session->setName(?string $name): void

  • Every session records the request that created it, without the caller doing anything: device holds the user agent (cut to the 255 characters the column takes, null when none was sent) and ip_creation the address it was created from. A name is never derived from either - it stays null until someone chooses one.

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
An api key is a session that is handed out deliberately instead of being created by logging in. It carries the same token, authenticates the same way and has the same lifetime controls - APIKey shares all of that with Session through the CanUseSession trait. What differs is that a key belongs to a single user and has no executing user, so its add() takes no $userExec. That is why the two are siblings rather than one extending the other: PHP would not allow the narrower signature on a subclass.

$key = APIKey::add($user, name: "Deployment pipeline");
$key->setCanExpire(false); // from CanUseSession, like setName() and extend()

$key->token(); // the plain value the client sends as its z_login_token, known after add() or byToken()

APIKey::byUser($user);  // the user's api keys
Session::byUser($user); // the user's logins

Every retriever is scoped to the class it is called on: Session::byId() does not find an api key and APIKey::byId() does not find a login, the same way Role and Group split the z_role table. The same holds for APIKey::byUuid() and APIKey::byUuids(), which are the safe way to address a key from outside the application - unlike the token, a UUID grants nothing to whoever reads it.

byToken() is the one exception. It resolves both kinds whichever class it is called on - returning an APIKey for a key and a plain Session for a login - so an authenticating request is judged by the right rules without the caller having to know which kind the token is.

  • Creates an api key for a user. The name is what keeps keys apart in a list, so it is worth passing.

    APIKey::add(User $user, ?string $name = null, ?string $reason = null): APIKey

Everything else a key needs it already has as a session: it is named through setName() and exempted from the login timeout through setCanExpire(false), which is what most keys want.

  • The lifetimes the profile page offers for a new key next to Never expires, in days mapped to their label.

    APIKey::LIFETIMES // [1 => "1 day", 3 => "3 days", ..., 365 => "1 year"]

docs.title: Bearer Authentication
docs.text:
A client that cannot keep a cookie, like a script or another service, sends its token in the Authorization header instead. Both a login and an api key authenticate this way.

Authorization: Bearer <token>

The bearer token wins over the z_login_token cookie. If it is invalid or expired the request is anonymous, it does not fall back to the cookie.

Only a header that carries exactly one token counts as a bearer token. A header of another scheme, like Basic, an empty Bearer, a value with more than one token like Bearer a b, and two Authorization headers (Apache merges them into one comma separated value) carry no token. The request then uses the cookie, if there is one. $req->bearerToken() returns the token of the header, or null.

A valid session does not log a deactivated user in. Whichever way the token arrived, a session or an api key, the request is anonymous ($user->isLoggedIn is false) as soon as the user's active is 0, for example after $user->remove(). The check runs on every request, so it takes effect immediately without ending the session.

docs.title: Lifetime Management
docs.text:
• Extends the session's lifetime by the given number of seconds on top of the base timeout and any existing extension. This only changes server-side validity and needs an active row, so an invalidated session cannot be revived.

    $session->extend(int $seconds): void

  • Sets the total extension time in seconds, replacing any previously set extension.

    $session->setExtensionTime(int $seconds): void

  • Fixes the point in time the session expires, or hands it back to the computed lifetime when null is passed. A fixed expiry replaces that lifetime entirely: neither loginTimeoutSeconds nor extended_seconds has a say while one is set, so extend() and setExtensionTime() write an extension that does not move the expiry. Takes a DateTime, like $user->verify() does; the getters stay strings. The column is a TIMESTAMP, so the expiry has to fall inside its range - from 1970 up to 2106-02-07 06:28:15 UTC on the supported MariaDB versions. A date outside it is rejected by the database rather than silently truncated.

    $session->setExpiresAt(?DateTime $expiresAt): void

    $session->setExpiresAt(new DateTime("+30 days"));
$session->setExpiresAt(null); // back to the computed lifetime

  • Subjects the session to expiring, or exempts it from it. A session passed false never expires and is therefore never invalidated on use, so exempting one revives a session that has expired but not yet been used. This is what turns an api key into a credential that keeps working, but it applies to any session. The exemption outranks a fixed expiry - it takes the session out of expiring altogether, rather than moving the point at which it does. It is stored inverted, in the is_permanent column.

    $session->setCanExpire(bool $canExpire): void

The login cookie has its own lifetime

is_permanent and expires_at are server-side. loginAs() sets the z_login_token cookie to expire after loginTimeoutSeconds (defaults to 7 days when unset) regardless, so a browser drops the cookie at that point even though the session itself lives on. The expiry is fixed when the cookie is set at login and is not re-issued when the session is extended, so extend() and setExtensionTime() keep the session alive on the server but not the cookie. Clients that send the token themselves are unaffected.

docs.title: Invalidation
docs.text:
• Immediately invalidates the session, preventing further use. The object is nulled, so any further call on it throws InvalidArgumentException("Instance no longer exists").

    $session->invalidate(): void

  • Ends every active login of a user in one statement, the session that issues it included. Api keys are credentials of their own and are left alone, so revoke those separately by calling invalidate() on each of APIKey::byUser(). This is the static counterpart to $user->clearSessions(), which is also what $user->updatePassword() runs - changing a password ends every login of the account, its keys keep working.

    Session::clearForUser(User $user): void

docs.title: Expiry Check
docs.text:
• Returns true if the session has expired. A session exempt from expiring never is; otherwise the expiry is the one fixed on the session, or, when it carries none, created plus the configured loginTimeoutSeconds (defaults to 7 days) plus any extended_seconds. The maths use PHP's strtotime() and time() on the database created value, so PHP and database timezones must agree.

    $session->isExpired(): bool

  • Returns the point in time the session becomes unusable, or null when the session is exempt from expiring. This is the effective expiry, whether it was fixed through setExpiresAt() or computed from the lifetime, which is absolute from creation and not sliding.

    $session->expiresAt(): ?string

docs.title: Two Factor Checks
docs.text:
A session remembers when it last passed a two factor check, in z_logintoken.last_two_factor, and how many wrong codes it may still send, in remaining_two_factor_tries.

  • Returns whether the session has to pass two factor again. false for an account without two factor, true while the session never passed a check or once the last one is older than $freshnessSeconds (defaults to two_factor_freshness_seconds, 900). A session whose user is gone always has to. This is what $req->requireFreshTwoFactor() asks.

    $session->requireRenew(?int $freshnessSeconds = null): bool

  • Returns when the session last passed a check, or null while it never did, and how many wrong codes it may still send (two_factor_tries to begin with, 5 by default).

    $session->lastTwoFactor(): ?string
$session->remainingTwoFactorTries(): int

  • Stamps a passed check on the session, and gives it its full budget of tries back.

    $session->recordTwoFactor(): void
$session->resetTwoFactorTries(): void

  • Spends one try on a wrong code and returns how many are left. At zero the caller is expected to sign the session out, the framework's own endpoints do.

    $session->spendTwoFactorTry(): int

  • A login that verified the code itself stamps the new session right away.

    $res->loginAs(int $userId, ?int $user_exec = null, ?string $name = null, ?string $reason = null, bool $recordTwoFactor = false)

docs.title: Session Data
docs.text:
• Returns the session's UUID. It is the only identifier of a session that is safe to hand out.

    $session->uuid(): string

  • Returns the plain session token, the value the client sends. Issued tokens are zub-sha256- plus 64 hex characters, 75 in total, and z_logintoken.token stores only zub-sha256- plus the SHA-256 of the plain value. The plain value of a hashed token exists only on an object created by add() or byToken(); on one loaded by any other retriever it is null. A token issued before hashing is stored as is and is still returned by every retriever, with a deprecation notice: compare against storedToken() instead. Tokens issued before this format stay in plain text and keep working, so do not validate one by its length. Sessions are never deleted, only set to active = 0 (logout, expiry, clearSessions()).

    $session->token(): ?string

  • Returns the value stored in z_logintoken.token: the hash for a session issued in the new format, the plain token for an older one. Use it, or LoginToken::hash($token), when comparing in your own SQL.

    $session->storedToken(): string

  • Returns the ID of the user who owns the session.

    $session->userId(): ?int

  • Returns the ID of the user being executed as (relevant for impersonation sessions).

    $session->userIdExec(): ?int

  • Returns the name of the session, or null if it has none.

    $session->name(): ?string

  • Returns the user agent the session was started from, or null if none was sent.

    $session->device(): ?string

  • Returns why the session was created, or null if no reason was given.

    $session->reason(): ?string

  • Returns the address the session was created from, or null if none could be determined.

    $session->ipCreation(): ?string

  • Returns the address the session was last used from, or null while it has not been used. It is rewritten on the first authenticated request that arrives from a different address, so a session that never moves is never written to.

    $session->ipLast(): ?string

  • Returns whether the session is subject to expiring at all. false means it is exempt, which is what setCanExpire(false) does.

    $session->canExpire(): bool

  • Returns the number of seconds the session has been extended by, or null if not extended.

    $session->extendedSeconds(): ?int

  • Returns the creation timestamp of the session.

    $session->created(): ?string

  • Returns when the session was last used, or null while it has not been used since it was created. Every authenticated request refreshes it, but at most once per session_last_used_throttle_seconds (defaults to 60), so the timestamp costs one write per throttle window rather than one per request - read it as "last seen around then", not to the second. Set the key to 0 to write on every request. A request from a new address is always written, because that is what updates ipLast().

    $session->lastUsed(): ?string

docs.title: Refreshing Session Data
docs.text:
• Reloads the session data from the database. The getters return the loaded data without reloading, so call it after a setter such as setName() or extend() to see the change.

    $session->refresh(): void

docs.title: Asset Proxy
docs.text: Since version 1.2.0, ZubZet serves CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and other static assets through an asset proxy instead of exposing them as files in your web root. A single internal route resolves each request against a list of registered source directories, which means framework- and package-bundled assets no longer have to be copied into every project.

docs.title: How assets are requested
docs.text:
The proxy listens on:

/_zubzet/asset-proxy/{path}

For example, /_zubzet/asset-proxy/css/bootstrap.min.css resolves Bootstrap's stylesheet from the first registered source that contains it.

docs.title: Referencing assets in views
docs.text:
Use the generateResourceLink helper available on every view's $opt array — it builds a correct, root-relative URL for you, versioned with ?v=<assetVersion>. The proxy lets a link carrying the configured assetVersion (not dev) be cached for a year as immutable, any other link only with revalidation through its ETag, answered with 304 while the file is unchanged; change assetVersion with every asset change, a framework or module update included:

@extends($layout)

@section("head")
    <link rel="stylesheet"
          href="<?php $opt["generateResourceLink"]("_zubzet/asset-proxy/css/bootstrap.min.css"); ?>">
@endsection

@section("content")
    <script src="<?php $opt["generateResourceLink"]("_zubzet/asset-proxy/js/jquery.min.js"); ?>"></script>
@endsection

The link ends in ?v=<assetVersion>, the only cache busting there is.

docs.title: Bundled assets
docs.text:
The framework registers these sources automatically at bootstrap, so they work out of the box:

Asset Proxy path jQuery _zubzet/asset-proxy/js/jquery.min.js Bootstrap (JS/CSS) _zubzet/asset-proxy/js/bootstrap.min.js, _zubzet/asset-proxy/css/bootstrap.min.css Font Awesome _zubzet/asset-proxy/css/font-awesome/all.min.css Z.js _zubzet/asset-proxy/Z.js

These come from the components/jquery, components/bootstrap, and components/font-awesome Composer packages — no files are copied into your project.

docs.title: Registering your own source
docs.text:
To expose an additional directory (for example, assets shipped by one of your own Composer packages), register it on the proxy with an absolute path and an optional URL prefix:

zubzet()->assetProxy->registerWebRootSource("/var/www/vendor/acme/ui-kit/dist", "ui-kit");

The file dist/app.css is then available at /_zubzet/asset-proxy/ui-kit/app.css. Registration is lazy — the directory is only touched when a matching request arrives. Sources are checked in registration order, and the first match wins. For an installed Composer package, (new BundledPackage("acme/ui-kit", "dist", "ui-kit"))->mount(zubzet()->assetProxy) resolves the path for you.

docs.title: Module assets and resolution order
docs.text:
Installed modules contribute their webroot/ directories as sources automatically. The full chain is checked in this order, first match wins:

  1. Module webroot/ sources, in module order
  2. Framework assets (IncludedComponents/assets/)
  3. The framework frontend directory (Z.js)
  4. Bundled Composer packages (jQuery, Bootstrap, Font Awesome)
  5. Sources you register via registerWebRootSource()

A module can therefore shadow a framework asset. Your application's own webroot/ is not part of this chain: the web server serves it directly, before PHP runs, so it always wins for real files.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The proxy is designed to serve only files that live inside a registered source:

  • Path traversal is blocked. Each request is resolved with realpath() and rejected unless the result stays within the registered source directory, so ../ sequences and symlink escapes cannot reach files outside the mount.
  • Only readable, existing files are served; anything else returns 404.
  • There is no allow-list and no access check. Everything else readable below a mounted source is served to anyone via GET, including dotfiles and the composer.json of mounted packages.
  • Source and config extensions are never served. Requests for .php, .phtml, or .ini files return 404 from every source, including ones you register yourself.
  • Content types are detected with league/mime-type-detection, falling back to application/octet-stream when the type is unknown.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: The booter settings are a way of getting your most basic settings. If you have something like the uploads folder or the database connection, that might be changed by a customer/admin after finishing this project, those values can be stored under your z_config folder as a key of z_settings.ini.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
If you want to use another key, simply create a new key in your z_settings.ini. To recall the value use $res->getBooterSettings("key"). If you don't pass a key, the whole array of values will be returned.

The signature is getBooterSettings($key = null, $useDefault = true, $default = null). The method is public on ZubZet, Request and Response and behaves exactly like the global config() helper, which proxies to it. An empty $key (null, "" or "0") returns the complete settings array, including the database and mail credentials. A missing key returns null by default. $useDefault is the second positional argument, so getBooterSettings("key", 5) does not set a default of 5: pass it by name (getBooterSettings("key", default: 5)). With $useDefault = false, a missing key throws an InvalidArgumentException with the message The setting '<key>' does not exist!.

docs.title: Settings file and order of precedence
docs.text:
The file is z_config/z_settings.ini, resolved relative to the working directory of the process and held in the built-in key config_file. It is read before anything else, so config_file itself cannot be changed through the constructor or the environment.

Later layers win: 1. Built-in defaults (paths, config_file, config_automated_file, framework roots) 2. z_settings.ini 3. The $params array passed to the ZubZet constructor (only for keys that already exist) 4. CONFIG_* environment variables (only with allow_env_config, see below) 5. The derived rootFolder and root, computed from rootDirectory and host 6. The automated settings file (z_config/z_automated_setting.ini, key config_automated_file), read with a plain parse_ini_string() without the ;/# protection of the main file

rootFolder is the link prefix $opt["root"] in views, the default prefix of rerouteUrl() (used by logout()) and the path of the maintenance bypass cookie.

host is required and has no default. It is the public base URL with scheme and optional port and without a trailing slash, e.g. http://localhost:4000, because root is built as host followed by rootFolder, which starts with a slash. Request::getCurrentURL() returns host plus REQUEST_URI (the incoming Host header is ignored) and getDomain() returns host without scheme, slashes and port. host also feeds the host and absRoot view options, the mail application_root and the password-reset link.

Settings can be read and written at runtime as zubzet()->key (zubzet()->settings is the whole store); a missing key throws, and a write affects only the current request and does not recompute root or rootFolder. Most settings are read when they are used, but the database connection copies its settings once at boot and a logger reads its settings when its channel is first created, so later writes do not reach them.

docs.title: INI syntax
docs.text:
z_settings.ini is parsed with parse_ini_string() without sections ([section] headers are ignored, all keys are flat), but every ; and # is protected before parsing and restored afterwards. A ; or # inside a value is therefore kept literally, so there are no inline comments: a trailing comment becomes part of the value.

host = https://example.com ; production

Here host is https://example.com ; production.

Values are normalised by parse_ini_string(): unquoted true, on and yes become 1; false, off, no, none, null and an empty value become an empty string; numbers stay strings. A double-quoted value is not normalised, so "true" stays the literal text true, which matters for settings compared with the string true.

A line that starts with ; or # is not a real comment either. It only survives as long as it parses as an ini line: with an = in it (; debug = on) it silently creates a bogus key (-----semicolon----- debug), and with characters such as (, ?, !, & or | the parse fails. Keep notes out of the file or use plain words without these characters.

A syntax error is not reported nicely. parse_ini_string() returns false, and booting dies with a PHP TypeError from overwriteAttributes() (it expects an array). This happens while the configuration is loaded, before the exception handling is installed, so the framework's error page and logging do not apply: you get PHP's raw fatal error (or a blank page, depending on display_errors). Check the web server or PHP error log if the app suddenly fails to boot after editing the INI.

docs.title: Environment variable overrides
docs.text:
With allow_env_config = true in the INI, a setting key is overridden by the environment variable CONFIG_KEY (CONFIG_ plus the upper-cased key, so dbpassword becomes CONFIG_DBPASSWORD; further examples are CONFIG_DBHOST, CONFIG_MAIL_SMTP, CONFIG_ASSETVERSION and CONFIG_FORGOTPASSWORDTIMESPAN).

If allow_env_config is absent, the variables are not read at all. The check is plain truthiness: any non-empty string other than 0 enables it, including the text false from a quoted INI value (allow_env_config = "false"), while an unquoted false is parsed to an empty string and disables it.

Only keys that already exist are overridden. The framework walks over the keys known from its built-in defaults and the INI, so a variable for any other key is silently ignored. This includes allow_env_config itself, which has to be set in the INI. Declare a placeholder in z_settings.ini for every setting you want to supply through the environment:

dbpassword = env

The value of the placeholder is arbitrary and replaced as soon as CONFIG_DBPASSWORD is set, the project stub uses ENV. Missing the placeholder is the usual reason why an environment variable seems to have no effect.

The value is taken as a raw string and skips the INI normalisation: in the INI file false, off and no are parsed to an empty string and true and on to 1, but an environment variable keeps its text as is. CONFIG_LOGGER_ENABLED=false is therefore the string false, which PHP treats as truthy, and the logger stays enabled. To switch a flag off, set the variable to 0 or to an empty value (CONFIG_LOGGER_ENABLED=0), to switch it on use 1.

docs.title: What do you actually put in here?
docs.text:
• Database connection details
  • Connections to other external tools like a Mailer, Storage or Api keys.
  • Basic Framework settings

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public function action_chatgpt(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $chatgptApiKey = $res->getBooterSettings("chatgpt_api_key");

    /* remaining code */

    return $res->render("admin/chatgpt");
}

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This helps manage credentials and settings more easily, while keeping sensitive data separate from everything else.

docs.title: Console Commands
docs.text: ZubZet provides a built-in console interface that allows you to manage and interact with the framework directly from the command line. Console commands enable automation, debugging, and execution of application logic outside the HTTP context.

docs.title: How to Run a Command
docs.text:
To execute a console command inside the Docker container, first access the container shell:

npm run shell

Then navigate to the root directory of your project (where the index.php file is located) and run:

php index.php {command}

The package registers no Composer scripts and no bin executable (its only require-dev entry is a test-coverage library), so the CLI is reached through the project: php index.php <command>, or php zubzet <command> and ./project <command> in a generated project. A command's return value becomes the process exit status (0 on success, 1 on failure).

docs.title: completion
docs.text: Dumps the shell completion script for the ZubZet console. This improves command-line usability by enabling tab completion.

docs.title: help
docs.text: Displays help information for a specific command or for the console in general. Symfony's global options (-h, -q, -v|-vv|-vvv, -V, --ansi, --no-ansi, -n) apply to every command.

docs.title: list
docs.text: Lists all available console commands; php index.php without a command prints the same list.

docs.title: run
docs.text: Executes a controller action directly from the console environment. This is useful for running application logic, maintenance tasks, or background operations without an HTTP request.

docs.title: info:startup
docs.text:
Prints a startup banner with the ZubZet version (as Composer reports it, e.g. v1.2.0, or unknown), application name, environment, PHP version, and asset version — a quick health check after deployment. A missing pageName, execution_type, assetVersion or host prints Unknown. Set <key> in settings! (host prints Unknown / Check docker-compose-base.yml) instead.

php index.php info:startup

Pass --pwd "$(pwd)" so clickable file links in the error page resolve to your host paths (the dev stack's npm run info does this for you). The value is stored in z_config/z_automated_setting.ini as automated_host_working_directory.

docs.title: project
docs.text:
Every generated project ships a project script in its root for the everyday tasks:

Command Description ./project start Build and start the Docker stack, then run composer install, db:seed and info:startup. ./project stop Stop the stack and remove it, including its volumes. ./project shell Open a shell inside the application container. ./project tests Run the Cypress suite headless; extra arguments (e.g. --spec) are passed through. ./project cypress Open the interactive Cypress UI.

Any other arguments are forwarded to php zubzet: inside the application container when it is running, otherwise directly with the host's PHP.

./project db:status

tests and cypress need Node.js and Cypress on the host. They are never installed automatically; if they are missing, the script prints the npm install command to run.

docs.title: Database commands
docs.text:
Command Description db:migrate Run all pending migrations (framework-bundled and your own under app/Database/migrations). db:seed Drop and recreate the database, run all migrations, then load seed data from app/Database/seed. All existing data is lost unless --skip-migrations is passed. db:status Show whether the migration lock is set; exit code 0 when unlocked, 1 when locked. db:sync Mark migrations as applied up to a version/date without running their SQL. db:unlock-migration Release a stuck migration lock.

db:seed accepts path filters (relative to app/Database/seed) to control which seed folders run. Every file starts selected, so --environments-included alone changes nothing; it only brings back paths removed by --environments-excluded:

# Only seed "Environments/Dev": exclude the folder, then re-include the subset
php index.php db:seed --environments-excluded=Environments --environments-included=Environments/Dev

# Seed everything except "Prod" (repeatable)
php index.php db:seed --environments-excluded=Prod

# Keep the database and only run the seed files (no drop, no migrations)
php index.php db:seed --skip-migrations

See Migrations for the full migration workflow.

docs.title: Repair commands
docs.text: Repair commands fix an installation that drifted into a broken state. They are never run automatically; run one when you hit the problem it names.

docs.title: repair:database-collation
docs.text:
Tables with different collations make queries across them fail, for example with Illegal mix of collations for operation 'UNION' on every authenticated request. This happens when tables were created under different server or database defaults, e.g. older tables from before a server upgrade next to newer ones.

The framework creates its tables as utf8mb4 with the collation utf8mb4_uca1400_ai_ci (ZubZet\Framework\Database\Connection::COLLATION). The command converts the framework tables (z_ prefix) to it with ALTER TABLE ... CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_uca1400_ai_ci:

php index.php repair:database-collation

Application tables and the database default are left alone. Add --include-app-tables to convert every table of the database and to set the database default to the same collation, so tables created later without an explicit collation match:

php index.php repair:database-collation --include-app-tables

Only tables whose own collation or any text column's collation differs are converted; a rerun with nothing left to convert changes nothing. Columns that deliberately use another collation (e.g. a case-sensitive utf8mb4_bin column) are converted as well.

Warning

Converting rewrites the whole table and blocks writes to it meanwhile, which can take a long time on large tables. Take a backup and run it in a maintenance window.

docs.title: auth:migrate-hashing
docs.text:
Wraps every legacy password hash in an Argon2id layer and marks the row onion; rows without a password are skipped. Idempotent, so it is safe to run more than once, but the update does not re-check the scheme, so a password changed during the run can be overwritten. See Password Handling.

php index.php auth:migrate-hashing

With --dry (-d) it only prints how many legacy passwords it found.

docs.title: module:setup
docs.text:
Merges missing default settings from installed modules into z_config/z_settings.ini. Append-only and idempotent: existing keys are never touched, and a rerun with nothing to merge changes nothing.

php index.php module:setup

docs.title: Your own commands
docs.text: Beyond run, the application (and every module) can ship dedicated Symfony commands in app/Commands/; they register automatically and appear in list. See Commands for the file convention and precedence rules.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage is a development feature: the underlying phpunit/php-code-coverage library is a development dependency of ZubZet and is not installed with your application by default. Install it before using the coverage commands:

composer require --dev "phpunit/php-code-coverage:9.*"

Without it, the coverage commands fail with an error explaining this requirement.

Collect a runtime code-coverage report:

php index.php testing:coverage:start
# ... exercise the app via tests or manual requests ...
php index.php testing:coverage:stop

start writes a session id to .coverage.session in the working directory; while that file exists, every web request and CLI call collects coverage (an Xdebug or PCOV driver is required). testing:coverage:stop writes the HTML report to .coverage/report/; add --cli (-c) to print a text report (PHPUnit summary plus a per-file tree, green from 90 %, yellow from 50 %, red below) to stdout instead. Merging many collected files is memory-hungry; CI runs it as php -d memory_limit=4G index.php testing:coverage:stop.

docs.title: What does a controller do?
docs.text: A controller is one part of the MVC pattern. It handles all the logic, but what does that mean? Usually the controller takes in data from one or multiple models as well as user input and does something with it. This could include sorting, searching, calculating and generally making the data ready to display or ready to put into the database in case of a form input for example.

docs.title: How to get a controller executed?
docs.text: Since there are no actual paths, controllers are tightly bound to the requested url. The first part of the URL, that is not part of getting to your project's root directory, determines which Controller will be used. If the request has no path segments, the controller named by the defaultIndex setting in z_config/z_settings.ini is executed with action_index. The value is the full controller class name, used as written, and when the key is unset it falls back to DashboardController, which the framework does not ship (without an application one / ends in a 404). New projects ship with defaultIndex = DashboardController. To serve localhost/ from the bundled IndexController (renders index.php in layout/default_layout.php), set defaultIndex = IndexController; without that it is only reachable at /index.

docs.title: File Routing
docs.text:
The url is separated into 4 relevant parts

  • Host/root for example localhost/ or www.example.com/
  • Controller name
  • Action name
  • Parameters

localhost/example/test/123/321

This would call the action_test in the ExampleController.php with the parameters 123 and 321.

docs.title: Controller Names and Case
docs.text:
The controller name is built from the first URL segment: only its first letter is upper-cased, the rest is kept exactly as sent, and Controller is appended.

URL Looks for /example/test ExampleController /Example/test ExampleController /EXAMPLE/test EXAMPLEController /frameworkApi FrameworkApiController

The file is found by this exact spelling, so on case-sensitive file systems (Linux) the file name must match it: ExampleController.php answers /example and /Example, but not /EXAMPLE, which ends in a 404. A controller with capitals inside its name (FrameworkApiController) is only reachable with the same capitals in the URL (/frameworkApi). The class name has to equal the file name without .php and lives in the global namespace (no namespace line). A controller usually extends z_controller, the alias of ZubZet\Framework\Core\Controller (which only adds makeFood() and makeCEDFood(); the bundled ErrorController does not extend it). An optional __construct(Request $req, Response $res) runs on a fresh instance before every action and every middleware or afterMiddleware method. Request, Response (Message\*), Rest (Support\Rest), User (the request user) and z_db (Database\Connection) are global class aliases that work like the fully qualified names in action signatures and route-closure type hints, so app code cannot declare global classes with these names.

Before the lookup, - in the segment becomes _, . becomes §2E and ä, ö, ü become ae, oe, ue (/my-page looks for My_pageController, /data/file.json runs action_file§2Ejson). The action name is the second segment, lower-cased, behind action_ (a public method; action_index when there is no second segment); PHP method names are case-insensitive, so action_byId also answers /group/byid. The HTTP method is not checked, any verb reaches any action_* method.

The segment is URL-decoded once and then looked up as a file name in the controller folders (userspace, modules, framework), with .php appended; it is not checked against a list of allowed names. Because . is replaced as described above, .. can never climb out of those folders. An encoded slash (%2F) is kept, though, and addresses a subfolder of a controller folder (/Admin%2FUsers looks for Admin/UsersController.php), but the default Apache setup (AllowEncodedSlashes Off) already answers such requests with a 404 before the framework runs. A name without a slash that is not found directly is searched for by file name in the subfolders of each controller folder, so a controller in a subfolder is reached by its plain name.

docs.title: Default Actions
docs.text:
To handle default behavior there are predefined actions.

Name Description action_index Will be executed if no action is specified in the request. localhost/example/ action_fallback Will be executed when the requested action is not found (also for an explicit route or middleware method that does not exist), without it the 404 page is shown. Can be used to have infinite actions. localhost/example/ghdafiehihwe

docs.title: Basic Controller
docs.text:
The following function action_test will be executed when requesting the path {root}/example/test/{parameters}.

<?php
    class ExampleController extends z_controller {

        public function action_test(Request $req, Response $res) {

        }

    }
?>

docs.title: Advanced Controller Example
docs.text:
<?php
    class EmployeeController extends z_controller {


        // This action will be executed when requesting the path `{root}/Employee`
        public function action_index(Request $req, Response $res) {
            return $res->render("employee/index");
        }

        // This action will be executed when requesting the path `{root}/Employee/list`
        public function action_list(Request $req, Response $res) {
            // Check the permissions of the currently logged-in user.
            $req->checkPermission("employee.list");

            // Handle an asynchronous POST-request with the parameter: action=delete-employee
            if ($req->isAction("delete-employee")) {
                $req->checkPermission("employee.delete");

                $employeeId = $req->getPost("employeeId");

                // Interacting with Models
                $req->getModel("Employee")->deleteById($employeeId);

                return $res->success();
            }

            // Rendering the View with all Employees as Array
            return $res->render("employee/employee_list", [
                "employees" => $req->getModel("Employee")->getAll()
            ]);
        }

        // This action will be executed when requesting the path `{root}/Employee/view`
        public function action_view(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("employee.view");

            // Retrives URL parameters (Offset, Length)
            $employeeId = $req->getParameters(0, 1);

            $employee = $req->getModel("Employee")->getById($employeeId);

            return $res->render("employee/employee_view", [
                "employee" => $employee
            ]);
        }
    }
?>

docs.title: Redirecting
docs.text: $res->rerouteUrl($url = "", $root = null) sends a location: header (implicit 302) and ends the script, as do $res->logout() and the REST helpers. $root defaults to the rootFolder setting, which is / when rootDirectory is empty and /{rootDirectory}/ otherwise. The header is built as $root . $url without any slash normalisation, so $url has to be written relative to the root folder, without a leading slash: rerouteUrl("employee/list"). A leading slash is not removed, so rerouteUrl("/employee") yields //employee with an empty root directory, which browsers read as a protocol-relative URL pointing at the host employee. Calling it without arguments redirects to the root folder; pass $root = "" to redirect to an absolute or external URL. $res->reroute($path, $alias = false, $final = false) instead dispatches internally to another controller and action without an HTTP redirect, so the browser URL stays (the query string is kept); explicit routes and group middleware apply to the new path, and $final = true ends the script afterwards, otherwise the calling action continues when reroute() returns (as after render() or json()). The new Request keeps GET, POST, cookies and body but has an empty store and urlParameters. For $alias see aliases. Response has no helpers for HTTP status codes, custom headers or downloads: use PHP's http_response_code() and header().

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Routing: registering explicit route definitions instead of name-based routing
  • Views: the templates rendered by $res->render
  • Permission System: the permissions behind $req->checkPermission
  • Parameter Abstraction: reading URL parameters and POST data
  • API reference: Request and Response

docs.title: CSRF Protection
docs.text:
Since version 1.3.0, the framework defends every request that can change state against Cross-Site Request Forgery.

A forged request is one the browser of a logged-in user sends because a page of another site told it to: the browser attaches the session cookie by itself. The defense reads only the headers the browser sets. There is no token, no cookie and no hidden form field, so forms, Z.Request, Z.Forms and hand-written fetch() calls need nothing extra.

GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are not checked

Links, redirects and embeds from other sites keep working, so do OAuth and payment callbacks and the links of your own mails opened in a webmail. In return, an action that changes state on a GET is unprotected until it opts back in, see Protecting a normally safe method.

docs.title: The headers
docs.text:
Header Set by Says Sec-Fetch-Site Current browsers, to https:// and localhost only How the page that started the request relates to its target: same-origin, same-site, cross-site, or none when no page started it (a typed URL, a bookmark, a link from a desktop application) Origin Browsers, on fetch(), its CORS preflight and every method but GET and HEAD; never on a link or another page navigation by GET The origin of that page, or null when the browser hides it

A page can make its Origin null, but it cannot forge any of these headers.

docs.title: When the check runs
docs.text: The router checks every request before the route files load, so no route, middleware or controller runs for a rejected one. This covers explicit routes, convention paths, the framework's routes under /_zubzet, the 404 page and the login that checkPermission() shows. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS pass the router unchecked; there is no other exception per method or route.

docs.title: Protecting a normally safe method
docs.text:
GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are skipped by CSRF::verify() on the assumption that they never change state. An action that breaks that assumption, like a GET logout, has to opt back in: call $req->csrfBlockAdditionalMethod() (or CSRF::verify("GET") directly) before doing anything state-changing. Without arguments it covers GET; pass the methods explicitly to cover others, like csrfBlockAdditionalMethod("GET", "HEAD"), since a HEAD request runs the same action and a page can send one with the session cookie. Method names are case insensitive. Passing a method name there removes it from the safe-method exemption for that call only, so the usual checks (Sec-Fetch-Site, Origin, csrf_allow and the trusted/blocked origin lists) run against it too. Like checkPermission(), csrfBlockAdditionalMethod() returns nothing: a rejected request gets the 403 page and the script ends, while CSRF::verify() only returns the result.

public function action_logout($req, Response $res) {
    // Logout is a GET action, but still state-changing, so it needs
    // CSRF protection too despite GET normally being exempt as safe.
    // HEAD runs the same action and a page can send it with cookies
    $req->csrfBlockAdditionalMethod("GET", "HEAD");

    return $res->logout();
}

A browser sends no Origin on a link, so a GET that opts back in only passes from the application's own origin or from no page at all (a typed URL, a bookmark), whatever csrf_allow and csrf_trusted_origins say. That suits a logout; an action that other sites have to link to cannot be protected this way and should take a POST instead.

A rejected request is answered by the 403 page of the error controller (error/403), the same one checkPermission() shows.

docs.title: How a request is judged
docs.text:
The source is the Origin header, lowercase. Without it, or with Origin: null, the source is unknown. The Referer is not looked at.

csrf_allow sets which Sec-Fetch-Site values pass on their own: same-origin lets same-origin and none through, same-site lets same-site through as well, any lets every value through (a public API for browsers on other sites; only csrf_blocked_origins still rejects). Without a cookie session nothing is there to forge, but with one, any switches the protection off.

  1. GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, not opted back in (see Protecting a normally safe method): passes.
  2. Neither Sec-Fetch-Site nor Origin is sent: passes. This is curl, a server or a webhook, and nothing else is checked.
  3. The source is unknown and csrf_allow is not any: passes only with Sec-Fetch-Site same-origin or none. Neither list can match an unknown source, so a page that hides its Origin (no-referrer, a sandboxed iframe) cannot slip past csrf_blocked_origins this way.
  4. Sec-Fetch-Site is present and not let through by csrf_allow: passes only when the source is listed in csrf_trusted_origins.
  5. Anything else: passes unless the source is listed in csrf_blocked_origins.

Both headers are compared lowercase and trimmed. A request with an Origin but no Sec-Fetch-Site (an old browser, plain http://) therefore only meets the blocklist. A source listed in both lists passes in step 4 and is rejected in step 5, depending on whether csrf_allow lets its Sec-Fetch-Site through.

A POST (or any other checked request) to https://app.example.com from:

Source Sec-Fetch-Site Default csrf_allow = same-site a page of https://app.example.com same-origin passes passes a typed URL, a bookmark none passes passes a page on https://www.example.com same-site rejected passes a page on https://www.example.com that hides its Origin (no-referrer) same-site rejected rejected a page on https://partner.com, listed in csrf_trusted_origins cross-site passes passes a page on https://partner.com that hides its Origin cross-site rejected rejected a page on https://evil.com cross-site rejected rejected curl, a server, an old browser sending an Origin absent passes passes

A GET, HEAD or OPTIONS passes in every row, unless the action opts back in.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning csrf_allow same-origin same-origin, same-site or any, case insensitive; any other value throws an error csrf_trusted_origins empty Comma separated origins that pass although csrf_allow does not let their Sec-Fetch-Site through csrf_blocked_origins empty Comma separated origins that are rejected although csrf_allow lets their Sec-Fetch-Site through, or it is absent 
csrf_allow = same-origin
csrf_trusted_origins = https://partner.com, https://docs.example.com
csrf_blocked_origins =

An entry is compared as written, only lowercased and trimmed, like the Origin header. Write it exactly as the browser sends the Origin: no path, no trailing slash, and no port unless it is not the default one (80 for http, 443 for https). https://partner.com:443 therefore never matches, while http://partner.com, https://partner.com:8443 and https://www.partner.com are other origins than https://partner.com. Write internationalized hosts in their xn-- form, as the browser sends them.

csrf_trusted_origins only lets the request through. Reading the answer, or sending JSON or custom headers, needs CORS on top. The CORS preflight is an OPTIONS and passes unchecked, the request that follows it is checked, so an origin that calls the application with fetch() has to be listed.

Only use csrf_allow = same-site when every subdomain of the site is yours, future and forgotten ones included: a subdomain hosting content of others (uploads, a bucket, one per customer), one with an XSS hole, or one whose DNS points to a cancelled service can then act with the sessions of your users. Block the risky ones with csrf_blocked_origins, or stay on same-origin and list the trusted ones.

docs.title: Configuration by scenario
docs.text:
The application runs on https://app.example.com.

# Scenario Configuration Notes 1 The same application runs on several subdomains Nothing Each subdomain passes its own requests (same-origin); a request from one to another is same-site and rejected unless listed 2 A bucket on bucket.example.com hosts foreign content, every other subdomain may csrf_allow = same-sitecsrf_blocked_origins = https://bucket.example.com 3 Subdomain x may, subdomain y may not csrf_trusted_origins = https://x.example.com Or csrf_allow = same-site with csrf_blocked_origins = https://y.example.com, which lets every other subdomain in as well and stops y in browsers without Sec-Fetch-Site too 4 Only site x.com may csrf_trusted_origins = https://x.com www.x.com is another origin and has to be listed on its own 5 Only site x.com and subdomain y may csrf_trusted_origins = https://x.com, https://y.example.com 6 Every subdomain may, plus site x.com csrf_allow = same-sitecsrf_trusted_origins = https://x.com 7 Every subdomain may, except x csrf_allow = same-sitecsrf_blocked_origins = https://x.example.com A page on x that hides its Origin is rejected too, as is every subdomain doing so 8 The application runs on a subdomain, the parent host may csrf_trusted_origins = https://example.com www.example.com is another origin 9 The application runs on a subdomain, another subdomain may csrf_trusted_origins = https://b.example.com 10 The nested subdomain x.y may, all others not csrf_trusted_origins = https://x.y.example.com Neither y.example.com nor a.x.y.example.com is covered 11 The same host may on port 3000, not on port 4000 csrf_trusted_origins = https://app.example.com:3000 Under csrf_allow = same-site, use csrf_blocked_origins = https://app.example.com:4000 instead

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No Sec-Fetch-Site. Old browsers (Safari before 16.4) and every browser over plain http:// to a host other than localhost send none, so only csrf_blocked_origins applies to them when they send an Origin. A checked request of theirs with a hidden Origin (null, for example from a page with no-referrer) is rejected, even from the application's own pages. Such browsers are otherwise protected only by the SameSite=Lax session cookie, which does not cover a link: an action that opts a GET back in, like the logout and z/login_as, is reachable from another site in them. Serve the application over https://.
  • Ports are not part of a site. A browser sends same-site from https://app.example.com:4000 to https://app.example.com, so under csrf_allow = same-site every port of every subdomain passes unless blocked.
  • csrf_allow = any switches the protection off for every site; only csrf_blocked_origins still applies. Use it for an API that has no cookie session.
  • No whole sites or wildcards. An entry is one exact origin. https://*.example.com or a bare site cannot be listed; list each origin, or use csrf_allow = same-site for the own site.
  • GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are not checked. An action that changes state on one of them is open to every site until it calls csrfBlockAdditionalMethod(). Prefer a POST for anything that changes state.
  • A hidden Origin is never trusted. A checked request without a known source passes only as same-origin or none, whatever csrf_allow and the lists say (except under csrf_allow = any). A partner that posts from a page with no-referrer has to stop hiding its Origin.
  • Files served by Apache directly (everything in the webroot that does not go through index.php, such as images, scripts and uploads) are not checked.

docs.title: When a legitimate request is rejected
docs.text:
Z.Request and Z.Forms give a 403 no special treatment, so look at the network tab.

Case Cause Another site The request comes from another site, or from another subdomain or port under csrf_allow = same-origin. List its origin in csrf_trusted_origins, or use csrf_allow = same-site when every subdomain is yours. A request without Origin (a page with no-referrer, a link to an action that opts back in) passes only from the application's own origin Invalid csrf_allow A checked request (step 1 does not apply) with a browser header throws an error (500) until the setting is same-origin, same-site or any Blocked origin The source is listed in csrf_blocked_origins

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: Every model query runs through one Connection object, reachable as db(). It is opened lazily on the first query, kept alive across the request, and re-opened by itself when the server drops it. This page covers the settings that shape it. All of them live in z_config/z_settings.ini (see Booter Settings) and all of them are optional apart from the endpoint and credentials below. For raw access, db()->getDatabaseConnection() returns the mysqli handle (e.g. for affected_rows), and executeMultiQuery() runs several statements without binding, bypassing the debug bar and slow-query log. It throws on failure; with $throwOnFailure = false it returns false instead.

docs.title: Endpoint and credentials
docs.text:
dbhost = database.example.com
dbport = 3306
dbname = app
dbusername = app
dbpassword = secret

dbhost, dbusername, dbpassword and dbname are required. If any of them is missing or empty, the first query throws a RuntimeException (Database connection requires valid configuration. Missing or empty config key(s): ...) naming the offending keys. None of them has a default, and dbpassword in particular must be non-empty: an account without a password is rejected, not connected to.

dbport is optional and has no framework default: when it is unset the driver's own default (3306) applies. It is honoured by the runtime connection and by migrations alike.

dbhost may also carry the port (host:3306), except with db_ssl turned on: the server certificate is matched against dbhost as a whole, and no certificate names a port, so with TLS the port belongs in dbport and a combined value is rejected with an error saying exactly that.

Migrations connect separately (through Doctrine DBAL) but read the same settings, so there is nothing to configure twice.

Migrations, and the seed, status, sync, unlock, repair-collation and hashing-migration commands, log in with dbusername_elevated and dbpassword_elevated when both are set. If either is empty, they use dbusername and dbpassword. The console builds every command, so the elevated login applies to each CLI invocation, run included. The switch happens at CLI startup for every command (including run) and lasts for the whole process, so models use the elevated user too.

docs.title: Timeouts and retries
docs.text:
db_connection_timeout = 900
db_max_retries = 3
db_wait_attempts = 10
db_wait_delay = 3

db_connection_timeout is the number of seconds after which an idle connection is checked before being reused (0 checks before every query; a non-numeric value throws an InvalidArgumentException at boot). Manual heartbeat() calls (also on models) are deprecated since 1.2.0 and can be removed.

db_max_retries is how many extra attempts a statement gets when it fails for a reason that is worth retrying: a deadlock, a lock-wait timeout, a Galera certification conflict, or a dropped connection (which is recovered by reconnecting through the endpoint and re-running the statement; each connect attempt times out after 5 seconds). Set it to 0 to disable retries entirely. executeMultiQuery() is never retried.

One statement may be applied twice

If a write reached the server but the acknowledgment was lost with the connection, the retry applies it again. Every exec() auto-commits, so the exposure is a single statement.

db_wait_attempts and db_wait_delay (seconds) bound how long the database commands wait for a database that is still starting; --no-wait fails at once.

docs.title: Encrypted transport (TLS)
docs.text:
Clusters that reject unencrypted clients (MariaDB's require_secure_transport, or anything reachable over a public network) need this turned on:

db_ssl = true

That is the whole configuration: the server certificate is verified against the trust store your system already uses, which knows every publicly issued certificate (for example Let's Encrypt). A private or self-signed authority is added to that same store (on Debian: drop it into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ and run update-ca-certificates), or handed to PHP via openssl.cafile.

The certificate is always verified. That is worth a sentence, because mysqli itself is lax here: given no authority it encrypts without verifying, and it never consults the system trust store on its own. The framework resolves that store for you so that db_ssl = true means verified, and raises an error rather than connecting unverified when no trust store can be found.

docs.title: Persistent connections
docs.text:
db_persistent = true

A persistent connection is kept open by the PHP worker after the request ends and handed to the next request, which skips the TCP, TLS and authentication handshake (measured against the e2e cluster: about 2.2 ms per encrypted connect versus 0.2 ms per reuse). It is safe to reuse: mysqli resets the session before handing it over and replaces a connection that no longer answers, so a node that died does not poison the pool.

It is off by default because of placement: a worker stays on whichever node it first reached, so a load-balanced cluster only rebalances as workers recycle. Turn it on where the handshake actually costs you, an encrypted or remote database being the typical case.

Restart your PHP workers after changing db_ssl

mysqli pools connections by host, port, user, password and database, not by transport, so a worker still holding a plaintext connection keeps using it after you turn db_ssl on. Reload PHP-FPM (or your web server) when you change the transport.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text:
ZubZet ships with the PHP Debug Bar preconfigured for the development environment. It overlays a small bar at the bottom of every rendered page and surfaces what happened during the request: SQL queries, rendered templates and parameters, log records with their full context, request data, timings, and memory usage.

The bar is always available in the test environment and never rendered anywhere else. SQL, parameter values, and log context can contain sensitive data, so the gate is strict by design.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
The debug bar is gated on execution_type in z_config/z_settings.ini:

execution_type = test

If execution_type is anything other than test (including unset), the bar is not bootstrapped, no assets are emitted, and no collectors run. There is no way to enable it for production.

The bar relies on the layout calling the head and body essentials. The default layout already does this. If you ship a custom layout and want the bar visible there too, include <x-zubzet::head :opt="$opt"/> inside your <head> and the body essentials inside your <body>:

<x-zubzet::body :opt="$opt"/>

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
Every SQL statement that runs through Connection::exec() (or Model::exec()) is captured with its placeholders interpolated, the bound values, the duration, and the row count; failed queries are not listed. Click a query to open a parameter table and copy the statement to the clipboard.

Bound values are shown as single quoted, addslashes()d literals (NULL for null) for display only; the statement itself ran with bound parameters.

INSERT INTO `model_test_insert` (`value`)
VALUES ('TestData')

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Every view passed to $res->render(...) is captured as a row in the templates tab, together with the layout name and the original options array.

core/render (layout: layout/default_layout.php)

Click the row to expand the params table. Values are formatted by the framework's data formatter, so arrays and objects are shown in a readable shape.

docs.title: Monolog
docs.text:
Every log record produced through logger() shows up as a row on the monolog tab (also records below logger_level, but none when logger_enabled is false), including the channel, level, message, full context, and processor extras (traceId, file, line, class, function).

The summary line is the trace id, channel, level, and message. Click the row to expand a key and value table with context.* and extra.* entries.

The tab uses the standard messages widget and includes a search input. Searching matches against the trace id, channel, level, message, and every context.* and extra.* entry as key=value, so you can quickly filter to a specific trace id, view path, or user id.

docs.title: Resolutions
docs.text:
Every convention lookup the Registry performed for the page is listed with its origin: the controller and every model, plus each loaded route file, labeled userspace, module:<package>, or framework, together with the winning file path. Lookups that resolved through the recursive subdirectory index carry a (recursive) suffix.

controllers: GuestbookController    module:zubzet/example-guestbook (/var/www/vendor/.../GuestbookController.php)
models: GuestbookStatsModel         module:zubzet/example-guestbook (recursive) (...)
routes: DefaultRoutes.php           framework (...)

With modules installed this answers "which root won this name" at a glance, so shadowing is never invisible: if a module view or controller unexpectedly takes over, the tab shows exactly where the file came from.

docs.title: Hiding framework queries
docs.text:
The framework runs many queries on its own behalf for authentication, sessions, permissions, migrations, and similar concerns. By default these are hidden so the queries tab only shows queries from your own application.

debugbar_hide_internal_queries = true

Set it to false to see every query, including the ones the framework runs internally.

Key Type Default Description execution_type string prod Must be test for the debug bar to render debugbar_hide_internal_queries boolean true Hide queries issued by models flagged with IsInternalModel (bundled z_* models except z_organizationModel) from the bar

docs.title: Marking your own models as internal
docs.text:
If you have models that you consider infrastructure rather than application logic, you can opt them into the same filter. Use the IsInternalModel trait on the model class:

use ZubZet\Framework\Database\IsInternalModel;

class CacheModel extends z_model {
    use IsInternalModel;

    public function purge() {
        $this->exec("DELETE FROM `cache_entries`");
    }
}

Queries issued through this model are filtered out of the queries tab whenever debugbar_hide_internal_queries = true. Direct db()->exec(...) calls that bypass the model layer keep the tag of the last model query (also z_logger after a log write), so they are hidden whenever that model was internal.
