docs.title: Adding your own log context
docs.text:
The monolog tab automatically renders the context array you pass to logger() and any extras added by processors. Anything you add is searchable.

logger("orders")->info("Order placed", [
    "orderId" => $order->id,
    "userId"  => $user->id,
    "total"   => $order->total,
]);

In the bar this expands into rows for context.orderId, context.userId, context.total, alongside the framework's own extra.traceId, extra.file, and friends.

See the Logging documentation for details on channels, processors, and custom loggers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# z_config/z_settings.ini
execution_type = test
debugbar_hide_internal_queries = true

public function action_show(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $order = model("order")->find($req->getParameters(0));

    logger("orders")->info("Order opened", ["orderId" => $order["id"]]);

    return $res->render("orders/show", ["order" => $order]);
}

When you visit the page the debug bar will show:

  • one query in the queries tab with the interpolated WHERE id = '...' clause
  • one render in the templates tab named orders/show (layout: layout/default_layout.php) with the order array as a parameter
  • one monolog row on the orders channel containing the context.orderId and the framework's extra.traceId

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: ZubZet controls how errors and uncaught exceptions are surfaced through two settings in z_config/z_settings.ini: showErrors (how much is promoted to an exception) and execution_type (which environment you are in). Together they decide whether a visitor sees a rich developer error page or nothing at all.

docs.title: showErrors levels
docs.text:
Value Constant Behavior 0 NONE display_errors and display_startup_errors are set to 0 and error_reporting to 0; nothing is promoted and PHP errors are neither shown nor logged; an exception thrown by an action is caught and the router runs the error/500 route. 1 EXCEPTIONS display_errors and display_startup_errors are set to 1 and error_reporting to E_ALL; PHP errors are logged and left to PHP's own handler, uncaught exceptions are handled and displayed; an exception thrown by an action is rethrown. 2 ALL Every reportable error and warning is logged and promoted to an ErrorException, which is rethrown like any action exception; display_errors, display_startup_errors and error_reporting are left untouched.

showErrors is required and has no default; the allowed values are the constants of BehaviorOption (BehaviorOption::isValidOption() checks a value), and setExceptionBehavior() applies the configured one at boot (calling it with an integer overrides the setting for the rest of the request). The configured value may be written as a string ("1"). Anything else, such as an out-of-range integer (3) or a non-numeric value, is treated as 0 and does not throw. The setting itself has to exist: a missing showErrors key throws an InvalidArgumentException ("The attribute 'showErrors' does not exist in the attribute store (yet)") during startup; errors thrown by the configuration or the maintenance gate happen before the handlers are installed, so Whoops and the logger do not see them. Only a direct call to setExceptionBehavior() with an explicit out-of-range integer throws InvalidArgumentException ("Invalid exception behavior option: X").

The router runs error/404 when the controller file does not exist or when neither the action nor action_fallback exists. An exception thrown while including the controller file always runs error/500; exceptions thrown while constructing or running the action follow the table above; PHP Errors are never caught there and reach the global exception handler. The bundled ErrorController answers action_403, action_404 and action_500 with the matching status code and renders the 403, 404 or 500 view in layout/min_layout; the three Blade views are identical except for the heading (Oops! Page not for you, Oops! Page not found, Oops! This page seems to be broken), the digits and the message (It seems like you don't have the permissions to visit this page!, The page you requested couldn't be found!, Sorry, we messed up!). To replace them, add an application ErrorController.php (it has to implement all three actions, otherwise a missing action keeps rerouting to the 404 page until the limit of 10 reroutes ends the request with "Error: Too many reroutes.") or application views named 403, 404 and 500.

docs.title: The Whoops error page
docs.text:
In the test environment (execution_type = test), ZubZet registers Whoops to render unhandled exceptions as an interactive page with the full stack trace, source snippets, and request context — a major step up from a plain error message while developing.

Test environment only

The Whoops page is intentionally limited to execution_type = test. In production (execution_type = prod) it is never registered, so stack traces are not exposed to visitors: uncaught exceptions are logged and rethrown to PHP's default handler.

docs.title: Clickable file links
docs.text:
Whoops can turn each stack frame inside the working directory into a link that opens the file in your editor. Two settings drive this:

  • development_editor — the editor URL scheme (default vscode), producing <editor>://file/<host path><relative file>:<line>.
  • automated_host_working_directory — your project's path on the host, so links resolve correctly even though the code runs inside a container; without it no links are made. The info:startup command sets this when run with --pwd "$(pwd)" (the dev stack's npm run info does this automatically).

docs.title: Sensitive data masking
docs.text: Whoops automatically masks request values whose keys look sensitive (containing pass, secret, token, session, auth, access, key, credential, private, bearer) across $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE, $_SESSION, $_SERVER, and $_ENV, so credentials are not printed on the error page.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Debug Bar — per-request queries, templates, and log records (also test-only).
  • Logging — persist errors and events to the database or a stream.

docs.title: Global Helper Functions
docs.text: To optimize developer experience and eliminate redundant boilerplate, global helper functions have finally been integrated. These helpers offer immediate and consistent access to core framework components and services. All previously available methods remain fully supported to ensure seamless backward compatibility. The functions below throw a RuntimeException at boot when a function of the same name already exists (except __(), which yields to an existing one).

docs.title: zubzet()
docs.text:
Returns the main instance of the ZubZet framework, or throws a NotInstantiatedException before it exists.

Syntax: zubzet()

docs.title: model()
docs.text:
Provides direct access to a specific model instance.

Syntax: model($modelName, $dir = null)

  • $modelName: The name of the model to be instantiated.
  • $dir: Optional directory to load the model from instead of the usual lookup.

Note: In controller actions, $reqObj->getModel($modelName) remains a supported alternative.

Example:

model("Test")->onTest();

docs.title: request()
docs.text:
Accesses the instance of the current request, or throws a NotInstantiatedException when there is none. It works on a snapshot of the superglobals taken at boot, so later writes to $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE or $_SESSION are invisible to it.

Syntax: request()

Example:

request()->getPost("POST_PARAMETER");

docs.title: response()
docs.text:
Accesses the instance of the current response, the same one that controller constructors, middleware and actions receive.

Syntax: response()

Example:

response()->sendEMail($to, $subject, $document);

docs.title: config()
docs.text:
Retrieves a configuration value by its key.

Syntax: config(?string $key = null, bool $useDefault = true, mixed $default = null)

  • $key: The configuration identifier. If it is empty, the complete settings array is returned, credentials included.
  • $useDefault: Whether to return a fallback value if the key is not found. Defaults to true; with false, a missing key throws an InvalidArgumentException.
  • $default: The value to return if $useDefault is true and the key is missing. Defaults to null.

Note: $useDefault is the second positional argument, so config("key", 5) does not set a default of 5. Pass the fallback by name: config("key", default: 5).

Note: Previously accessible via $req->getBooterSettings(...) inside controller actions; this approach remains fully supported.

Example:

config("dbusername");

docs.title: configNumeric()
docs.text:
Retrieves a configuration value that has to be a number.

Syntax: configNumeric(string $key, int $default)

  • $key: The configuration identifier.
  • $default: The value to return if the key is missing.

Note: Non-numeric values are rejected with an InvalidArgumentException instead of being cast. A typo or a value like off would otherwise silently become 0 and disable whatever the setting controls.

Example:

configNumeric("db_max_retries", 3);

docs.title: user()
docs.text:
Returns the request user, built once per request when the framework is constructed, from the bearer token or the z_login_token cookie. It is also available as $req->getRequestingUser(), $req->booter->user, $opt["user"] in views and as the global alias User, which is not the record class Authentication\Permission\User (import that one with use).

Syntax: user()

Note: This streamlines the previous method of calling $req->getRequestingUser() within controller actions. Check user()->isLoggedIn (true only when token, session and an active z_user row all resolve) to detect anonymous visitors. userId is the account the session acts as (null when anonymous), orgId the user's organization id (null when anonymous or without one), getSessionToken() the current session token (null when anonymous), execUserId the real user behind a login as session (equal to userId for a normal login) and fields the complete z_user row including password, salt, password_scheme and custom columns (empty when anonymous).

Example:

user()->userId;

docs.title: db()
docs.text:
Provides the database instance for a specified connection, or throws a NotInstantiatedException before it exists.

Syntax: db(string $connection = "default", bool $allowUnsetConnection = false)

  • $connection: The name of the database connection (defaults to "default", any other name throws an InvalidArgumentException).
  • $allowUnsetConnection: Return null instead of throwing while the connection does not exist yet (early in boot).

Note: Database access is no longer restricted to using $this->z_db within models; db(), zubzet()->z_db and $this->z_db are the same shared connection.

Example:

db()->exec("SELECT * FROM z_user");

docs.title: logger()
docs.text:
Returns a Monolog logger instance for the given channel, or throws a NotInstantiatedException before the framework instance exists.

Syntax: logger(string $name = null)

  • $name: The channel name. Defaults to "app" if omitted.

Loggers are created on first use and cached for subsequent calls with the same name. See Logging for full configuration details.

Example:

logger()->info("Something happened");
logger("payments")->warning("Timeout", ["orderId" => $id]);

docs.title: view()
docs.text:
Renders a view template directly.

Syntax: view(string $document, array $opt = [], array|string $options = [])

  • $document: The path to the view file.
  • $opt: Data array passed to the view.
  • $options: Additional rendering options, or a layout name as a string.

Note: This serves as a streamlined alternative to rendering via the response object using $resObj->render(...).

Example:

view("adminpanel/dashboard");

docs.title: encryptSecret()
docs.text:
Encrypts a secret with the encryption_key setting, for example before storing it in the database. See Secrets.

Syntax: encryptSecret(string $plaintext): string

  • $plaintext: The value to encrypt.

Example:

$stored = encryptSecret($secretKey);

docs.title: decryptSecret()
docs.text:
Decrypts a value created by encryptSecret(). Throws a ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\DecryptionException when the key is wrong or the value is malformed or was modified. See Secrets.

Syntax: decryptSecret(string $encrypted): string

  • $encrypted: A value returned by encryptSecret().

Example:

$secretKey = decryptSecret($stored);

docs.title: __()
docs.text:
Translates a message id into the active locale. See Translations for the catalogues and how the locale is picked.

Syntax: __(string $id, array $parameters = [], ?string $domain = null, ?string $locale = null): string

  • $id: The message id. An id no catalogue defines is returned unchanged.
  • $parameters: Placeholder values, keyed the way the catalogue spells the placeholder.
  • $domain: The catalogue domain, messages when omitted.
  • $locale: A locale override, the active locale when omitted.

The framework only declares it when no global __() exists yet, so an application or library that brings its own keeps it.

Example:

echo __("dashboard.welcome", ["{name}" => $name]);

docs.title: deprecated()
docs.text:
Raises a deprecation notice for a code path that still works but should no longer be used. The notice goes through PHP's error handling like a deprecation of PHP itself: with showErrors = 2 it is promoted to an exception, with showErrors = 1 it is logged as a DEPRECATION event and displayed, and with showErrors = 0 it is silent, like every other PHP notice.

Syntax: deprecated(string $version, string $message): void

  • $version: The version the deprecation starts with, e.g. "1.3.0".
  • $message: What is deprecated and what to use instead.

The framework only declares it when no global deprecated() exists yet, so an application or library that brings its own keeps it.

Example:

public function legacyLookup(string $key) {
    deprecated("1.3.0", "legacyLookup() is replaced by lookup(), which also handles prefixed keys");
    return $this->lookup($key);
}

docs.title: e()
docs.text:
Escapes a string for safe HTML output. It strips tags (everything between < and >, so 1<2 and 3>2 becomes 12) and then escapes the remaining special characters through the render engine, so its output matches what {{ }} produces in a view.

Syntax: e(?string $value): ?string

  • $value: The string to escape. null is passed through unchanged, so optional values can be escaped without an extra check.

Use it whenever a value ends up in HTML outside of a template echo, for example in attributes built in PHP.

shortenStr($str, $maxlength = 10) cuts at word boundaries and appends ..., but returns a string that fits with a trailing space; getCaller($depth = 1) only works for 0 and 1; var_swap(&$x, &$y) swaps two variables. makeSlug() drops every character outside A-Za-z0-9-_ and space without transliterating, so Größe becomes gre; emptyToNull(&$value) also nulls 0, '0', false, [] and the string null. The global constants TIMESPAN_DAY_n hold n days in seconds (TIMESPAN_DAY_1 is 86400) for n = 1, 2, 3, 7, 10, 14, 20, 21, 30, 60, 90, 180, 182 and 365; the FILE_SIZE_* constants are listed in File Uploads.

Example:

<a title="<?= e($opt["title"]) ?>">

docs.title: Health Endpoint
docs.text:
Since version 1.3.0, the framework ships a public health check:

GET /_zubzet/health

It performs an explicit database roundtrip (SELECT 1) and reports the result as JSON. The response never contains error details, so the endpoint is safe to expose publicly for uptime monitoring, downtime alerts, and readiness checks during application startup.

docs.title: Responses
docs.text: Condition Status Body Application and database reachable 200 {"status": "healthy"} Database unreachable 503 {"status": "unhealthy"}

docs.title: Disabling
docs.text:
The endpoint is enabled by default. Turn it off in z_settings.ini:

health_endpoint_enabled = false

When disabled, the route is not registered and /_zubzet/health answers 404.

docs.title: Using a layout in your project
What is a layout?
docs.text: When talking about a layout, a reusable page structure is meant. To an extent, most content pages look very similar. Think navigation or footer. A perfect opportunity for generalization. A view is rendered into a layout: the layout is the page shell, the view fills in the content.

docs.title: How a layout works
docs.text:
A layout is a .blade.php file that defines the page shell and marks where a view's sections go with @yield: 

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
    <head>
        <x-zubzet::head :opt="$opt"/>
        @yield("head")
        <link rel="stylesheet" href="<?php echo $opt["root"]; ?>assets/css/bootstrap.min.css">
    </head>
    <body class="d-flex flex-column min-vh-100">
        <header>
            <nav class="navbar navbar-expand-lg navbar-light bg-light">
                <a class="navbar-brand">Adminpage</a>
            </nav>
        </header>

        <main class="container mt-5">
            @yield("content")
        </main>

        <footer class="my-2 footer fixed-bottom">
            <p class="text-center text-body-secondary">© 2024 Company</p>
        </footer>

        <x-zubzet::body :opt="$opt"/>
    </body>
</html>
- @yield("content") is where the view's @section("content") lands, the main page body. - @yield("head") is where the view's optional @section("head") lands, inside the document <head>. A layout without it drops the view's head section. - <x-zubzet::head :opt="$opt"/> and <x-zubzet::body :opt="$opt"/> pull in the framework essentials (a <meta charset> and viewport tag, jQuery, Popper, Bootstrap, bs-custom-file-input, Font Awesome including its v4 class names, Z.js with Z.Request.rootPath, rootHost and absRoot, a watcher that reloads the page once the z_login_token cookie is gone, and the debug bar). Include them in every full page layout: the head component inside <head> before @yield("head"), so view heads can use jQuery and Z, the body component at the end of <body>. Pass the render data through with :opt="$opt"; :custom-bootstrap="true" on the head component skips only the Bootstrap JS tag. Z.js needs jQuery, the global bsCustomFileInput, Bootstrap 4 and Font Awesome, which the head component loads.

A view then selects and fills this layout: 

@extends($layout)

@section("head")
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="<?php echo $opt["root"]; ?>assets/css/page.css">
@endsection

@section("content")
    <h1>Dashboard</h1>
@endsection
Because the view carries @extends($layout) rather than naming a specific layout, the same view works with whatever layout you hand it, which is what makes switching layouts per request possible.

docs.title: How to use one in your project?
docs.text: When using $res->render, a third optional parameter accepts a path to a layout, or an array whose only read key is layout. If no parameter is given, the render engine will look for a layout with the standard name in your views folder. The standard location for a layout is {your z_views folder}/layout/default_layout.blade.php. If you wish to use a different location, you'll need to use the third parameter to specify a different path. This also allows you to use multiple layouts within the same project and even switch dynamically for content pages. The framework bundles layout/default_layout (the default), layout/min_layout (the same head but the framework body scripts after the content, used by the login and the 403, 404 and 500 pages), and layout/empty and layout/mail_layout (only the view's content without any HTML, for partials and mails; mail_layout is the default of sendEmailToUser()). A same-named file in your views folder replaces a bundled one. The default and min layout link {root}assets/img/favicon.png, a static file your app has to supply.

docs.title: Example usage
docs.text:
public function action_index(Request $req, Response $res) {
    return $res->render("admin/index", [], "admin/layout");
}

docs.title: Setting a default layout for part of your app
docs.text: When $res->render is called without an explicit layout, the framework picks one in this order: per-instance default → global default → layout/default_layout. Use $res->setDefaultLayout("admin/layout") (the request's single Response) or the static Response::setGlobalDefaultLayout("admin/layout") from a controller __construct, a route middleware or an action to change that default for a section of the app; both set methods discard any layouts pushed before, so the given one becomes the only entry. Both scopes also expose pushDefaultLayout / popDefaultLayout (and the global equivalents) so nested components can install a layout and restore the previous one when they're done: pop removes and returns the top entry and throws an \UnderflowException on an empty stack, so every push needs exactly one pop, in LIFO order.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text:
ZubZet provides a built-in logging system powered by Monolog. It allows you to record application events, errors, and diagnostic information either to a database table or to a stream (file or stderr). The framework automatically logs certain system events such as logins, page views, and REST errors. Which of them are stored depends on logger_level.

Loggers are created lazily on first use and cached for the lifetime of the request, so there is no overhead for channels that are never written to.

docs.title: Disabling Logging
docs.text:
Logging is enabled by default. To disable it, set the following in z_config/z_settings.ini:

logger_enabled = false

When disabled, all logger() calls still work but write to a NullHandler — log messages are silently discarded without any errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All logger settings are configured in z_config/z_settings.ini.

Key Type Default Description logger_enabled boolean true Enables or disables the logging system entirely logger_type string database The logger backend, database or stream (case-sensitive); any other value throws an InvalidArgumentException logger_level string notice Minimum log level to record: a name (case-insensitive) or number, see below; an unknown name throws an InvalidArgumentException logger_stream_url string php://stderr Stream target — only used when logger_type = stream logger_slow_request_ms number 1000 Requests at least this slow (>=) are logged as SLOW_REQUEST at shutdown (not after an uncaught exception; console commands count too); a negative or non-numeric value disables it logger_slow_query_ms number 300 exec() queries (so execQuery(), not executeMultiQuery()) taking at least this many milliseconds (>=, so 0 logs every query; measured from prepare to execute, retries included, result fetch excluded) are logged as SLOW_QUERY (without disturbing getInsertId() or the current result); an INI file cannot disable it, so use a high threshold

docs.title: Log Levels
docs.text:
Log levels follow the Monolog/PSR-3 standard. Set logger_level to a level name — only records at or above that level are stored.

logger_level value Description debug Detailed diagnostic information info Normal operational events notice Significant but expected events warning Exceptional but non-critical events error Runtime errors critical Critical conditions alert Action must be taken immediately emergency System is unusable

The framework logs its own events on the zubzet channel (Logger::ZUBZET) at different levels. The event names are the constants of ZubZet\Framework\Logger\LogEventType and become the record message. With the default notice, the info events are dropped by the handler and not stored; set logger_level = info to record them.

Level Framework events info RENDER (every rendered view, mail renders included; context location, view, viewName, layout, layoutName), USER_LOGGED_IN (userId), USER_LOGGED_IN_ANOTHER (userId, userId_exec), USER_LOGGED_OUT (userId), USER_CREATED (userId, email; written by z_userModel::add(), so also by signup, User::add() and the admin add-user page), ACCOUNT_UPDATED (userId; admin edit-user adds the old email, two-factor changes a reason), PASSWORD_RESET_REQUESTED (userId; only when the email matched an account), PASSWORD_RESET (userId, reason) warning SLOW_REQUEST (duration_ms, uri), SLOW_QUERY (duration_ms, query without bound values), REST_ERROR (code, message), ACCOUNT_LOGIN_RATE_LIMITED (userId) error EXCEPTION (class, message, file, line, trace)

PHP errors are logged as ERROR (error), PARSE (critical), WARNING (warning), DEPRECATION/NOTICE (notice) or STRICT (debug), depending on their severity (any other severity is logged as ERROR with level warning), with the context message, file and line. Failed password attempts, verification success, logouts of anonymous requests and admin actions (roles, permissions, database browsing) write no event, and sendEmail() failures are echoed instead of logged. @-suppressed errors and fatal errors are not logged.

docs.title: Writing Log Entries
docs.text:
Use the global logger() helper function anywhere in your application.

// Log to the app channel
logger()->info("User submitted a contact form", ["email" => $email]);

// Log to a named channel
logger("payments")->warning("Payment gateway timeout", ["orderId" => $id]);

logger() without arguments defaults to the "app" channel (Logger::APP). Any string can be passed to create a named channel — each channel is cached after the first call.

docs.title: Available Methods
docs.text:
logger()->debug("message", $context);
logger()->info("message", $context);
logger()->notice("message", $context);
logger()->warning("message", $context);
logger()->error("message", $context);
logger()->critical("message", $context);
logger()->alert("message", $context);
logger()->emergency("message", $context);
logger()->log($level, "message", $context);

The second parameter $context is an optional associative array with additional data to attach to the log record. PSR-3 {placeholder} interpolation in the message is not active.

Keys that should accompany every later record of a channel go into extra instead, via logger()->contextAdd([...]), contextMergeFrom($name = "app") (the source channel wins on shared keys; an empty name or a channel that was never created throws), contextInspect(fn($context) => ...) (the return value replaces the context) and contextClear(). All of them return the logger and can be chained, and a key named traceId, file or line overrides the built-in value.

Every record carries a 32-character hex extra.traceId, generated on first use and shared by the whole request. The framework reads no incoming trace header, so propagate one with Logger::setTraceId($id) (not validated, only later records carry it); Logger::getTraceId() returns it.

docs.title: Registering a Custom Logger
docs.text:
If you need full control over a logger — custom handlers, formatters, or processors — you can build a ZubZet\Framework\Logger\Logger instance (it extends the Monolog Logger) manually and register it under a channel name using LoggerFactory::register(). Once registered, it is returned by logger() like any other channel, but it gets none of the logger_* handler and processor setup (no traceId or call-site extra unless you add a processor).

use Monolog\Handler\RotatingFileHandler;
use ZubZet\Framework\Logger\Logger;
use ZubZet\Framework\Logger\LoggerFactory;

$customLogger = new Logger("audit");
$customLogger->pushHandler(new RotatingFileHandler("/var/log/audit.log", 30));

LoggerFactory::register("audit", $customLogger);

// Anywhere in your application
logger("audit")->info("User exported data", ["userId" => $id]);

If a logger with that name was already created by the framework, register() overwrites it in the cache. logger() builds channels from the logger_* settings via LoggerFactory::getOrCreateLogger(), while LoggerFactory::getLogger($name) only returns a cached channel or null.

The parameter is typed Logger|LoggerInterface, but register() and logger() are declared to return the ZubZet Logger. A plain Monolog Logger or any other PSR-3 logger is therefore accepted and cached, yet register() and every later logger() call for that name throw a TypeError on return. Always register a ZubZet\Framework\Logger\Logger.

docs.title: Database Logger
docs.text:
Stores log records in the z_interaction_log database table. This is the default logger type.

logger_type = database

Each log entry is stored as a row with the following columns:

Column Type Description id INT Auto-incrementing primary key text MEDIUMTEXT The plain log message value MEDIUMTEXT Full log record as a JSON string (see below) userId INT ID of the currently logged-in user (nullable) userId_exec INT ID of the executing user when using "login as" (nullable) created TIMESTAMP Timestamp of the log entry

If the database connection is not available or the insert fails (for example a missing table mid-migration), the entry is silently skipped. Nothing purges z_interaction_log, so delete old rows yourself.

docs.title: value Column Structure
docs.text:
The value column contains the JSON-encoded Monolog record. The processor adds traceId, file, line, class and function to extra (omitted below), and the environment keys userId, execUserId and source ("web" or "cli") are appended at write time:

{
    "message": "User logged in",
    "context": { "userId": 42 },
    "level": 200,
    "level_name": "INFO",
    "channel": "zubzet",
    "datetime": { "date": "2026-04-08 12:00:00.000000", "timezone_type": 3, "timezone": "UTC" },
    "extra": {
        "userId": 42,
        "execUserId": 42,
        "source": "web"
    }
}

Context values are not normalized. The record is encoded with JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE, JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES, JSON_INVALID_UTF8_SUBSTITUTE and JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR; if encoding fails, a fallback record containing only the message and the encoding error is stored instead.

docs.title: Stream Logger
docs.text:
Writes log records as JSON to a file or PHP stream, one record per line.

logger_type = stream
logger_stream_url = php://stderr

logger_stream_url accepts any valid PHP stream URL or file path (relative paths resolve against the working directory):

logger_stream_url = php://stderr
logger_stream_url = php://stdout
logger_stream_url = /var/log/app.log
logger_stream_url = z_config/app.log

Each log entry is a single JSON object followed by a newline character (an empty context or extra is written as {}). Missing directories are created and there is no rotation; the php://stderr default ends up in the PHP or webserver error log. The environment keys are appended to extra automatically before formatting:

{"message":"User logged in","context":{"userId":42},"level":200,"level_name":"INFO","channel":"zubzet","datetime":"2026-04-08 12:00:00","extra":{"userId":42,"execUserId":42,"source":"web"}}

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# z_config/z_settings.ini
logger_type = database
logger_level = info

public function action_order(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $orderId = model("order")->createOrder($req->getPost("items"));

    logger()->info("Order placed", ["orderId" => $orderId]);

    return $res->success(["orderId" => $orderId]);
}

docs.title: Maintenance Mode
docs.text: A standalone gate that runs immediately after configuration loads, before the logger, exception handler, asset proxy, routing, and database. When active it sends 503 Service Unavailable (Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8, Retry-After: 300, always the HTML page, even for JSON, REST and asset-proxy requests) and exits without any shutdown handlers, DB queries or log writes. Safe to enable while running a live migration.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Value HTTP requests CLI commands disabled Pass through Pass through soft Blocked unless bypass cookie Pass through enabled Blocked Pass through full Blocked Blocked

Set this mode in the settings file or, with allow_env_config, using an ENV variable (CONFIG_MAINTENANCE_MODE). It is read on every request, so editing it takes effect immediately. There is no CLI command or admin toggle for it.

maintenance_mode = enabled

Defaults to disabled. Case-insensitive. Unknown values fall back to disabled, including the INI word off, which normalises to an empty string.

docs.title: Bypass cookie
docs.text: In soft mode, requests with a maintenance cookie pass through. Only the presence of the cookie key is checked (MaintenanceHandler::checkBypassCookie()), so any value bypasses, even an empty one. Admins can set it via the admin panel, which sends the value true for the rootFolder path with SameSite=Lax (plus Secure when host starts with https://, never HttpOnly). It expires after 24 hours. The page is unreachable while the gate blocks, so set the cookie before switching to soft.

docs.title: CLI behavior
docs.text: In full mode, CLI commands write Service Unavailable to stderr and exit with code 1. Use this to pause cron jobs alongside HTTP traffic.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
The HTTP body comes from the first usable file:

  1. app/Views/maintenance.html Project override
  2. (framework) src/Maintenance/maintenance.html Framework default

The bundled page (title Maintenance, heading We'll be back soon) says the website is undergoing maintenance, asks to check back later, hints to contact the web administrator and reloads itself every 5 minutes. A template is skipped if empty or if it contains <?php (the gate uses file_get_contents, never include).

The template is only used for HTTP responses. CLI hits always receive the bare Service Unavailable string regardless of mode.

docs.title: Admin panel
docs.text: /z/maintenance shows the current status and exposes a button to set the bypass cookie. Requires the admin.maintenance permission. Only reachable in disabled or soft-with-cookie; in enabled or full you must edit the INI directly to toggle off.

docs.title: What does a model do?
docs.text: A model depicts all interactions with your data structure. This is usually either the database or a file. The model can be used to retrieve data as well as set it.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text: If you have already created a model, you can simply use $req->getModel("Modelname"), $res->getModel("Modelname") or model("Modelname") (the controller itself has no getModel()) in a controller action to call the model. Otherwise, if you are within a model and need to call another model, you can use $this->getModel("Modelname"). An optional second argument of getModel() replaces the app/Models/ directory and must end with a directory separator.

docs.title: File and class
docs.text:
A model lives in app/Models/<Name>Model.php and is a plain global-namespace class <Name>Model (no namespace declaration). getModel("<Name>") and model("<Name>") append Model automatically, so getModel("Employee") loads app/Models/EmployeeModel.php.

A dotted name such as model("admin.Users") loads app/Models/admin/UsersModel.php (directory parts lower-cased, class UsersModel); an app file shadows a bundled model of the same name (z_adminDashboard, z_file, z_general, z_logger, z_login, z_migration, z_organization, z_permission, z_user), and a missing model throws an Exception (Model: <Name>Model does not exist!). The loader require_onces the file, so class names must be unique even across sub-directories, and creates one instance per model and request with db() and zubzet(), so properties persist; never instantiate a model yourself or pass user input as the name.

docs.title: Built-In Functionality
docs.text: Every model extends z_model, an alias of ZubZet\Framework\Core\Model, and inherits its many useful methods, including the query builder helpers (trait CanBuildQuery) and getModel() (trait CanRetrieveModel), plus the protected $z_db (the Connection) and $booter. You can simply use the already existing methods and build on them.

docs.title: Example Model
docs.text:
<?php

    class EmployeeModel extends z_model {

        public function getAll(): array {
            $sql = "SELECT *
                    FROM `employee`";
            return $this->exec($sql)->resultToArray();
        }

        public function getById($employeeId): array {
            $sql = "SELECT *
                    FROM `employee`
                    WHERE `id` = ?";
            return $this->exec($sql, "i", $employeeId)->resultToLine();
        }

    }
?>

The method exec is probably the most important one for your model. It incorporates all the steps for a prepared statement in one simple line. The first parameter is the sql command as a variable or string literal. The second parameter is a string literal of all the variable types. Each char represents one variable. All parameters afterwards are expected to be variables and replace the question marks within the sql command.

docs.title: Prepared types
docs.text: Type Description Use Cases i An integer Mostly IDs, but also other numeric values s A string Names, Dates, Emails d A double A rational number b A blob Binary data like an image. (Not recommended)

docs.title: Example Database Request
docs.text:
$sql = "SELECT * 
        FROM `employee` 
        WHERE `first_name` = ?
        AND `age` = ?";
$this->exec($sql, "si", "Klaus", 30);

docs.title: Execute Features
docs.text:
exec returns the Connection, so these helpers chain directly. The result and insert id are shared per request, so a query from any model replaces the previous one. mergeAsGroup(), checkIfUnique(), checkIfExists(), executeMultiQuery(), execQuery() and switchUser() exist only on db(), not on models. The result helpers only work after a SELECT, as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE leave no result set.

Type Description resultToLine() Returns the next row of the last result as an associative array, or null when no row is left. resultToArray() Returns all remaining rows of the last result, each as an associative array keyed by column name with numeric columns as PHP numbers; an initial array can be passed to append to. getInsertId() Get the last insert id; every exec() overwrites it (SELECTs included), but inserts done by the internal log do not. mergeAsGroup($groupBy, $subElement = null) db() only: groups the remaining rows by the $groupBy column (numeric-string keys become integers); each group holds the full rows, or just the $subElement values when set. checkIfUnique($table, $field, $value, $ignoreField = null, $ignoreValue = null), checkIfExists($table, $field, $value) db() only: true when no row (respectively at least one row) has $field = $value; names are backtick-wrapped but not escaped, values are bound as s. The ignore pair excludes the edited row (AND $ignoreField <> ?), so a null $ignoreValue makes checkIfUnique return true. countResults Returns the number of results in the last query. countTableEntries($table) Returns COUNT(*) of the table. getResult() The raw mysqli_result\|bool\|null of the last query. getFullTable($table, $fields = "*") Returns all rows of SELECT $fields FROM $table; both are inserted unescaped. getTableWhere($table, $fields, $where) Like getFullTable with WHERE $where, also inserted unescaped; optional $types and $values bind placeholders in $where.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Why not simply write queries without question marks?

Only bound values are escaped, the query text is sent exactly as written. When not preparing your variables, it is very likely that your code is vulnerable to SQl injections, one of the most common security mistakes made when dealing with databases.

If you always use exec with the question marks in your queries, you save yourself from a lot of headaches.

Learn more about SQL injections from the official PHP documentation. An interesting and even partly entertaining read.

docs.title: Models, Views and Controllers (Structure)
docs.text: A model-view-controller (MVC) is an architectural design pattern that organizes an application's logic into distinct layers, each of which carries out a specific set of tasks.

docs.title: What's a model?
docs.text: The model depicts all interactions with your data structure. This is usually the database or a different data medium. The model can be used to retrieve, update and remove data.

docs.title: What's a controller?
docs.text: It handles all the sites logic. Routing is Based on the name of the controller and its actions. This Interacts with models and renders views.

docs.title: What's a view?
docs.text: A view contains the html the user should see. All additional resources like css, images or javascript are also loaded from views. Views do usually not contain a footer, navigation, header or other elements that belong to the overall layout of the page. For this, layouts should be used as without a layout, a view can't be renderer. Read more about layouts here.

docs.title: Parameters, post, get, file and cookies
URL Parameters
docs.text: When using virtual links, parameters as “subfolders” is a great way of transfering values, that are also very readable. See the following link schema as an example of what is meant by parametres within the virtual link: controller/action/param0/param1/param2/...

docs.title: Read the parameters using code
docs.text: To read the virtual url parameters use $req->getParameters. It works using an offset and a length: length 1 returns the single segment (false when absent) or, with a value to compare against, a boolean from a loose ==; any other length returns an array slice, null all remaining segments. getReadableParameter() splits an SEO segment such as title-64 at the last dash into text and id (without a dash the whole segment is the id, without a segment both are empty strings), and getUrlParts() returns all raw segments below the root directory, not URL-decoded (a double slash gives an empty one). getParameters() always skips the first two segments (controller and action), so for routes of another shape use getRouteParameter(). getCurrentURL() returns host plus the raw REQUEST_URI with query string, getRoot() the root setting (host plus root directory, also Z.Request.rootHost) and getRootFolder() the rootFolder path such as /; getDomain() returns host without scheme, port and path, and isCli() is true for console runs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example URL: www.yourwebsite.com/{controller}/{action}/a/b/c

Get the first parameter: $req->getParameters(0, 1); Returns: "a"

Get all the parameters after the second one: $req->getParameters(1); Returns: ["b", "c"]

Check if the first parameter is "test": if($req->getParameters(0, 1, "test")) { ... Returns: false

Get the first parameter when using a fallback action $req->getParameters(-1, 1); Returns "action"

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
// Example execution `{root}/{controller}/employee/view/2`
public function action_employee(Request $req, Response $res) {

    // Checks if the first URL parameter (offset 0, length 1) is "view"
    if ($req->getParameters(0, 1, "view")) {

        // Retrieves the second URL parameter (offset 1, length 1), which is the employeeId
        $employeeId = $req->getParameters(1, 1);

        return $res->render("employee/employee_view", [
            "employee" => $req->getModel("Employee")->getEmployeeById($employeeId)
        ]);
    }

    return $res->render("employee/list");
}

docs.title: GET, POST, COOKIES, FILE as a method
docs.text: The framework includes some extra functionality when it comes to the above mentioned features and you should use the framework instead of the traditional way. This is because the framework employes extra filtering and processing methods as well as error handling already for you.

docs.title: Getting POST and GET parameters
docs.text: $req->getGet and $req->getPost are methods to get form parameters. These also enable to set default parameters, returned when the key is unset or null; without a key they return the whole array. Note: Post parameters get decoded automatically if their values have the special prefix <#decURI#>. This decoding is applied recursively to nested values, replaces the value in $_POST itself and allows to transmit special characters (Z.js sends its fields that way).

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
$req->getCookie gets a cookie of the request; $res->unsetCookie removes it there, $res->setCookie does not add it before the next request. It has a second parameter to set a default if the cookie is not set.

$res->setCookie has the same parameters as the native setcookie function of php. It should be used, because in the future may more logic build into the framework that deals with cookies.

Note: setCookie is a plain pass-through (setcookie(...func_get_args())) and applies no security defaults. Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite are only set if you pass them, so a bare $res->setCookie("name", "value") is sent without any of the three and is readable by JavaScript and sent over plain HTTP. Use the options-array form and set them yourself:

$res->setCookie("name", "value", [
    "expires" => time() + 3600,
    "path" => "/",
    "secure" => $res->cookieSecure(),
    "httponly" => true,
    "samesite" => "Lax",
]);

$res->cookieSecure() is true when the host setting starts with https://. The framework's own cookies pass these attributes explicitly through an internal helper, see CSRF protection.

$res->unsetCookie($name, $path = "/", $domainScope = "") removes the cookie from the request input and sends an expired one (empty value, timestamp 1). The path and domain must match those it was set with; $res->getCookieDomainScope() returns .<domain> when login_scope_allow_subdomains is the string true, otherwise an empty string (host-only).

docs.title: File
docs.text: $req->getFile uses $_FILE like $req->getPost uses $_POST. getFiles() and getCookies() are the key-less forms of getFile() and getCookie(), and getFile($key, $default) returns $default for a missing key like the other getters.

docs.title: Body and raw input
docs.text: $req->getBody() returns the raw request body, or null when it is empty or exactly "0". $req->getJson() decodes it into associative arrays, see JSON body. $req->store is a public array that the framework never fills and reroute() replaces the Request, so it is empty afterwards. SERVER, SESSION, REQUEST and body have no getters, read them from $req->input; there is no getMethod(), getHeader(), isPost() or isAjax(), use $req->input->SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] or the HTTP_* keys. $req->ip() returns the first set of HTTP_CLIENT_IP, HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR and REMOTE_ADDR (then the getenv() variants), referer() and userAgent() the header or null, and getExecutionTime() the seconds since REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT (null if missing).

docs.title: Accept-Language
docs.text:
$req->acceptLanguage() returns the locales of the request's Accept-Language header, best first. Entries are ordered by their q value, malformed entries and q=0 are dropped, and each tag is brought into its canonical case, so en-us and EN-US are one entry. The header is client controlled, so only the first 50 entries are read.

$req->acceptLanguage(); // "de-CH,de;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" -> ["de-CH", "de", "en"]

Translations use it to pick the locale of a visitor without one of their own.

docs.title: Bearer token
docs.text: $req->bearerToken() returns the token of an Authorization: Bearer <token> header, or null when the header is missing, uses another scheme or does not carry exactly one token (Bearer, Bearer a b). The framework authenticates by it before the login cookie.

docs.title: JSON body
docs.text:
$req->getBody() returns the raw request body. $req->getJson() decodes it as JSON, objects into associative arrays, and throws otherwise. An UnexpectedValueException carries the HTTP status to answer with as its code:

Status Reason 405 The method is not POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE 415 The Content-Type is not exactly application/json, or names a charset other than utf-8 413 The body is longer than $maxBytes (default 1 MiB)

A body that is not well formed JSON (a BOM, an empty body, invalid UTF-8 or nesting deeper than $maxDepth, default 32) throws a \JsonException instead; answer it with 400.

The strict Content-Type is what keeps a cross site form out: a form can send text/plain and form types, but never application/json. Integers beyond PHP_INT_MAX come back as strings instead of lossy floats.

try {
    $data = $req->getJson();
} catch(\UnexpectedValueException $e) {
    http_response_code($e->getCode());
    return $res->json(["error" => $e->getMessage()]);
} catch(\JsonException $e) {
    http_response_code(400);
    return $res->json(["error" => $e->getMessage()]);
}

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Aliases and virtual links: shorter or alternative versions of your virtual links
  • File uploads: validating and processing files received via $req->getFile

docs.title: Password Handling
docs.text: ZubZet hashes passwords with PHP's native Argon2id. The framework stores enough information alongside every hash to verify it, to recognise older hashes, and to upgrade them to the current algorithm automatically. Application code normally never touches a hash directly: the User API covers creating users, setting passwords, and checking a login.

docs.title: Where passwords are stored
docs.text:
Credentials live on the z_user table:

Column Purpose password The stored credential, VARCHAR(255) (an Argon2id hash for current accounts). password_scheme Which format password is in: native, legacy, onion, or wordpress. NULL for accounts without a password: User::add() inserts NULL and sets native once a password is set. salt VARCHAR(255), per row salt for legacy and onion rows. NULL for native and wordpress, because those hashes embed their own salt; every upgrade to native resets it to NULL. last_password_rehash_at TIMESTAMP NULL: when the stored hash was last produced (password change or rehash); the migration backfilled it from created for rows with a password. Useful for credential age policies.

There is no separate salt for native hashes. A native password value already contains the algorithm, the cost parameters, and a random salt in one self describing string, which is what makes transparent upgrades possible.

docs.title: The schemes
docs.text:
The password_scheme column tells the verifier how to read a stored value, so the formats can coexist while older accounts upgrade on their own.

Scheme password holds salt Notes native An Argon2id hash from password_hash(). NULL The target format for every account. legacy The raw SHA-512 hex produced by the framework's previous scheme. set Verify only. Upgraded to native on the next login. onion A native Argon2id hash wrapping the legacy value. set A dormant account moved onto Argon2id ahead of its next login. Upgraded to native when the owner logs in. wordpress A hash imported from WordPress, $wp$2y$… (6.8 and later) or $P$… (phpass, earlier). NULL Verify only. Upgraded to native on the next login. See Importing WordPress users.

docs.title: Adding users and setting passwords
docs.text: For building features and APIs, work through the User object. The plaintext is hashed for you, and the resulting account is always native.

docs.title: Create a user with a password
docs.text:
use ZubZet\Framework\Authentication\Permission\User;

$user = User::add("person@example.com", "the-plaintext-password");

User::add() also accepts null for the password to create an account whose credential is set later (for example invite or single sign on flows):

$user = User::add("person@example.com", null);
// ... later ...
$user->updatePassword("the-plaintext-password");

docs.title: Set or change a password
docs.text:
$user->updatePassword("the-new-plaintext-password");

This writes a fresh native Argon2id hash, clears the salt, stamps last_password_rehash_at, and invalidates the user's existing sessions.

docs.title: Check a password during login
docs.text:
$user = User::byEmail($email);

if ($user && $user->verifyPassword($plaintext)) {
    // success
}

User::verifyPassword() returns a boolean and is self healing: on a correct login it transparently upgrades a stale stored hash to a current native hash (see Self healing upgrades). It is the password check used by the framework's own login flow.

docs.title: Reset codes
docs.text:
The forgot-password flow stores a code per request in z_password_reset (userId, refId, reason, active, created; reason is always forgot). The reset page accepts a code while its row is active = 1 and created is newer than the booter setting forgotPasswordTimeSpan. After a successful reset the code is deactivated. A code is ZIT- plus 64 random hex characters, a new request does not deactivate earlier codes, and login/forgot_password has no rate limit and answers {"result":"success"} or {"result":"error"}, so it reveals whether an email is registered. The email is matched exactly, without an active or verified filter. An invalid reset code dies with the bare text ERROR: This code is not or no longer valid!; a successful reset ends all sessions of the user without logging them in, and the server checks no confirmation field (the view compares both in JS only, with a client-side minlength="4").

forgotPasswordTimeSpan is a relative time string such as 60 minutes (the project stub ships exactly that), which is handed to strtotime('-' . $value). When the setting is unset, that call fails and the cut-off becomes 1970-01-01 00:00:00, so an active code never expires. Always set it if codes should have a lifetime.

docs.title: The hash and verify API
docs.text: User is built on the lower level ZubZet\Framework\Authentication\PasswordHash\Password class, which you can use directly when you are not working with a User object.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
use ZubZet\Framework\Authentication\PasswordHash\Password;

$stored = Password::hash($plaintext); // Argon2id

Password::hash() rejects input outside MIN_LENGTH_BYTES to MAX_LENGTH_BYTES (3 to 1024 bytes by strlen, the upper bound being a denial of service guard) by throwing InvalidArgumentException("Invalid password length.").

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
$result = Password::verify($plaintext, $stored);

if ($result->isCorrect()) {
    // password matched
}

Password::verify() returns a Verification value object rather than a bare boolean, so a single call can also report whether the stored hash should be refreshed:

Method Returns isCorrect() Whether the password matched. isUpgradeNeeded() Whether the stored hash is stale and should be replaced. upgradePassword() The fresh native hash to persist. Guard with isUpgradeNeeded() first; calling it when no upgrade is pending throws a LogicException.

The hash inside upgradePassword() is computed only when you call it, so a plain isCorrect() check never pays for an upgrade it does not use. An empty stored value, a password outside the length limits and an unknown scheme (including null) give a wrong result instead of throwing.

For legacy and onion values, pass the scheme and a non-empty salt (otherwise an InvalidArgumentException is thrown) so the verifier knows how to read them:

$result = Password::verify($plaintext, $stored, Password::LEGACY, $salt);

docs.title: Importing WordPress users
docs.text:
To take over the accounts of a WordPress site, copy each user_pass value into password unchanged and set password_scheme to wordpress. The stored string says which WordPress format it is, so one scheme covers both:

Prefix Produced by Verified as $wp$2y$ WordPress 6.8 and later bcrypt over an HMAC-SHA-384 pre-hash of the trimmed password, as wp_hash_password() does. $P$ (or $H$) WordPress before 6.8, and any account that has not logged in since the upgrade to 6.8 The phpass portable hash: salted MD5 iterated 2^count times.

Both verify through the ordinary login path and are replaced by a native Argon2id hash on the first successful login. Nothing else WordPress may store (plain MD5 from before WordPress 2.5, or unprefixed hashes written by a plugin that overrides the algorithm) is recognised; those users need a password reset. The phpass format is weak at rest, and the onion command only covers legacy rows, so consider a reset for $P$ accounts that stay dormant after the import.

Two framework rules apply to imported accounts as they do to every other: passwords shorter than MIN_LENGTH_BYTES are rejected, and WordPress trims the password before hashing, so the verifier trims it as well.

docs.title: WordPress hashes upgrade themselves
docs.text: No separate migration step is needed for imported accounts. A wordpress row goes through the same self healing path as a legacy or onion row: on the first correct login, User::verifyPassword() verifies the WordPress hash, writes a fresh native Argon2id hash in its place, sets the scheme to native and stamps last_password_rehash_at. From then on the account is indistinguishable from one created in ZubZet. The WordPress verifiers are only ever consulted for rows still marked wordpress, so they can be removed once that count reaches zero.

docs.title: Self healing upgrades
docs.text:
ZubZet keeps stored hashes current without ever asking users to reset a working password. On a successful login, the stored hash is upgraded to a fresh native Argon2id hash when any of the following is true:

  • the account is still legacy or onion, or
  • the account is native but was hashed below the current cost.

The second case relies on PHP's password_needs_rehash(). When you raise the Argon2id cost (see below), existing users are migrated one at a time as they log in, with no bulk operation and no forced reset.

docs.title: Future proofing the work factor
docs.text: The work factor is PHP's Argon2id default cost. Hardware gets faster over time, so the recommended practice is to re measure every year or two and raise the cost when appropriate. Because the cost is embedded in each stored hash, raising it does not invalidate existing passwords: password_needs_rehash() simply reports the older hashes as stale, and the self healing path upgrades them on the next login.

docs.title: Migrating an existing installation
docs.text:
When you upgrade the framework, the schema migration runs automatically and marks every existing password row as legacy. Those accounts keep working unchanged and upgrade themselves to native on the next login.

Rehash on login only reaches accounts that actually log in. To bring accounts that have not logged in yet onto Argon2id as well, run the onion migration once:

php index.php auth:migrate-hashing

This wraps every legacy hash in an Argon2id layer and marks the row onion, so the whole table moves onto the modern algorithm rather than only the active accounts. It is idempotent, so it is safe to run more than once, and the first successful login peels an onion row back to a single native hash.

Wrapping an existing hash inside a stronger one is the same layered "onion" technique Facebook has publicly described for modernising its own password storage, which is where the name comes from.

docs.title: A short history
docs.text:
For years ZubZet hashed passwords with SHA-512 plus a per user salt and an additional transformation step, provided by a dedicated hashing library. That scheme served the framework reliably and shipped in production for a long time.

Version 1.2.0 modernises password storage onto PHP's native Argon2id, the algorithm recommended by the current OWASP Password Storage guidance. Argon2id is memory hard and purpose built for password storage, the native PHP functions are maintained as part of the language and run in constant time, and every stored value embeds its own algorithm, cost, and salt. That self describing format is what lets ZubZet recognise existing hashes and upgrade them transparently, and it makes raising the work factor in the future a one line change.

Existing passwords are safe and keep working. They are verified through the legacy path and re hashed onto Argon2id automatically the next time their owner logs in, so adopting the modern format needs no password reset.

docs.title: Basic explanation
docs.text: A user can have multiple roles, and each role can have multiple permissions. These can be managed in the admin panel.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Roles are the things that holds permissions. A role can be created with the Z-Admin panel ({root}/z). For a user to have access to the permissions of the role it needs to have the role assigned. The assignment can also be done with the Z-Admin panel.

docs.title: Structure of a permission
docs.text: Permissions are structured as multiple keywords connected by periods. For example: admin.user.create. This is descriptive as it can be seen that this permission is for admins with access to the user management and creating users. This style of writing permissions allows also the usage of wildcards. To admin.user.create someone with these permissions will have access to it: *.*, admin.*, admin.user.* and admin.user.create. *.* is a wildcard for all permissions, including single-word ones such as support. Use it on you own risk. A trailing .* also covers the prefix itself and everything below it (a.b.* satisfies a.b and a.b.c, not a.x). Wildcards only count on the granted side: a * inside a name or a lone * is plain text. The checks in PHP compare names case-sensitively, byAccessToAll and byAccessToAnyOf follow the database collation. Names are free text up to 255 characters.

docs.title: Blocking forbidden pages
docs.text: The Request object has a method called checkPermission. By calling it, anonymous users are sent to login/index and logged in users without the permission given as the parameter to the 403 page, and the current request is cancled with exit. checkSuperPermission($permission) is the same check but also accepts the permission of the original user of a loginAs session, like checkPermission($permission, false, true). With true as second parameter both return false instead. The reserved name console passes only on the CLI and otherwise ends in the 403 page, whatever the user holds. So it is wise to call this at the very beginning of an action.

docs.title: Controller example:
docs.text:
// Kicks the current request out of the action when it does not have "employee.view"
public function action_view(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $req->checkPermission("employee.view");

    return $res->render("employee/employee_view");
}

// Returns a bool if the user has the permission
public function action_view(Request $req, Response $res) {
    if(!$req->checkPermission("employee.view", true)) { 
        return $res->render("forbidden");
    }

    return $res->render("employee/employee_view");
}

docs.title: Requiring an organization
docs.text:
requireOrganization works like checkPermission, but ensures that the user belongs to an organization instead of checking a permission. A logged out user is sent to the login, and a logged in user without an organization is sent to the 403 page. A removed organization no longer counts.

public function action_view(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $req->requireOrganization();

    return $res->render("employee/employee_view");
}

// Returns a bool instead of showing the login or 403 page
if(!$req->requireOrganization(true)) {
    return $res->render("forbidden");
}

To check for a specific organization, use $organization->hasMember($user) or $user->isMemberOf($organization).

docs.title: Checking permissions while rendering the page
docs.text: To check if the requesting user has a permission, the user object in $opt can be used. It has a method called checkPermission that returns a boolean. Note that this is another method than checkPermission from the request object. This one returns false for anonymous users, never redirects the user and can be used for example to determin if specific should be visible to the user on a page it generally has access to. checkSuperPermission($permission) also accepts the original user of a loginAs session, and checkPermissionOf($permission, $userId) checks any user id without a login check. Permissions are loaded once per user id per request and not refreshed when they change.

docs.title: View example:
docs.text:
@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <!-- Returns a bool if the user has the permission -->
    <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("employee.delete")) { ?>
        <button id="delete">Delete</button>
    <?php } ?>

    <!-- Remaining code -->
@endsection

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: As the client and the server are completely separated, they need to have a way communicated. It is basically a standardized way of transfering, in our case JSON data, from the server to the client.

docs.title: How to use this?
docs.text:
The REST response pipeline is the Rest class, but you'll typically reach for one of the response helpers instead:

Call Purpose $res->generateRest Sends a REST payload wrapped in a meta envelope and exits by default $res->generateRestError Logs a REST_ERROR warning, sends only the error object and exits (HTTP status stays 200) $res->error Convenience for generateRest with result=error and the message, an optional payload array is merged like success does, exits $res->success Convenience for generateRest with result=success, exits; payload keys are merged after result and can override it $res->formErrors Merges all array arguments (others are ignored) into {"result":"formErrors","formErrors":[...]} inside the meta envelope, exits; each entry holds name, type and optional info $res->json Sends a raw JSON payload (no meta wrapper); does not exit

generateRest takes a payload array whose keys are added after meta (a payload key named meta replaces it). The second parameter of generateRest called $die determines if the script exits after generating the REST response. The parameter is optional with a default value of true. The pretty-printed JSON is sent without a Content-Type header or HTTP status code, unlike json.

docs.title: generateRest
docs.text:
$res->generateRest([
    "response" => "RESPONSE",
    "error" => "ERROR"
]);

{ "meta": { "endpoint": "REST API", "request": "URL", "timestamp": 9999999 }, "response": "RESPONSE", "error": "ERROR" }

docs.title: generateRestError
docs.text:
$res->generateRestError(404, "MESSAGE");

{ "error": { "code": 404, "message": "MESSAGE" } }

docs.title: success
docs.text:
$res->success([
    "information" => "MESSAGE"
]);

{ "meta": { "endpoint": "REST API", "request": "URL", "timestamp": 9999999 }, "result": "success", "information": "MESSAGE" }

docs.title: error
docs.text:
$res->error("MESSAGE");

{ "meta": { "endpoint": "REST API", "request": "URL", "timestamp": 9999999 }, "result": "error", "message": "MESSAGE" }

docs.title: json
docs.text:
Use json when you need to send a raw JSON payload without the REST meta wrapper. It sets Content-Type: application/json (and no status code) and echoes json_encode($data). Unlike the other helpers above it does not exit — call exit yourself if you need to stop the request here. JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR is always applied, so unencodable values raise a JsonException, after the header was already set.

$res->json([
    "ok" => true,
    "items" => [1, 2, 3],
]);

{"ok":true,"items":[1,2,3]}

Pass extra json_encode options as the second argument: 

$res->json($data, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT);

docs.title: Routing in ZubZet
docs.text: Since version 1.0.0, ZubZet not only includes the internal routing system (controller-based actions) but also provides a route definition system. The routing definition system is powered by FastRoute. (ZubZet 1.2.0 switched the underlying engine from Slim to FastRoute — your route definitions are unchanged.)

docs.title: What does "Routing" mean?
docs.text: Routing is the process of defining how your application responds to different HTTP requests. When a client (e.g., a browser or API consumer) sends a request to your server, the router decides which piece of code (controller and method) should handle that request. This makes it possible to build clean, structured, and maintainable applications where every endpoint has a clear definition.

docs.title: How to use the routing system?
docs.text: To define your routes, you first need a Routes folder in your project’s app directory. Inside this folder, you can create multiple files. Each file can contain routes, and all of them will be automatically registered by the framework. Every *.php file directly in app/Routes/ is loaded (subdirectories are not) in alphabetical order, before the module and framework route files, and the file name carries no meaning. A request is matched against these routes first (by REQUEST_METHOD, without a method-override parameter, and the URL-decoded path without query string and trailing slash); only if none matches, it falls back to the controller-based actions (or the console on the CLI), so a wrong HTTP verb never produces a 405. There is no route cache, the route files run on every request, and a duplicate or shadowed route throws a FastRoute BadRouteException while they load.

docs.title: How to register a route?
docs.text:
In a route file, after use ZubZet\Framework\Routing\Route;, you can register a route with the following syntax:

Route::{method}({endpoint}, [{ControllerClass}::class, {ControllerAction}]);

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
1. method → One of the supported HTTP methods:

    • any(endpoint, action) → Match GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS and HEAD
    • get(endpoint, action) → Match GET requests
    • post(endpoint, action) → Match POST requests
    • put(endpoint, action) → Match PUT requests
    • delete(endpoint, action) → Match DELETE requests
    • patch(endpoint, action) → Match PATCH requests
    • options(endpoint, action) → Match OPTIONS requests
    • define(method, endpoint, action) → Define any method (upper-cased, ANY works too); there is no head() helper and get() does not register HEAD

  2. endpoint → The URL path where the route will be accessible (e.g., /users, /products/{id}), in FastRoute syntax: {id:\d+} restricts a placeholder with a regex (default [^/]+) and a trailing [...] segment is optional (/users[/{id}]). You can also define Route Parameter using curly braces (e.g., /users/{id}), which you read with $req->getRouteParameter(). Group prefixes and endpoint are concatenated, a leading slash is added, repeated slashes collapse and the trailing slash is removed (empty becomes /).

  3. ControllerClass → The PHP class that contains the logic for handling the request. It must be a global-namespace class stored as <ControllerClass>.php in z_controllers, because it is looked up by file name.

  4. ControllerAction → The specific method inside the controller that should be executed. Any public method works, the action_ prefix is not required. Instead of the pair, the action can be a closure whose parameters are resolved by type (Request, Response, or array for the route parameters), so 0 to 3 parameters work in any order; any other parameter gets its default value, else null. Static arguments are ignored for closures and $req->getRouteParameter() stays empty, use the array parameter.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Route::get('/users/{id}', [UserController::class, 'show']);

This means:

When a client makes a GET request to /users/42, the router will call the show() method inside the UserController and make {id} (42) available as Route Parameter.

docs.title: Case and Spelling
docs.text:
Since version 1.3.0, routes match regardless of case: GET /Users/42 reaches the route above as well. Route parameters keep the spelling of the request, so {id} of /USERS/AbC is AbC.

The pattern of a route parameter ignores case too, /codes/{code:[A-Z]+} also matches /codes/abc.

docs.title: Route Groups
docs.text:
Sometimes multiple routes share the same prefix (for example, /api/v1/...). Instead of repeating the prefix in every route, you can define a group:

Route::group('/api/{apiVersion}', function () {
    Route::get('/users', [UserController::class, 'index']);
    Route::post('/users', [UserController::class, 'store']);
});

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
• The group prefix (/api/{apiVersion}) will automatically be applied to all routes inside the group.

  • In this example:

    1. GET /api/{apiVersion}/users → UserController::index
    2. POST /api/{apiVersion}/users → UserController::store

docs.title: Nested Groups
docs.text:
You can also nest groups inside each other:

Route::group('/api/{apiVersion}', function () {
    Route::group('/users', function () {
        Route::get('', [UserController::class, 'index']);      // GET /api/{apiVersion}/users
        Route::get('/{id}', [UserController::class, 'show']);  // GET /api/{apiVersion}/users/{id}
    });
});

The prefixes are concatenated in order, and the routes inherit the middleware of all enclosing groups.

This allows you to build modular and structured route definitions that are easy to maintain.

docs.title: Middleware and AfterMiddleware
docs.text:
ZubZet allows you to attach middleware and afterMiddleware to both routes and groups.

  • Middleware → Executed before the route runs. Example use cases: authentication, user validation, request logging.
  • AfterMiddleware → Executed after the route has been processed; its return value is ignored, and it does not run if the action ends the script (exit, for example generateRest() or rerouteUrl()). Example use cases: response formatting, cleanup, analytics logging.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Route::get('/test', [TestController::class, 'route'])
    ->middleware([TestController::class, 'Route_Middleware_Accept'])
    ->afterMiddleware([TestController::class, 'Route_Afterware']);
  • The middleware and afterMiddleware use the same format as routes: [ControllerClass::class, ControllerAction] arrays, never closures, and are called like actions with ($req, $res, ...$arguments).
  • A route or group registers when its fluent chain is destroyed, so end the statement after the last call and do not store the result in a variable.

docs.title: Middleware Rules
docs.text:
• A middleware must return true in order for the request to continue.
  • If a middleware returns anything other than true, the execution stops immediately:
    • No further middlewares are run
    • The route handler itself is not executed
    • No afterMiddleware is executed

Example flow with multiple middlewares:

  1. Authentication → returns true ✅ → continue
  2. UserRegistry → returns true ✅ → continue
  3. LoginLogging → returns true ✅ → route runs

But if Authentication returns anything else (it sets no status code and renders nothing itself, so it has to produce its own response):

  • Execution stops right there
  • Neither UserRegistry, the route, nor any afterMiddleware will be executed

docs.title: Middleware on Groups
docs.text:
You can also attach middleware to entire groups. All routes inside the group will inherit the defined middleware and afterMiddleware.

Route::group('/api/{apiVersion}', function () {
    Route::get('/users', [UserController::class, 'index']);
    Route::get('/users/{id}', [UserController::class, 'show']);
})
->middleware([AuthController::class, 'checkAuth'])
->afterMiddleware([LogController::class, 'logRequest']);

This means:

Every request to /api/{apiVersion}/users or /api/{apiVersion}/users/{id}:

  1. First passes through checkAuth (middleware)
  2. Then executes the route
  3. Finally runs logRequest (afterMiddleware)

With several groups, group middleware run from outer to inner before the route's own middleware; afterMiddleware run the route's own first, then the groups from inner to outer.

A group also guards the controller-based actions below its prefix, so a group without routes is enough for them:

Route::group('/admin')->middleware([AuthController::class, 'checkAuth']);

checkAuth runs before every action of the AdminController, in every spelling that reaches it: /admin/users, /Admin/users and /%41dmin/users alike. The prefix is compared the way the controller name is resolved: decoded, with - as _, . as §2E and ä, ö, ü as ae, oe, ue, regardless of case. A group /admin-panel therefore also covers /admin_panel/.... Direct executePath() calls (CLI run, checkPermission() redirects, error pages) skip explicit routes and group middleware. All matching groups run outer to inner, afterMiddleware in the same order, and a middleware returning anything but true ends the script with exit.

An empty prefix covers every URL. Otherwise a prefix covers a URL only if it equals the URL or is followed by / in it, and the whole prefix is compared literally against the path, which always starts with /. Three kinds of prefix therefore never guard a controller-based URL: one with a trailing slash (/admin/), one without a leading slash (admin) and one with a {placeholder} (/api/{apiVersion}). Placeholders are only resolved for routes, not for controller URLs. Nested groups concatenate their prefixes without a separator, so every nested prefix needs its own leading slash and none may end with one. A nested group stores only its own middleware; the parent matches the URL separately.

The groups for controller-based URLs are stored by their full prefix, spelled exactly as declared. Two groups with the same full prefix (Route::group('/admin') declared twice, or a nested /admin inside a group / that adds up to the same string) therefore do not add up: the later declaration replaces the earlier one, and only its middleware and afterMiddleware guard the controller actions below that prefix. Merge them into one group instead. This only affects the controller fallback, the routes inside each group still run with the middlewares of every group around them. Prefixes that differ only in spelling (/admin and /Admin) are separate entries, so both apply to the same URL.

docs.title: Route Parameters
docs.text:
Within the routing system, you can define dynamic route segments using curly braces, e.g. {parameter}. These placeholders are automatically treated as route parameters.

To access a parameter inside a controller action, you can use:

$req->getRouteParameter("key");

If you call $req->getRouteParameter() without passing a key, it will return all route parameters as an array. A key that does not exist gives null. The parameters, including the placeholders of group prefixes, are set before every stage (action, middleware, afterMiddleware) and reset for the next one, so controller-based actions and their group middleware see an empty array. Values are URL-decoded before matching, so an encoded %2F can span segments.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Route::get('/api/{apiVersion}', [ExampleController::class, 'Example']);

class ExampleController extends z_controller {

  public function Example(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $version = $req->getRouteParameter("apiVersion");

    if ($version == "v1") {
        print_r("Correct Version v1");
    } else {
        print_r("Wrong Version");
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Static Arguments
docs.text:
Since version 1.2.0, you can attach static arguments to a route, middleware, or afterMiddleware directly in its definition. Unlike route parameters (which come from the URL), static arguments are fixed values baked into the route — handy for reusing one handler with different configuration.

Pass an array as the third argument:

Route::get('/reports/sales', [ReportController::class, 'render'], ['sales', 2026]);

The values are handed to the action after Request and Response:

public function render(Request $req, Response $res, string $type, int $year) {
    // $type === 'sales', $year === 2026
}

Middlewares and afterMiddlewares accept static arguments the same way; each stage receives only its own list, and a string-keyed array is passed as named arguments:

Route::get('/admin', [AdminController::class, 'index'], ['dashboard'])
    ->middleware([AuthController::class, 'requireRole'], ['admin'])
