    ->afterMiddleware([AuditController::class, 'log'], ['admin-view']);

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Some secrets have to be stored by the application and read back later. A typical case: your application lets each customer connect their own S3 bucket, so the customer enters an access key and a secret key that you have to save in the database and use on every upload. Unlike a password, such a value cannot be hashed, because the application needs the original to talk to S3.

ZubZet encrypts these values at rest with a key from z_config/z_settings.ini. The database only ever holds the encrypted value, so a leaked dump or backup alone does not reveal the customers' credentials. The application decrypts a value right before using it.

docs.title: Setting the key
docs.text:
Encryption needs PHP's OpenSSL extension, which the framework declares as a requirement in its composer.json.

Add an encryption_key of at least 32 bytes to z_config/z_settings.ini. The length is counted in bytes, so a key of plain ASCII characters, like the generated one below, needs 32 characters:

encryption_key = 2f6c1d9e8a7b4c3d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b4c5

Generate a random one, for example with:

php -r 'echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32)), PHP_EOL;'

Wrap a key that contains = or !, such as a base64 one, in double quotes, otherwise z_settings.ini cannot be parsed:

encryption_key = "0WLTPAWOP15mDT/gBrdw/RMbctM7TFVXaPViz3y8AtA="

Keep the key out of the repository and never lose it

Anyone with the key and the database can decrypt every value, so provide it through the environment (CONFIG_ENCRYPTION_KEY with allow_env_config = true, see Installation) instead of committing it. Environment variables only override settings that exist in z_settings.ini, so keep an empty encryption_key = line there; without it CONFIG_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ignored. Values encrypted with a key cannot be decrypted without it: changing or losing the key makes every stored value unreadable.

docs.title: Storing a secret
docs.text:
The global helpers encryptSecret() and decryptSecret() cover the usual case. Encrypt the value before it reaches the model, and decrypt it only where it is used:

// Saving the bucket credentials a customer entered
model("Bucket")->saveCredentials(
    $companyId,
    $req->getPost("accessKey"),
    encryptSecret($req->getPost("secretKey")),
);

// Using them for an upload
$bucket = model("Bucket")->getByCompany($companyId);
$secretKey = decryptSecret($bucket["secret_key"]);

The same methods are available on the ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\Encryption class:

use ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\Encryption;

$encrypted = Encryption::encryptSecret($secretKey);
$secretKey = Encryption::decryptSecret($encrypted);

Every call to encryptSecret() uses a fresh random IV, so encrypting the same value twice gives two different results. Compare decrypted values, never encrypted ones, and do not search or index the encrypted column.

docs.title: Detecting a wrong key
docs.text:
Values are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, which authenticates the ciphertext. Decryption therefore never returns garbage: when the key is wrong, or the stored value was modified, truncated or is not an encrypted value at all, decryptSecret() throws a ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\DecryptionException.

use ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\DecryptionException;

try {
    $secretKey = decryptSecret($bucket["secret_key"]);
} catch(DecryptionException $e) {
    // Wrong encryption_key, or the stored value is damaged
}

A missing encryption_key, or one shorter than 32 bytes, throws a RuntimeException, so a misconfiguration is noticed before anything is stored. Decryption checks the value first: a value that is not in the encrypted format throws the DecryptionException even when the key is missing.

Stack traces

PHP copies the first 15 bytes of every argument into an exception's stack trace, which the framework logs. From PHP 8.2 on, #[\SensitiveParameter] hides the secret and the key there. On PHP 8.0 and 8.1 set zend.exception_ignore_args = On in php.ini.

docs.title: Storage format
docs.text:
An encrypted value is plain text of the form zenc:aes-256-gcm: followed by base64url. Encrypting the 40 character S3 secret key wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY stores this in the database:

zenc:aes-256-gcm:ydhF8rgskJ4UnMKoACkDLA2jApTRBmneKl8pqgVYTBb2QOiipP6hs7KLeNTy1JEWkeW2FWxaulfmY_H4PNn46oyTAh4

zenc marks the value as encrypted, aes-256-gcm names the cipher, and the rest holds the random IV, the authentication tag and the ciphertext. The value only contains A-Z, a-z, 0-9, -, _ and :, so it can be stored in a VARCHAR or TEXT column and passed through URLs, JSON or environment variables without escaping. It is about (length × 4 / 3) + 55 characters long, 108 for the key above; a TEXT column avoids having to size it.

Any string can be encrypted, including binary data. To store several values together, encrypt them as JSON:

$stored = encryptSecret(json_encode(["accessKey" => $accessKey, "secretKey" => $secretKey]));
$credentials = json_decode(decryptSecret($stored), true);

The cipher key is derived from encryption_key with HKDF-SHA256, so the setting may be any sufficiently long random string, in double quotes if it contains = or !.

docs.title: Changing the algorithm
docs.text: Every value names the cipher it was encrypted with, so the framework can switch to a different algorithm without breaking stored values. A cipher is a class implementing ZubZet\Framework\Security\Secrets\Cipher\Cipher, registered under a fixed identifier in Encryption::CIPHERS. A new default only affects values encrypted from then on; existing values keep decrypting with the cipher they name, as long as it stays registered. Only authenticated ciphers qualify, otherwise a wrong key could no longer be detected.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: Texts are translated with symfony/translation. An application keeps its texts in catalogues, one file per domain and locale, and looks them up with __(). The framework ships catalogues of its own for the admin panel and the form texts of Z.js, in English and German.

docs.title: Catalogues
docs.text:
Catalogues live in app/Translations/ and are named {domain}.{locale}.{format}:

app/Translations/
    messages.en.json
    messages.de.json
    messages.de_CH.json
    mails.de.php

The formats are json, php, csv and ini. messages is the default domain. A region gets its own catalogue with an underscore, de_CH, and only needs the keys it spells differently: whatever it leaves out falls back to de.

Nested keys are joined with dots:

{
    "dashboard": {
        "welcome": "Welcome back, {name}!"
    }
}

Modules ship catalogues the same way. An application key beats the same key of a module, and a module key beats the framework's. So redefining a single framework text, say form.error_required, only takes that key in the application catalogue.

docs.title: Translating
docs.text:
__("dashboard.welcome", ["{name}" => $user->email()]);

Syntax: __(string $id, array $parameters = [], ?string $domain = null, ?string $locale = null): string

  • $id: The message id, e.g. dashboard.welcome. An id no catalogue defines is returned unchanged.
  • $parameters: Placeholder values, keyed the way the catalogue spells the placeholder, braces included.
  • $domain: The catalogue domain, messages when omitted.
  • $locale: A locale override, the active locale when omitted.

In a Blade view, {{ __("dashboard.welcome", ["{name}" => $name]) }} escapes the result like any other echo.

An application that already defines a global __(), for example through another library, keeps its own: the framework only declares the helper when no function of that name exists yet.

docs.title: Locale
docs.text:
The active locale is picked in this order:

  1. The locale of the logged in user, z_user.locale_bcp_47, e.g. de.
  2. The best entry of the request's Accept-Language header that a catalogue covers. The entries are tried by their quality, and each is matched against the locales of the loaded catalogues with the RFC 4647 lookup, so de-AT finds de when there is no de_AT catalogue. This takes the PHP intl extension.
  3. The first of fallback_locales.

Translation::locale() returns the active locale. Given a user, Translation::locale($user) puts that user's locale_bcp_47 first, for texts addressed to someone else, such as a mail:

use ZubZet\Framework\Translation\Translation;

$locale = Translation::locale($recipient);
__("email.password_reset.subject", locale: $locale);
Setting Default Meaning fallback_locales en Comma separated locales. The first is the locale of last resort, and a message missing in the active locale is looked up in them in order.

The parsed header is available on its own as well, see $req->acceptLanguage().

docs.title: Frontend Texts
docs.text:
The form texts in Z.Lang, like Submit, Saved! and the validation errors, come from the form.* keys of the catalogue:

Key Text form.submit, form.saved, form.unsaved Submit button and save hints form.choose_file File input form.error_required, form.error_filter, form.error_length, form.error_unique, form.error_exist, form.error_range, form.error_file_to_big Validation errors

<x-zubzet::head/> writes them into Z.Lang for the active locale, so an application translates them like its own texts or overwrites them in the layout after the head component. submit, choose_file, addElement and CEDRemove are read when a form is built, so set them before creating forms. The errors in (also from checked()), integer, date and regex have no form.* key; their English texts stay in Z.Lang and are overwritten there. addElement (a fas fa-plus icon), CEDRemove (✕), saveError (Error while saving), error_password_reset (An error occurred. Did you use the correct email address?) and error_password_mismatch (The password are not the same!) have no catalogue entry and keep these Z.js defaults.

docs.title: Two Factor Authentication
docs.text:
An account can protect its logins with a second factor: a time based one time password (TOTP) from an authenticator app. The framework handles the enrollment, asks for the code during the login and can guard single actions behind a recent check. The codes are generated and verified with spomky-labs/otphp.

Users turn it on and off themselves on their profile page. The methods behind it are documented on the User and Session objects.

docs.title: Enrollment
docs.text:
Turning two factor on takes two steps, so a secret that never reached the authenticator cannot lock anyone out:

  1. $user->startTwoFactor() stores a fresh secret and returns it together with a provisioning URI, the two shapes an authenticator takes it in. The profile page shows the URI as a QR code. The account does not count as protected yet.
  2. $user->confirmTwoFactor($code) turns two factor on once a code from the authenticator matches the stored secret.

Turning it off again takes a current code as well. An admin with admin.user.edit can turn it off for an account on the user page of the Z-Admin panel, which is the way back in for an owner who lost their authenticator.

A code is accepted one 30 second step either side of the current one, so a clock that drifts a little still works.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
When the password of an account with two factor is correct, the login creates no session yet. It answers with a challenge instead:

{"result": "success", "twoFactor": true, "challenge": "zub-..."}

The challenge is redeemed at POST _zubzet/two-factor/login with the fields challenge and code. A correct code creates the session, already stamped with a passed check. A challenge is valid for two_factor_challenge_seconds (defaults to 600) and can be redeemed once. Wrong codes count against the same limit as wrong passwords (maxLoginTriesPerTimespan within maxLoginTriesTimespan).

Z.Presets.Login does all of this on its own: it opens the two factor modal, sends the code and continues like a normal login once it is accepted. The modal markup ships with <x-zubzet::body/>, so every layout that uses the login has to render it (see Layouts).

docs.title: Guarding an Action
docs.text:
A login can live for days. For a sensitive action, $req->requireFreshTwoFactor() demands that the session passed a check recently:

public function action_delete_account(Request $req, Response $res) {
    $req->requireFreshTwoFactor();

    // Only reached with a recent check, or for an account without two factor
}

The check counts as recent within two_factor_freshness_seconds (defaults to 900). A different window can be passed as the first argument. Accounts without two factor always pass, there is nothing to renew. An api key starts without a stamp, so for an account with two factor it does not pass until it renews the check at POST _zubzet/two-factor/refresh.

Without further arguments a stale session is answered with a JSON error carrying twoFactorRenew and the request ends. To answer the client yourself, pass boolResult: true:

if(!$req->requireFreshTwoFactor(boolResult: true)) {
    return $res->error("Two factor required", ["twoFactorRenew" => true]);
}

Z.Request.action(), Z.Request.root() and Z.Forms react to twoFactorRenew on their own: they open the modal, send the code to POST _zubzet/two-factor/refresh, which stamps the current session, and tell the user to try again. Z.Presets.RefreshTwoFactor(onDone) opens the same modal on demand.

Every session may send two_factor_tries (defaults to 5) wrong codes on a renewal or when turning two factor off. After the last one it is signed out. A passed check gives the session all its tries back.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning two_factor_freshness_seconds 900 How long a passed check counts as recent for requireFreshTwoFactor() two_factor_challenge_seconds 600 How long the challenge of a login's two factor step can be redeemed two_factor_tries 5 How many wrong codes a session may send on a renewal or when turning two factor off

The texts of the modal come from Z.Lang in Z.js and can be overwritten in the layout after the layout essentials are embedded: error_two_factor_incomplete, two_factor_renewed and error_password_wrong for the password change.

docs.title: What does a view do?
docs.text:
A view contains the HTML the user should see, along with the CSS, images and JavaScript that page needs. Views do usually not contain a footer, navigation, header or other elements that belong to the overall layout of the page. For this, layouts should be used, as without a layout a view can't be rendered. Read more about layouts here.

Database access and heavy logic should not be used in the view, as that belongs into other parts of the application.

docs.title: The render engine
docs.text:
Since v1.3.0 ZubZet renders views with Katana, a standalone implementation of the Blade templating language. A view is a .blade.php file placed in your project's z_views directory (default app/Views), otherwise it will not be found when called from the render method.

Blade gives you a concise syntax for the things you do in every template: escaping output, loops, conditionals, reusable components and page inheritance. This page covers the parts you reach for day to day, which is most of what you need. For the complete directive reference, the Laravel Blade documentation is the final backstop (Katana implements the common Blade set, see Not available in Katana).

Blade is a superset of PHP

Every .blade.php file is still a PHP file. Plain PHP works verbatim: <?php ... ?>, <?= $x ?> and any function call run exactly as they would in a normal template. Blade directives like @if or @foreach are just shorthand that compiles down to that same PHP, so you never have to give up raw PHP, Blade only adds to it. If you prefer to stay inside Blade's syntax, @php ... @endphp is identical to <?php ... ?>.

docs.title: A first view
docs.text:
A view extends a layout and fills in its content: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <h1>Hello World</h1>
@endsection
@extends($layout) plugs the view into the layout the controller chose. The framework passes the layout name in as $layout, so you never hardcode it. @section("content") is the main body, and the layout decides where it lands. An optional @section("head") adds page specific tags to the document <head> (a stylesheet, a meta tag). Read more about how the two fit together in Layouts.

docs.title: Passing data
docs.text:
Whatever you pass to render is available in the view, both as a top level variable and inside the $opt array: 

// Controller
public function action_index(Request $req, Response $res) {
    return $res->render("employee/index", [
        "name" => "Ada",
    ]);
}

{ View: app/Views/employee/index.blade.php }
@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <h1>Hello {{ $name }}</h1>   { or $opt["name"] }
@endsection
The framework also injects a set of helpers into $opt for every render, overwriting caller-supplied keys of the same name (except title): $opt["root"] (the application's root path, always ending with a slash, so paths are appended without one), $opt["host"], $opt["absRoot"] (host plus root path), $opt["user"], $opt["request"], $opt["response"], $opt["title"] (the pageName setting unless the caller passes one), $opt["generateResourceLink"]($url, $root = true) (prints the root, $url and ?v=<assetVersion>, dev uses time() and an unset setting leaves ?v= empty; $root = false omits the root), $opt["echo"]($val) (prints nl2br(htmlspecialchars($val))). A missing view or layout throws nothing: the bundled 500 view is rendered in layout/min_layout instead. render() echoes the page once and returns nothing; it sets no status or header and does not exit, so that 500 view is sent with the current status. For a view to communicate back to a controller, asynchronous methods must be used (see Backend Requests).

View names and the file extension

The view above is addressed as "employee/index" while the file on disk is app/Views/employee/index.blade.php. The extension is optional and dot notation works too, so "employee/index", "employee/index.blade.php" and "employee.index" all resolve to the same file. A view in your project overrides a framework view of the same name.

docs.title: Echoing data
docs.text:
{{ $name }}              { escaped output, HTML safe }
{!! $trustedHtml !!}     { raw, unescaped output }
{ this is a comment and is not rendered }
{{ $title ?? "Untitled" }}   { any PHP expression works inside the braces }
{{ }} escapes its output the same way the framework's e() helper does, so it is safe for user input by default. Use {!! !!} only for HTML you trust.

Plain PHP echoes are not escaped

Only {{ }} escapes. <?= $x ?> and <?php echo $x; ?> print the value as it is, so wrap values you do not control in e() (<?= e($x) ?>) or use {{ }} instead. This also applies to $opt values such as $opt["title"]. Mail views follow the same rule.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
@if($user->isLoggedIn)
    <span>Welcome back</span>
@elseif($showGuestBanner)
    <span>Hello, guest</span>
@else
    <a href="{{ $opt["root"] }}login">Log in</a>
@endif

@unless($employees)
    <p>No employees yet.</p>
@endunless

@isset($employee)
    <p>{{ $employee["name"] }}</p>
@endisset

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
@foreach($employees as $employee)
    <li>{{ $employee["name"] }}</li>
@endforeach

{ @forelse handles the empty case in a single construct }
@forelse($employees as $employee)
    <li>{{ $employee["name"] }}</li>
@empty
    <li>No employees found.</li>
@endforelse

@for($i = 0; $i < 3; $i++)
    <span>{{ $i }}</span>
@endfor
Inside any loop the $loop variable is available, exposing $loop->index, $loop->iteration, $loop->first, $loop->last, $loop->count and $loop->remaining: 
@foreach($employees as $employee)
    <li class="{{ $loop->first ? 'is-first' : '' }}">
        {{ $loop->iteration }}. {{ $employee["name"] }}
    </li>
@endforeach

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
@switch($status)
    @case("active")
        <span class="badge">Active</span>
        @break
    @case("pending")
        <span class="badge">Pending</span>
        @break
    @default
        <span class="badge">Unknown</span>
@endswitch

docs.title: Raw PHP
docs.text:
Because Blade is a superset of PHP, these two are equivalent. Use whichever reads better: 

<?php $total = array_sum($amounts); ?>

@php
    $total = array_sum($amounts);
@endphp

<p>Total: {{ $total }}</p>

docs.title: Including partials
docs.text:
Split shared markup into its own view and pull it in wherever you need it: 

@include("partials.employee_card", ["employee" => $employee])

@includeIf("partials.banner")             { only if the view exists }
@includeWhen($showTips, "partials.tips")  { only when the condition is true }
An included partial receives the current view's data plus anything you pass in the second argument. Because the render engine resolves names across your project and the framework, a partial can live in either.

docs.title: Auth directives
docs.text:
ZubZet binds Blade's @auth and @guest to its own permission system. With no argument they test whether a user is logged in, and with an argument they test a permission (dotted and wildcard aware). @guest is the negation of @auth: 

@auth
    <a href="{{ $opt["root"] }}account">My account</a>
@endauth

@auth("employee.edit")
    <a href="{{ $opt["root"] }}employee/edit">Edit</a>
@endauth

@guest
    <a href="{{ $opt["root"] }}login">Log in</a>
@endguest
See the Permission System for how permissions are defined.

docs.title: Conditional HTML attributes
docs.text:
Blade has small helpers for the attributes you toggle most often, so you do not have to write the <?php echo $x ? "checked" : "" ?> dance: 

<div @class(["card", "card-active" => $isActive, "card-muted" => !$isActive])>...</div>

<input type="checkbox" @checked($subscribed)>
<option value="de" @selected($lang === "de")>German</option>
<button @disabled($isSaving)>Save</button>

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Components are reusable pieces of UI you drop in with an <x-...> tag. Create one as a .blade.php file under app/Views/components, then use it by file name: 

{ app/Views/components/alert.blade.php }
@props(["type" => "info"])
<div class="alert alert-{{ $type }}">
    {{ $slot }}
</div>

{ in any view }
<x-alert type="warning">
    Your session is about to expire.
</x-alert>
Attributes on the tag (type="warning") become variables inside the component ($type), and the content between the open and close tags is available as {{ $slot }}. @props declares the inputs a component expects and their defaults. A component in your project's components directory overrides a framework component of the same name.

docs.title: Framework components
docs.text:
The framework ships its own components under the zubzet namespace. The two you see in every layout are the page essentials: 

<x-zubzet::head :opt="$opt"/>   { jQuery, Bootstrap, Font Awesome, Z.js, the debug bar head }
<x-zubzet::body :opt="$opt"/>   { the session watcher, the two factor modal and the debug bar body }
The zubzet:: namespace keeps these separate from your own components, so an app component named head never collides with <x-zubzet::head/>. You normally only place them in layouts, see Layouts.

docs.title: Account components
docs.text:
The account components render the pieces of the profile page the admin panel ships under z/profile, so you can place them on a page of your own: 

<x-zubzet::account.change-password/>                        { current, new and repeated password plus the submit button }
<x-zubzet::account.sessions class="list-group-flush"/>      { every login of the current user, each with a rename and a revoke button }
<x-zubzet::account.clear-sessions class="btn btn-danger"/>  { ends every login of the current user }
<x-zubzet::account.api-keys/>                               { the create form, the key list with the same two buttons, and the modal showing a fresh token }
<x-zubzet::account.two-factor/>                             { two factor state, the setup with its QR code, and turning it off }
They read the current user themselves and post to the framework's own _zubzet/profile/* routes (change-password, clear-sessions, revoke-token, rename-token, create-api-key, start-two-factor, confirm-two-factor, disable-two-factor, all post only, with revoke-token and rename-token taking the kind as type), so they need neither data nor a route from you, work on any page, and render nothing for a guest. Framing is yours: none of them brings a card or a heading, <x-zubzet::account.clear-sessions/> brings no classes at all and takes its label from the slot. Every attribute you pass lands on the element the component renders.

The login and the two factor gate ask for the code in a modal. Its markup is <x-zubzet::authentication.two-factor/>, which <x-zubzet::body/> already renders, so it only has to be placed by hand in a layout that leaves out the body essentials.

docs.title: Pushing to the layout with stacks
docs.text:
A view can push markup into a named stack that the layout renders elsewhere, which is handy for adding a page specific script without a dedicated section: 

{ layout }
<head>
    ...
    @stack("scripts")
</head>

{ view }
@push("scripts")
    <script src="<?php $opt["generateResourceLink"]('js/chart.js'); ?>"></script>
@endpush

docs.title: What changed from the previous engine
docs.text:
Before v1.3.0 a view was a PHP file that returned an array of head and body closures, and the layout was chosen from the outside. Now a view is a Blade template that extends a layout. The migrator rewrites this for you (see Migrating to 1.3.0), and the mapping is:

Before (closure array) Now (Blade) return ["body" => function($opt) { ... }] @section("content") ... @endsection return ["head" => function($opt) { ... }] @section("head") ... @endsection the layout picked externally @extends($layout) inside the view copy and pasting shared markup @include and components (<x-...>) hand written foreach loops only @foreach, @forelse, $loop and more (raw PHP still works)

Beyond a cleaner syntax, the engine unlocks real template inheritance, reusable components and shared partials that the old closure format could not express.

docs.title: Not available in Katana
docs.text: Katana implements the common Blade directives, which is everything on this page. A handful of Laravel specific directives are not available, because they depend on parts of Laravel the framework does not use: @csrf, @method, @error, @can / @cannot, @lang / @choice, @vite, @dump / @dd and @inject. Use the framework's own equivalents (for example @auth("permission") in place of @can) or plain PHP.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Katana, the render engine ZubZet uses.
  • Laravel Blade documentation, the full reference for the Blade language.
  • Layouts, how views and layouts fit together.

More examples for views can be found in the framework's src/IncludedComponents/views directory.

docs.title: Migrations in ZubZet
docs.text:
With the release of version 1.1.0, a dedicated Migration system has finally been integrated into ZubZet.

This implementation introduces a comprehensive overhaul of how database changes are handled. Migrations now feature a robust set of tools and improvements designed to make database management more powerful, secure, and intuitive for developers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The migration system is responsible for managing database schema changes in a controlled and repeatable way.

By centralizing these processes, the system provides several key advantages:

  • Enhanced Flexibility: Migrations are more feature-rich, allowing for complex schema evolutions.
  • Streamlined Workflows: A variety of dedicated commands are available to cover every stage of the migration lifecycle.

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text: The following commands are integrated into the ZubZet CLI to manage your database lifecycle efficiently.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
The Import command is used to execute pending migrations and synchronize the database schema.

Syntax: php zubzet db:migrate

This command applies all pending migrations of the project, the framework and modules, sorted together by date, then index, then name, ensuring each migration is executed exactly once. If none is pending, the import prints No pending migrations found. and exits with code 0 without locking. Every other run prints Importing migration: <file> per file and ends with Migration finished at: <time> (took <n>s). By default, the system will attempt to run all available migrations, regardless of the current environment settings, unless specific configurations are applied.

docs.title: Safety and Validation
docs.text:
To prevent database inconsistency, the system performs a pre-execution validation:

  • Integrity Check: If the process detects a skipped migration (a migration file dated on or before the last executed one that was never imported), it lists the affected files as a warning. Because --force is enabled by default, the import then continues and runs them as pending migrations in timeline order. With --force false the import prints Aborting import due to skipped migrations. Use --force to ignore. and is aborted immediately with exit code 1.
  • Lock Check: If the database is locked, the import prints Migrations are currently locked. Aborting import. and exits with code 1, followed by a hint to check for parallel runs, manual migrations or a lock to clear manually.
  • Atomic Validation: This check is performed before any changes are made, ensuring that your database never enters a partial or inconsistent state.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
If a SQL statement of a migration fails, the import prints Error importing <file>: <message> and exits with code 1. The failure is not rolled back and the lock is not released:

  • Migrations imported before the failing one stay applied and are recorded as executed.
  • The failing migration is not recorded. Statements of that file that ran before the error stay applied, as every statement is committed on its own.
  • The database stays locked. Fix the cause, run db:unlock-migration and import again.

If a migration cannot be loaded or built (for example a PHP migration whose class is missing), the import prints Migration import failed: <message>, releases the lock and still exits with code 0. The remaining pending migrations are not run, while those imported before it stay applied. Check the output instead of the exit code in scripts.

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text:
• environments-included | -i {environment_name} Determines which environment-specific migrations are processed during the import.

    Details: The default environment is always included automatically. You can include multiple environments by repeating the flag. Once given, migrations of any other environment are skipped with Skipping migration (not in included environments): <file>. Environment-skipped migrations are not recorded and stay pending; the environment is checked before skip and manual. Usage: db:migrate -i production -i testing

  • environments-excluded | -e {environment_name} Defines specific environments that should be explicitly skipped during the migration process, each with Skipping migration (in excluded environments): <file>.

    Details: Use this to suppress migrations intended only for certain stages (e.g., dev or staging) when updating a production database. It is checked after -i, and default can be excluded too. Usage: db:migrate -e production

  • dry | -d Lists the pending migrations without executing SQL, locking the database or recording them as executed (the Table was locked. and Table was unlocked. lines are still printed).

    Details: Highly recommended for verifying exactly which migration files will be applied before executing them on a live system. Migration files are not loaded in dry mode, so their skip, environment, and manual markers are not evaluated — every pending migration is reported as importable. Usage: db:migrate -d

  • exclude-external Filters the import to only include local project migrations.

    Details: When this flag is active, any migrations provided by the ZubZet Framework and by modules are ignored. Usage: db:migrate --exclude-external

  • force | -f [true|false] Bypasses the integrity check for skipped migrations.

    Details: Enabled by default, so skipped files only produce a warning (listing each file) and the process runs all pending migrations, including the skipped ones, in timeline order. Omitting the option or passing it without a value (-f / --force) keeps it enabled. Pass any value PHP does not read as true (e.g. --force false, --force=false, -f 0 or -f no) to restore the strict behavior, which aborts the import when a skipped migration is detected. Usage: db:migrate --force false

  • enforce-external-timeline Applies the skipped-migration check to external migrations too.

    Details: External migrations (those of the ZubZet Framework and of installed modules) are normally exempt from the skipped-migration check, so a pending one older than the last executed migration still runs without being reported. With this flag they are checked like local project migrations and count as skipped. Whether a skipped migration aborts the import is still decided by --force. Usage: db:migrate --enforce-external-timeline

docs.title: File Convention
docs.text:
Every migration file must be located in the following directory:

app/Database/migrations

Note: The path is relative to the working directory, the folder is created when missing and subfolders are scanned too. Apart from the migrations of the framework and modules, files located outside of this directory are not considered by the migration system. This strict structure ensures that the framework can reliably scan, order, and track the status of your database schema changes.

docs.title: Filename Convention
docs.text:
Each migration filename must follow a defined and consistent format to ensure the correct execution order.

Structure

YYYY-MM-DD_{INDEX}_{NAME}.{php/sql}

Component Description

  • YYYY-MM-DD | Required A valid date in ISO format (year-month-day). This acts as the primary sorting criteria. Impossible dates are not rejected but roll over (2025-02-30 becomes 2025-03-02, which is the date stored).
  • INDEX | Optional A numeric index used to distinguish and order multiple files created on the same day. 0 is not recognized as an index and would become part of the NAME, so start at 1.
  • NAME | Required A descriptive name identifying the purpose of the migration (e.g., create_users_table). It must not be empty.

The year must be 2000 or later; earlier dates abort with a History error. Migrations touching z_* tables must be dated after the bundled one creating them (the bundled timeline starts at 2021-02-04_zubzet.sql).

Examples

2026-03-03_1_CreateUserTable.php
2026-03-03_AddStatusToOrders.sql

Important: If a migration file does not follow this filename convention, the migration system will throw an error and abort the import process immediately to prevent sequence errors.

Identity: A migration is identified by its NAME part only (everything after the date and the optional index, including the file extension). Whether a file is pending or already executed is decided by comparing this name with the z_version table, so the date and index are ignored. A file with the same NAME on another date or with another index therefore counts as already executed and is never run. Use a new NAME for every new migration. Two files with the same filename in different roots or subfolders abort import and sync.

docs.title: Supported Migration File Types
docs.text:
The Migration system supports two different file formats, which can be mixed freely within your project. Other files are ignored.

  • SQL Migration Files (.sql)

    You can use .sql files to define raw SQL statements. All statements found in these files are executed directly against the database in the order they appear. A .sql migration always has the environment default and cannot be marked skip or manual.

    Statements are split at semicolons, the SQL of a PHP migration's run() as well. Semicolons inside string literals ('...', "..."), quoted identifiers (`...`) and comments (--, #, /* ... */) do not end a statement. /*! ... */ and /*+ ... */ are executable and kept. A DELIMITER $$ line changes the terminator as in the mysql client, so triggers and procedures with a BEGIN ... END body work.

  • PHP Migration Files (.php)

    For advanced logic, ZubZet supports PHP-based migrations. These files allow you to use the Schema QueryBuilder and conditional logic.

    Class Structure: Every PHP migration must extend the base Migration class and implement the execute() method.

    use ZubZet\Framework\Database\Migration\Migration;

class Migration_2025_10_01_MigrationEnv extends Migration {

    public function execute(): void {
        $this->setEnvironment("production");

        $table = $this->tableCreate("migration_env");
        $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
        $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
        $table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => true]);
    }
}

    Classname Convention: The migration system automatically resolves the class name based on the filename:

    • The prefix Migration_ is added to the filename (without extension).
    • Any hyphens (-) in the filename are converted to underscores (_).

      Example: 2026-03-03_Test.php becomes class Migration_2026_03_03_Test

    Migration Settings The following settings can be applied inside the execute() method to control migration behavior:

    • Skip Marks the migration as skipped. It will not be imported (Skipping migration (marked to skip): <file>), but it will be marked as executed in the database to prevent it from ever running in future updates.

      Usage: $this->skip();

    • Environment Assigns the migration to a specific environment (e.g., production, testing)

      Usage: $this->setEnvironment(name); Default: default

    • Manual Marks the migration as manual. When the import reaches this file, it will print Migration requires manual execution: <file>, stop with exit code 0 and leave the database locked.

      Note You must manually verify changes, synchronize the state (limit it with --end and --endVersion, otherwise later pending migrations are marked as executed too), and then re-run the import to continue. Usage: $this->setManual(true);

    Schema Operations ZubZet utilizes Doctrine DBAL for its Schema QueryBuilder. You can find the full documentation here.

    • tableCreate(string $name)

      Creates a new table. Returns a Table object to define columns and indexes.

      Example

      SQL: 

      CREATE TABLE `testTable` (
    `id` INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    `name` VARCHAR(255),
    `active` TINYINT(1) DEFAULT 1,
    `created` TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

      Doctrine: 

      $table = $this->tableCreate("testTable");
$table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
$table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
$table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255]);
$table->addColumn("active", "boolean", ["length" => 1, "default" => 1]);
$table->addColumn("created", "timestamp", ["columnDefinition" => "TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"]);

    • tableDrop(string $name)

      Drops an existing table

      Example

      SQL: 

      DROP TABLE `testTable`;

      Doctrine: 

      $this->tableDrop("testTable");

    • tableRename(string $oldName, string $newName)

      Renames a table

      Example

      SQL: 

      ALTER TABLE testTable RENAME TO newName;

      Doctrine: 

      $this->tableRename("testTable", "newName");

    • run(string $sql)

      Adds a raw SQL string at this position of the call order. The table methods only record actions and all SQL is generated afterwards; it then runs split at ; like a SQL file.

      Example 
      $this->run('
    CREATE TABLE `testTable` (
        `id` INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
        `name` VARCHAR(255)
    );
');

    • tableAlter(string $name)

      Modifies an existing table structure (adding/removing columns). Returns a Table object and throws for a table that did not exist before this file ran (the schema is read once per file).

      Example

      SQL: 

      ALTER TABLE z_user ADD description LONGTEXT DEFAULT NULL;

      Doctrine: 

      $this->tableAlter("tableTest")
      ->addColumn("description", "text", ["notnull" => false]);

    More examples can be found here

docs.title: Unlock Migration
docs.text:
The Unlock Migration command is used to manually clear the database lock that is left behind when a migration process crashes or is interrupted.

Warning: Only use this command if you are certain that no migration process is currently running. Using this while a migration is active can lead to database inconsistency.

Syntax: php zubzet db:unlock-migration

This command removes the lock state from the z_migration_lock table (Migration table unlocked.), allowing new migrations to be executed again. It creates missing migration tables first and prints Migration table is not locked. when nothing is locked.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• A migration crashed and the database remains locked
  • A manual migration was interrupted and you've resolved the issue
  • You need to resume the migration process after fixing an error

docs.title: Seed
docs.text:
The Seed command is used to completely recreate the database and then insert seed data, making it ideal for test and development environments where a clean, reproducible database state is required.

Running this command will permanently delete all existing data in your database. It is not reversible. Do not use this on production unless you explicitly intend to wipe the entire system.

The database is dropped and recreated unless you pass --skip-migrations. This needs the DROP and CREATE database privileges, so configure dbusername_elevated and dbpassword_elevated (both must be set, otherwise dbusername and dbpassword are used) when your regular account lacks them.

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text:
By default, db:seed executes all .sql and .php files found recursively in app/Database/seed (created when missing) and in the app/Database/seed folder of each installed module, whatever their names, in byte-wise path order (uppercase before lowercase, 10_ before 2_, so zero-pad numeric prefixes). Seeds are not recorded, so running db:seed --skip-migrations twice inserts the data twice.

  • skip-migrations | -s Skips the migration process and executes only the seeding step.

    Details: With this flag the database is not dropped or recreated, so existing data is kept and the seed files are executed on top of it. Use this flag when you want to populate the database with seed data without re-running migrations. This is useful when your database schema is already up-to-date and you only need to insert or update seed data without resetting the database. Usage: db:seed -s

  • environments-excluded | -e Excludes matching seed folders or files from execution.

    Details: Matches are path-based (relative to app/Database/seed). You can exclude a complete folder (for example Environments) or a single file including its extension (for example Environments/Testing/Chat.sql). Wildcards are not supported. Usage: db:seed -e Environments

  • environments-included | -i Re-includes matching seed folders or files after exclusions are applied; -i alone does not narrow the run, because every file starts selected, and an empty selector matches nothing.

    Details: This allows a two-step flow: first exclude a broad path, then include a specific subset again (folder or single file). Usage: db:seed -e Environments -i Environments/Testing

Execution Workflow When executed, the command performs the following sequence:

  1. Drop: Delete the existing database.
  2. Create: Recreated the database from scratch.
  3. Migrate: Rebuilds the schema (see Import) by running db:migrate in-process with default options; its result is ignored, and since this disables the console's auto exit, the process then always exits with 0, even when a seed file failed
  4. Populate: Executes all seed files found in app/Database/seed; a failing file prints Error executing seed file <path>: <message> and stops the run

With --skip-migrations, steps 1 to 3 are skipped and only the seed files run.

docs.title: Supported Seed File Types
docs.text:
The Seed system supports two different file formats, which can be mixed freely within your project.

  • SQL Seed Files (.sql)

    You can use .sql files to define raw SQL statements. The content of each file is buffered behind a -- SEED FILE: <path> marker and run through executeMultiQuery() (no ; splitting) before the next PHP seed file and at the end, so an SQL error is reported against that PHP file, and one in the final run is not caught.

  • PHP Seed Files (.php)

    For complex data generation or dynamic logic, ZubZet supports PHP-based seed files. These files must extend the base Seed class.

    Class Structure: Each seed class must implement a run() method where all database operations are defined. 

    use ZubZet\Framework\Database\Migration\Seed;

class TestSeed extends Seed {

    public function run() {
        $this->insert("model_test_insert", [
            "value" => "test value"
        ]);
    }
}

    Classname Convention:

    • The class name must equal the file name (without .php) exactly, including its case. The file is loaded with require_once and the class is instantiated by that name, so it must live in the global namespace (no namespace declaration); a duplicate class name across files is a fatal redeclare.
    • Hyphens (-) in the file name are not converted. Since they are not valid in class names, use file names that are valid PHP class names, like TestSeed.php.

      Example: TestSeed.php ➔ class TestSeed extends Seed

    QueryBuilder Usage: PHP seed files utilize CakePHP\Database for building queries through the CanBuildQuery trait (dbSelect, dbInsert, dbUpdate, dbDelete, getQueryBuilder).

    For more detailed information about the Query Builder, see: QueryBuilder

    Registering Queries To ensure reliable execution, every query must be explicitly registered within the system.

    • Automatic Registration: $this->insert($table, array $data) builds a single dbInsert() query from one row of column => value pairs and registers it with addQuery(). It returns nothing and has no $types parameter and no multi-row form. No further action is needed. 

      $this->insert("model_test_insert", ["value" => "test value"]);

      The query is only queued. It runs after run() has finished, in the order it was added, via db()->execQuery() as a prepared statement with bound values.

    • Manual Registration: For custom queries built via the QueryBuilder, you must use: 

      $this->addQuery($query);

      Queries that are not added via addQuery() will not be executed. This includes queries created with $this->dbInsert(...), $this->dbUpdate(...) or $this->dbDelete(...), which only build the query and do not register it. For several rows, call insert() once per row.

    If you need direct access to the underlying connection (\Cake\Database\Connection), use: 

    $connection = $this->getQueryBuilder();

    addQuery() accepts a Cake\Database\Query and appends it to the public $queries array.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
The Sync command marks migrations as executed in the migration history without actually applying any changes to the database schema.

  • Manual Adjustments: You already manually updated the database and need to tell the system "this is done."

  • Aligning History: You are setting up an existing database with a new codebase and want to skip old migrations that are already present in the schema.

  • Conflict Resolution: Fixing a broken migration state after manual intervention.

skip and manual markers are ignored, there is no skipped-migration detection, and outside --dry the command always releases the migration lock afterwards, without checking it first, so it also clears a stuck lock. Files outside the start/end range print Skipping migration (before start date|before start version|after end date|after end version): <file>; with nothing pending it prints No pending migrations to synchronized found. and still exits 0. A failure while synchronising prints Synchronization failed: <message> and exits 1.

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text:
• start {start_date} Specifies the start date from which migrations should be synced.

    Usage: db:sync --start 2026-03-01 Format: YYYY-MM-DD, compared strictly, so 2005-1-1 is rejected with exit code 1.

  • startVersion {index} Specifies the numeric index from which the sync should start.

    Note: Requires the --start option to bet set (otherwise exit code 1); it is only compared for files dated exactly on the start date. Usage: db:sync --start 2025-12-01 --startVersion 2

  • end {end_date} Specifies the end date up to which migrations should be synced.

    Usage: db:sync --end 2026-03-01 Format: YYYY-MM-DD, compared strictly like --start.

  • endVersion {index} Specifies the numeric index up to which the sync should run.

    Note: Requires the --end option to bet set (otherwise exit code 1); it is only compared for files dated exactly on the end date. Usage: db:sync --end 2025-12-01 --endVersion 2

  • environments-included | i {environment_name} Determines which environment-specific migrations are processed.

    Details: The default environment is always included automatically. Usage: db:sync -i production -i testing

  • environments-excluded | e {environment_name} Defines which environments should be explicitly ignored during the sync.

    Usage: db:sync -e staging

  • dry | d Simulates the sync process. It shows which files would be marked as executed without updating the database history.

    Details: Date and version filters still apply, but migration files are not loaded, so environment markers are not evaluated. Usage: db:sync -d

  • include-external Includes migrations provided by the ZubZet Framework in the sync process.

    Usage: db:sync --include-external

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
The Status command provides a quick health check of the database lock state.

To prevent race conditions, broken schemas, and inconsistent data, ZubZet applies a strict database lock during every migration process. This ensures that no two migration instances can run in parallel.

docs.title: Lock States
docs.text:
The command prints Migration Lock Status: LOCKED or Migration Lock Status: UNLOCKED and reports one of the following states:

  • LOCKED (exit code 1) – A migration is currently in progress, or a previous migration was interrupted (e.g., a Manual Migration), leaving the database protected against concurrent execution.
  • UNLOCKED (exit code 0) – The database is clear (also when z_migration_lock does not exist yet; the command creates no tables). No migration is currently active, and new migrations can be started safely.

The exit code makes the command usable as a check in scripts, e.g. db:status && db:migrate.

Warning

If the status remains LOCKED even though no migration is running, it usually means a Manual Migration was reached or a process crashed.

To resolve this, you must:

  1. Fix the underlying issue (manually adjust the database schema if needed).
  2. Clear the migration lock using the unlock command: 
    db:unlock-migration
  3. Resume the migration process: 
    db:migrate

Usage 

db:status

docs.title: Production Deployment
docs.text:
When deploying to a Production environment, ensuring that the migration history is perfectly aligned with the actual database schema is critical before applying new changes.

The standard workflow for a safe production update follows these two essential steps:

docs.title: 1. Synchronize (db:sync)
docs.text:
First, align the internal migration history. This ensures that any schema states already present in the database are correctly marked as "executed," preventing the system from attempting to re-run legacy migrations.

Usage: db:sync

docs.title: 2. Migrate (db:migrate)
docs.text:
Once the history is synchronized, execute the pending migrations to bring the production database up to the latest version.

Usage: db:migrate

Warning

To avoid unexpected downtime, always perform a Dry-Run first to preview exactly which files will be affected.

docs.title: Internal Tables
docs.text: To support the migration system, ZubZet automatically creates two internal database tables. These tables are required for locking and version tracking and are managed fully by the framework.

docs.title: z_migration_lock
docs.text:
This table is used to track whether the database is currently locked for migrations.

It stores:

  • Whether a migration lock is active (is_locked)
  • The timestamp of when the lock was created (locked_at, informational)

This lock ensures that only one migration process can run at a time, preventing parallel execution and inconsistent states. The check and the insert are separate statements and a lock never expires, so only db:unlock-migration clears a stale one.

docs.title: z_version
docs.text:
This table is used to track executed migrations.

It stores:

  • The basename (migration_name), date (migration_date), index (migration_version, 0 when the filename has none), sha1 file hash (file_hash) and created time of each executed migration (the hash is never compared, so edits to an executed migration go unnoticed; the active column is never read)

By keeping a record of executed migrations, ZubZet ensures that migrations are never executed more than once.

Both tables are created automatically when the migration system is used and require no manual setup. They are an essential part of ensuring safe, repeatable, and reliable database migrations in ZubZet.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Table
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableCreate("TestTable");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => true]);
}

This would result in the following MySQL query:

CREATE TABLE TestTable (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB

docs.title: Example 2: Table with Timestamps and Defaults
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableCreate("TestTable");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => true]);
    $table->addColumn("active", "boolean", ["default" => true]);
    $table->addColumn("created", "datetime", [
        "default" => "CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"
    ]);
    $table->addColumn("updated", "datetime", [
        "default" => "CURRENT_TIMESTAMP",
        "columnDefinition" => "TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"
    ]);
}

This would result in the following MySQL query:

CREATE TABLE TestTable (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    active TINYINT(1) DEFAULT 1 NOT NULL,
    created DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    updated TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB

docs.title: Example 3: Table with Foreign Key Reference
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableCreate("orders");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("userId", "integer", ["notnull" => true]);
    $table->addColumn("total", "decimal", ["precision" => 10, "scale" => 2]);
    $table->addColumn("status", "string", ["length" => 50, "default" => "pending"]);
    $table->addColumn("created", "datetime", ["default" => "CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"]);
    $table->addIndex(["userId"], "idx_orders_user");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    userId INT NOT NULL,
    total NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending' NOT NULL,
    created DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    INDEX idx_orders_user (userId),
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB

docs.title: Example 4: Table with Unique Constraint
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableCreate("users");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("email", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => false]);
    $table->addColumn("username", "string", ["length" => 100, "notnull" => true]);
    $table->addUniqueIndex(["email"], "uq_users_email");
    $table->addUniqueIndex(["username"], "uq_users_username");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

CREATE TABLE users (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(255) DEFAULT NULL,
    username VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email (email),
    UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_username (username),
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB

docs.title: Example 1: Add a Column
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->tableAlter("users")
        ->addColumn("description", "text", ["notnull" => false]);
}

This would result in the following MySQL query:

ALTER TABLE z_user ADD description LONGTEXT DEFAULT NULL

docs.title: Example 2: Add Multiple Columns
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableAlter("users");
    $table->addColumn("phone", "string", ["length" => 20, "notnull" => false]);
    $table->addColumn("address", "text", ["notnull" => false]);
    $table->addColumn("birthdate", "date", ["notnull" => false]);
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

ALTER TABLE z_user
    ADD phone VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT NULL,
    ADD address LONGTEXT DEFAULT NULL,
    ADD birthdate DATE DEFAULT NULL

docs.title: Example 3: Add Column with Index
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableAlter("orders");
    $table->addColumn("status", "string", ["length" => 50, "default" => "pending"]);
    $table->addIndex(["status"], "idx_orders_status");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

ALTER TABLE orders ADD status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending' NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON z_user (status)

docs.title: Example: Rename a Table
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->tableRename("old_table_name", "new_table_name");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query:

ALTER TABLE old_table_name RENAME TO new_table_name

docs.title: Example: Drop a Table
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->tableDrop("obsolete_table");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query:

DROP TABLE obsolete_table

docs.title: Example 1: Insert Data
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $table = $this->tableCreate("categories");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => true]);

    $this->run("
        INSERT INTO categories (name) VALUES
        ('Electronics'),
        ('Clothing'),
        ('Books');
    ");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

CREATE TABLE categories (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL, 
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO categories (name) VALUES
    ('Electronics'),
    ('Clothing'),
    ('Books');

docs.title: Example 2: Complex SQL Operations
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->run("
        ALTER TABLE users
        ADD COLUMN active TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 AFTER email,
        MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR(255) NULL,
        ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_user_email (email);
    ");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

ALTER TABLE users
    ADD COLUMN active TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 AFTER email,
    MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR(255) NULL,
    ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_user_email (email);

docs.title: Example: Full Migration with Multiple Operations
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    // Create a new table
    $table = $this->tableCreate("products");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("name", "string", ["length" => 255, "notnull" => true]);
    $table->addColumn("price", "decimal", ["precision" => 10, "scale" => 2]);
    $table->addColumn("active", "boolean", ["default" => true]);
    $table->addColumn("created", "datetime", ["default" => "CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"]);

    // Alter an existing table
    $this->tableAlter("orders")
        ->addColumn("product_id", "integer", ["notnull" => false]);

    // Rename a table
    $this->tableRename("old_categories", "categories");

    // Drop an obsolete table
    $this->tableDrop("temp_data");

    // Insert seed data
    $this->run("
        INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES
        ('Product A', 19.99),
        ('Product B', 29.99);
    ");
}

This would result in the following MySQL query: 

CREATE TABLE products (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    price NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    active TINYINT(1) DEFAULT 1 NOT NULL,
    created DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE `utf8_unicode_ci` ENGINE = InnoDB;

ALTER TABLE z_user ADD product_id INT DEFAULT NULL;

ALTER TABLE old_categories RENAME TO categories;

DROP TABLE temp_data;

INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES
    ('Product A', 19.99),
    ('Product B', 29.99);

docs.title: Example 1: Environment-Specific Migration
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->setEnvironment("production");

    $table = $this->tableCreate("production_logs");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
    $table->addColumn("message", "text");
    $table->addColumn("created", "datetime", ["default" => "CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"]);
}

docs.title: Example 2: Skip Migration
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->skip();

    // This migration will be marked as executed but not actually run
    $table = $this->tableCreate("skipped_table");
    $table->addColumn("id", "integer", ["autoincrement" => true]);
    $table->setPrimaryKey(["id"]);
}

docs.title: Example 3: Manual Migration
docs.text:
public function execute(): void {
    $this->setManual(true);

    // Import will stop here and wait for manual verification
    $this->run("
        UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1;
    ");
}

docs.title: Column Types Reference
docs.text:
Doctrine DBAL supports the following common column types:

Type Description Options integer Integer values autoincrement, unsigned smallint Small integer autoincrement, unsigned bigint Large integer autoincrement, unsigned string VARCHAR length (required) text LONGTEXT - boolean TINYINT(1) default decimal DECIMAL precision, scale float FLOAT precision datetime DATETIME default timestamp TIMESTAMP default date DATE default time TIME default blob BLOB - json JSON -

docs.title: Common Column Options
docs.text:
Option Description Example notnull NOT NULL constraint ["notnull" => true] default Default value ["default" => "value"] length String length ["length" => 255] autoincrement Auto increment ["autoincrement" => true] unsigned Unsigned integer ["unsigned" => true] precision Decimal precision ["precision" => 10] scale Decimal scale ["scale" => 2] columnDefinition Raw SQL definition ["columnDefinition" => "..."]

For more details, see the Doctrine DBAL Documentation.

docs.title: Query Builder in ZubZet
docs.text:
Since version 1.0.0, ZubZet includes a built-in Query Builder. It is based on CakePHP\Database.

The Query Builder allows you to build SQL queries programmatically in a safe and structured way, directly from your models.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Inside a model or a PHP seed class (controllers do not have them), you can now use helper methods like dbSelect, dbUpdate, dbDelete, and dbInsert, provided by the trait CanBuildQuery. These methods internally delegate to the CakePHP Query Builder.

Example methods inside a model:

public function dbSelect($fields = [], $table = [], array $types = []) {
    return $this->getQueryBuilder()->selectQuery($fields, $table, $types);
}

public function dbUpdate($table = null, array $values = [], array $conditions = [], array $types = []) {
    return $this->getQueryBuilder()->updateQuery($table, $values, $conditions, $types);
}

public function dbDelete(?string $table = null, array $conditions = [], array $types = []) {
    return $this->getQueryBuilder()->deleteQuery($table, $conditions, $types);
}

public function dbInsert(?string $table = null, array $values = [], array $types = []) {
    return $this->getQueryBuilder()->insertQuery($table, $values, $types);
}

public function getQueryBuilder() {
    return db()->queryBuilderConnection;
}

docs.title: Executing Queries
docs.text:
Once you have built a query, you can execute it with the exec method (which ignores $types and $params for a Query) or db()->execQuery($query); both return the Connection, so the result helpers can follow directly: 

$query = $this->dbSelect(...);

$this->exec($query);

Values bind as strings unless typed: integer, biginteger and smallinteger bind as integers, float and decimal as doubles, and where(fn($exp) => $exp->eq($field, $value, "integer")) pins the type. Multi-row inserts use new InsertQuery($this->getQueryBuilder()) with into(), insert() and repeated values().

docs.title: Select Example
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users') // Build a SELECT query on table "users", fetching only the columns "id" and "name"
              ->where(['id' => 42]); // Add a WHERE condition: only rows where "id" equals 42

$result = $this->exec($query); // Execute the query and return the result

This will execute a query equivalent to:

SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = 42;

docs.title: Insert Example
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbInsert('users', [ // Build an INSERT query for the "users" table
    'name'  => 'John Doe', // Set column "name" to "John Doe"
    'email' => 'john@example.com' // Set column "email" to "john@example.com"
]);

$this->exec($query); // Execute the query to insert the new record

Equivalent SQL:

INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('John Doe', 'john@example.com');

docs.title: Update Example
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbUpdate('users', [ // Build an UPDATE query on the "users" table
    'email' => 'new@example.com' // Set column "email" to "new@example.com"
])->where(['id' => 42]); // Add WHERE condition: only update the row where "id" equals 42

$this->exec($query); // Execute the query to apply the update

Equivalent SQL:

UPDATE users SET email = 'new@example.com' WHERE id = 42;

docs.title: Delete Example
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbDelete("users") // Build a DELETE query on the "users" table
            ->where(["id" => 42]); // Add WHERE condition: only delete the row where "id" equals 42

$this->exec($query); // Execute the query to remove the record

Equivalent SQL:

DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42;

docs.title: Untrusted identifiers
docs.text: Values are bound as prepared statement parameters, but table and column names are inserted into the SQL as written. ZubZet does not enable identifier quoting (quoteIdentifiers) on the query builder connection, so an identifier is never escaped or validated. Table and column names must never come from user input.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• All query methods (select, insert, update, delete) return a CakePHP SelectQuery, InsertQuery, UpdateQuery or DeleteQuery.
  • Queries are executed via $this->exec($query).

For more examples, see the Examples page.

docs.title: More Information
docs.text:
The Query Builder in ZubZet is built on top of CakePHP\Database. You can use all features provided by CakePHP’s query builder.

Important:

  • There is no direct database connection handled by CakePHP itself inside ZubZet.
  • This means that simply creating a query with $this->getQueryBuilder() will not execute it.

  • You must explicitly run the query via:

    $this->exec($query);

  • The CakePHP Query Builder instance (one Cake\Database\Connection, shared by all models) can always be accessed with:

    $this->getQueryBuilder();

This ensures that all queries you build are properly executed through ZubZet’s database layer.

docs.title: Query Builder Examples
docs.text: This page provides detailed examples for building queries with the CakePHP Query Builder in ZubZet.

docs.title: Simple Equality
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name', 'email'], 'users')
              ->where(['status' => 'active']);

SELECT id, name, email
FROM users
WHERE status = 'active'

docs.title: Multiple Conditions (AND)
docs.text:
By default, multiple conditions in where() are combined with AND:

$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->where([
                  'status' => 'active',
                  'role' => 'admin'
              ]);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE status = 'active' 
AND role = 'admin'

docs.title: Chained WHERE (AND)
docs.text:
You can also chain multiple where() calls:

$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->where(['status' => 'active'])
              ->where(['role' => 'admin']);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE status = 'active'
AND role = 'admin'

docs.title: Using OR
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->where([
                  'OR' => [
                      'role' => 'admin',
                      'id' => 1
                  ]
              ]);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE (
    role = 'admin' OR
    id = 1
)

docs.title: Combined AND and OR
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->where([
                  'status' => 'active',
                  'OR' => [
                      'role' => 'admin',
                      'id' => 1
                  ]
              ]);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE (
    status = 'active' AND (
        role = 'admin' OR
        id = 1
        )
    )

docs.title: WHERE IN List
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->whereInList('id', [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE id in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

docs.title: WHERE NOT IN List
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name'], 'users')
              ->whereNotInList('id', [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);

SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE id not in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

docs.title: Greater Than (>)
docs.text:
$query = $this->dbSelect(['id', 'name', 'age'], 'users')
              ->where(['age >' => 18]);

SELECT id, name, age
FROM users
WHERE age > 18

docs.title: Complex Query Example
docs.text:
Here's a complete example combining multiple features:

$query = $this->dbSelect([
                  'u.id',
                  'u.name',
                  'u.email',
                  'order_count' => 'COUNT(o.id)',
                  'total_spent' => 'SUM(o.total)'
              ], ['u' => 'users'])
              ->leftJoin(['o' => 'orders'], ['u.id = o.user_id'])
              ->where([
                  'u.status' => 'active',
                  'u.created >=' => '2025-01-01',
                  'o.status IN' => ['completed', 'shipped']
              ])
              ->group(['u.id', 'u.name', 'u.email'])
              ->having(['COUNT(o.id) >=' => 3])
              ->orderDesc('total_spent')
              ->limit(10);

$result = $this->exec($query);

SELECT
    u.id,
    u.name,
    u.email,
    COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
    SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o
ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE (
    u.status = 'active' AND
    u.created >= '2025-01-01' AND
    o.status in ('completed','shipped')
)
GROUP BY u.id, u.name, u.email
HAVING COUNT(o.id) >= 3
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10

docs.title: Auto form validation and database updates
docs.text: This framework has the ability to create automatic generated forms with user feedback. These forms can be validated automatically on the server and if errors occur the feedback is sent back to the user. If no errors occur the data can be used to update a database table.

docs.title: Front-end
docs.text:
To create the form on the frontend, use Z.js, the framework's bundled frontend script. It is served through the asset proxy and included automatically by the framework's default head component, so the global Z object is available in every properly set up layout. An example form can be created with this code: 

var form = Z.Forms.create({dom: "form"});

var inputFirstName = form.createField({
    name: "first_name",
    type: "text",
    text: "First name",
    required: true
});

var inputLastName = form.createField({
    name: "last_name",
    type: "text",
    text: "Last name",
    required: true
});

docs.title: Creating a form
docs.text:
The form is created with Z.Forms.create. The dom attribute takes the id of an html element in which the form in embedded. For this to work the element needs to be loaded so this script should not execute directly at the start of the page. If the element will spawns later the form can be added to it with the dom attribute element.appendChild(form.dom);.

Further options of Z.Forms.create:

  • doReload: reloads the page after a successful submit, default false (true when Z.Forms.create() gets no options object at all), forced to true once a CED is added.
  • saveHook(response): called with the parsed response after a success only. formErrorHook(response) is called after the fields of a formErrors response were marked.
  • hidehints: suppresses the sticky banner above the form that shows the unsaved, saved and error hints. form.hint(alertClass, content) shows it manually with a Bootstrap alert class and HTML content, form.unhint() hides it.
  • sendOnSubmitClick: default true; with false the submit button no longer calls form.send(), so you must call it yourself.
  • customEndpoint: URL the submit button posts to instead of the current action. form.send(customUrl) takes the URL directly.

form.send() clears the field errors and posts the form data as multipart/form-data (a call is ignored while a request runs or within 300 ms of the previous one; form.debug = true logs the FormData and the response to the console) and handles the JSON result of the response: success runs saveHook, reloads if doReload is set and shows the saved hint, formErrors marks the fields (names without a field are ignored, a field with several errors shows the last one) and runs formErrorHook, error (or a response that is not valid JSON) shows the generic Z.Lang.saveError hint, never the message sent by $res->error().

form.createActionButton(text, style, action) adds a button after the submit button and returns it. style has to be a single class such as btn-secondary.

docs.title: Creating fields
docs.text: Attribute Description name Corresponds to the name in the post request. type The input type. Any valid HTML standard type is accepted, as well as textarea, select, multi-select, autocomplete, button and hidden. Without a type the input gets an invalid type attribute. This attribute does not affect server-side value parsing. text Label HTML, default a non-breaking space. value Initial value, used over default when truthy (0 or an empty string falls back to it), and the label of a button (full width, class from style, default btn-primary). For multi-select, pass an array (e.g. ["1","4"]) or <?= json_encode([...]) ?>. food Required for select and multi-select types. It defines the options available and is formatted as an array: [{value: 1, text: "one"}, {value: 2, text: "two"}, ...], where value falls back to text and an entry with type: "optgroup" starts a group. This array can be generated via $controller->makeFood. required Marks the field as required in the UI only: a red asterisk and the class input-required are added to the label, and a select drops its empty --- option. No client-side validation is performed and the browser's required attribute is not set. Enforce it on the server with ->required(). width Defines the width of the form element in 1/12 units of the total width (col-md-N, default 12, 0 for hidden); a field that no longer fits into 12 units starts a new row. Effective on medium or larger devices. On small devices, the width is always 100%. attributes Allows adding additional attributes for the generated input element (e.g., min, max for number inputs), set after the defaults so they can override them. Example usage: attributes: {'min': 1, 'max': 10}. prepend Adds HTML in an input-group-prepend before the input field. This can be used for prefixes, labels, or other indicators. Example usage: prepend: 'Prefix' creates an input field with a preceding text or symbol. hint Muted help text as HTML under the input. placeholder Input placeholder; for multi-select the text of the first option, for file the text before a file is chosen is customFileInputText (default Z.Lang.choose_file). default Value restored by field.reset(), also the initial value when value is empty. autofill When false (default) every input gets autocomplete="new-password" to suppress browser autofill. disabled Starts the field disabled. The input is greyed out and cannot be edited until field.enable() is called. hidden Starts the field hidden. It is left out of the layout until field.show() is called. The field still exists and submits its value.

docs.title: Simple input example
docs.text:
var inputAmount = form.createField({
    name: "amount",
    type: "number",
    attributes: {
        min: 0,
        max: 100,
        step: 10
    }
});

docs.title: Manipulating fields
docs.text:
The return value if form.createField is the created field. It has the attributes input (the dom input element), label and dom (the wrapper around label, input and error text). It also has on which is an alias for addEventListener on the input dom element. The value can be read and set with value: a multi-select returns a copy of its array, a checkbox a boolean, and the setter of a file field only changes the label text. field.markInvalid(error) and field.markValid() show or clear the Z.Lang.error_<type> message and the is-invalid class, and markInvalid scrolls the field into view.

form.addCustomHTML(). With this you can add Html inside of the form, in its own div; the next field starts a new row.

docs.title: Escaping untrusted strings
docs.text:
Several strings are inserted into the page as HTML (innerHTML), not as plain text. Escape anything that is not hard-coded, such as user input or database content, before you pass it in, otherwise it is an XSS hole. In PHP use htmlspecialchars() or e() before dumping the value into the script.

Inserted as HTML, escape these:

  • text (the label) and hint of a field
  • prepend
  • the value of a button field and the text of createActionButton()
  • form.hint(alertClass, content)
  • form.addCustomHTML(html)
