docs.title: Shop Application
docs.text:
In the last guide, we explored how to enhance your website's security by implementing roles and permissions to restrict user access effectively.

In this guide, we’ll focus on handling backend requests in your application. Using a Shop example, we will demonstrate how to implement functionality for removing data from the database, triggered by a delete button on the page. This will provide you with the foundation for managing interactive actions securely and efficiently.

docs.title: Resources
Setting up our Application
docs.text: To start working with permissions, we first need the basic structure of our application. This guide provides pre-built files in the "Resources" section, including templates for controllers, models, and views. Using these resources ensures an organized setup and allows us to focus on implementing functionality and backend requests efficiently.

docs.title: How Do Backend Requests work?
docs.text: The framework includes a robust and fully implemented request system. Backend requests enable communication between the view and the controller. When an action is triggered in the view, such as clicking a delete button, a request is sent to the controller. The controller processes this request, performs the necessary operations—such as deleting an item from the database—and sends a response back to the view. This ensures that user actions on the front end dynamically and securely interact with the back-end logic and data.

docs.title: How to send a Backend Request?
docs.text:
To send a backend request, we need to update our view to handle user actions. Here, we’ll make the delete button functional by adding an event listener to manage button clicks.

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Name</th>
                <th>Price</th>
                <th>Delete</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <?php foreach ($opt["products"] as $product) { ?>
                <tr>
                    <td><?= $product["name"] ?></td>
                    <td><?= $product["price"] ?></td>
                    <td>
                        <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
                            <button class="delete-product">Delete</button>
                        <?php } else { ?>
                            <i>No Permissions</i>
                        <?php } ?>
                    </td>
                </tr>
            <?php } ?>
        </tbody>
    </table>
@endsection

To send a backend request, we need to update our view to handle user actions. Here, we’ll make the delete button functional by adding an event listener to manage button clicks.

What are classes?

Classes are identifiers used in HTML elements to apply styles with CSS or add behavior with JavaScript. They can be shared across multiple elements for consistency.

Additionally, there are IDs, which are unique identifiers meant to target a single element on a page.

First, assign a class to the delete button so it can be uniquely identified: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Name</th>
                <th>Price</th>
                <th>Delete</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <?php foreach ($opt["products"] as $product) { ?>
                <tr>
                    <td><?= $product["name"] ?></td>
                    <td><?= $product["price"] ?></td>
                    <td>
                        <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
                            <button class="delete-product">Delete</button>
                        <?php } else { ?>
                            <i>No Permissions</i>
                        <?php } ?>
                    </td>
                </tr>
            <?php } ?>
        </tbody>
    </table>
@endsection
The class="delete-product" ensures that only these buttons are targeted for the delete functionality.

What is jQuery?

jQuery is a fast, small, and feature-rich JavaScript library designed to simplify HTML document traversal, event handling, animations, and AJAX interactions. It provides an easy-to-use API that works across a multitude of browsers, making it a popular choice for enhancing web development with minimal code.

More information can be found on the official jQuery website.

Next, use jQuery to add an event listener for the buttons with the delete-product class. To enhance security, we ensure the script is only displayed to users who have the appropriate permissions. This prevents unauthorized users from accessing or triggering backend functionality.

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Name</th>
                <th>Price</th>
                <th>Delete</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <?php foreach ($opt["products"] as $product) { ?>
                <tr>
                    <td><?= $product["name"] ?></td>
                    <td><?= $product["price"] ?></td>
                    <td>
                        <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
                            <button class="delete-product">Delete</button>
                        <?php } else { ?>
                            <i>No Permissions</i>
                        <?php } ?>
                    </td>
                </tr>
            <?php } ?>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
        <script>
            $(".delete-product").click(function() {

            });
        </script>
    <?php } ?>
@endsection
What do EventListeners do?

EventListeners are JavaScript functions that wait for a specific event, such as a click or a keypress, to occur on an element. When the event happens, the listener executes a predefined action or function, enabling dynamic interactions on a webpage.

This script attaches a click() event listener to all elements with the delete-product class, setting up the functionality needed to handle the delete action dynamically.

Now we need to get our product-identifier ('id'). For that we need to save the id`s of the products inside the product-html-element. We are doing it like that: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Name</th>
                <th>Price</th>
                <th>Delete</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <?php foreach ($opt["products"] as $product) { ?>
                <tr>
                    <td><?= $product["name"] ?></td>
                    <td><?= $product["price"] ?></td>
                    <td>
                        <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
                            <button class="delete-product" data-id="<?= $product['id'] ?>">Delete</button>
                        <?php } else { ?>
                            <i>No Permissions</i>
                        <?php } ?>
                    </td>
                </tr>
            <?php } ?>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
        <script>
            $(".delete-product").click(function() {
                var id = $(this).data("id");
            });
        </script>
    <?php } ?>
@endsection

With the data-id attribute, we can embed custom values into our HTML elements. For example, using var id = $(this).data("id");, we can retrieve the id of the selected product and store it in a variable.

Next, we send the product ID to the backend using the Z.Request.action method: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Name</th>
                <th>Price</th>
                <th>Delete</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <?php foreach ($opt["products"] as $product) { ?>
                <tr>
                    <td><?= $product["name"] ?></td>
                    <td><?= $product["price"] ?></td>
                    <td>
                        <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
                            <button class="delete-product" data-id="<?= $product['id'] ?>">Delete</button>
                        <?php } else { ?>
                            <i>No Permissions</i>
                        <?php } ?>
                    </td>
                </tr>
            <?php } ?>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <?php if($opt["user"]->checkPermission("library.edit")) { ?>
        <script>
            $(".delete-product").click(function() {
                var id = $(this).data("id");

                Z.Request.action('delete-product', {
                    productId: id
                }, (res) => {
                    if(res.result == 'success') {
                        location.reload();
                        return;
                    }
                    alert("An error occurred");
                });
            });
        </script>
    <?php } ?>
@endsection
The Z.Request.action method sends the request to the backend, with delete-product as the identifier to specify the action to perform. The product ID is passed as data to identify the item to delete. The response is then handled by checking if the result is success. If so, the page reloads to update the table; otherwise, an error message is displayed.

docs.title: How to handle a Request in the Backend?
docs.text:
Backend Requests sended with the Z.Request.action method, will always land on the Action, we are currently in with the view. To handle now the request we need to check if the action in our controller is set to our identifier of our request (delete-product). We are doing it like this: 

<?php
    class ShopController extends z_controller {

        public function action_list(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("shop.view");

            if ($req->isAction("delete-product")) {

            }

            $products = $req->getModel("Shop")->getProducts();

            return $res->render("shop/shopping_cart", [
                "products" => $products
            ]);
        }
    }
?>
To handle the backend request, we first check if the request matches the delete-product identifier using $req->isAction("delete-product"). This ensures we are processing the correct action.

Next, we secure the request and retrieve the productId sent from the frontend: 

<?php
    class ShopController extends z_controller {

        public function action_list(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("shop.view");

            if ($req->isAction("delete-product")) {
                $req->checkPermission("shop.delete");
                $productId = $req->getPost("productId");

            }

            $products = $req->getModel("Shop")->getProducts();

            return $res->render("shop/shopping_cart", [
                "products" => $products
            ]);
        }
    }
?>
Here, $productId = $req->getPost("productId") retrieves the product ID from the request data. We then delete the product by calling the deleteProduct method in the ShopModel and passing the productId as a parameter:

<?php
    class ShopController extends z_controller {

        public function action_list(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("shop.view");

            if ($req->isAction("delete-product")) {
                $req->checkPermission("shop.delete");
                $productId = $req->getPost("productId");

                $req->getModel("Shop")->deleteProduct($productId);
            }

            $products = $req->getModel("Shop")->getProducts();

            return $res->render("shop/shopping_cart", [
                "products" => $products
            ]);
        }
    }
?>

Finally, we send a response back to the frontend. The framework provides several response methods, such as:

  • $res->success() Indicates the request was successful.
  • $res->error() Indicates the request failed.

In this case, since the request is successful, we use $res->success() and return immediately to prevent further code execution:

<?php
    class ShopController extends z_controller {

        public function action_list(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("shop.view");

            if ($req->isAction("delete-product")) {
                $req->checkPermission("shop.delete");
                $productId = $req->getPost("productId");

                $req->getModel("Shop")->deleteProduct($productId);
                return $res->success();
            }

            $products = $req->getModel("Shop")->getProducts();

            return $res->render("shop/shopping_cart", [
                "products" => $products
            ]);
        }
    }
?>

This ensures a clear response is sent to the frontend, confirming whether the deletion was successful, and prevents unnecessary processing after the response. For additional response options, refer to the REST API documentation.

docs.title: Why Set active = 0 Instead of Deleting the Product from the Database?
docs.text:
The deleteProduct function in our ShopModel is implemented as follows: 

public function deleteProduct($productId) {
    $sql = "UPDATE `product`
            SET `active` = 0
            WHERE `id` = ?";
    $this->exec($sql, "i", $productId);
}
Instead of removing the product entirely, this function simply sets the active status to 0 in the database. This approach is more prudent because it allows us to retain the data even after a product is "deleted."

This makes it possible to restore mistakenly deleted products and adds a layer of security for user interactions, for example, in cases where users may post inappropriate content and then try to delete it immediately.

However, in our getProducts function, we make sure to only retrieve items that have an active status of 1, so that "deleted" products are not visible in the regular product listings.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Z.Request.action: Sends a request to the backend, requiring an identifier. Additional data can be provided optionally.
  • $req->isAction(""): Checks whether there is a backend request that needs to be handled.
  • active=0: It is preferable to set the active status of database entries to 0 rather than deleting them permanently.

This guide demonstrates how to implement backend requests for our website, enabling efficient data management directly from the frontend.

docs.title: Todo Application
docs.text:
In the last guide, we explored how to make backend requests and manage them effectively on the server side.

In this guide, we will learn how to create forms within our website. Using a simple Todo application as an example, we will demonstrate how to implement functionality to add data to our database using forms.

docs.title: Resources
Setting up our Application
docs.text: To begin working with forms, we first need to establish a basic structure for our application. You can start by copying the controllers, models, views, and database files into the section of your project. Using these resources ensures an organized setup, allowing us to focus on implementing functionality and forms effectively.

docs.title: How to create a Form?
docs.text:
What are Forms?

A form is an interactive element within a web page that allows users to input and submit data. Using the ZubZet framework, forms can be dynamically created and validated, ensuring efficient data collection and seamless integration with backend processing and database storage.

With the help of the framework, creating a form is straightforward. This form comes with several advantages, including easy management, a wide range of features, and an appealing design.

docs.title: Creating a Form in a View
docs.text:
To create a form in a view using ZubZet's framework, start by defining an HTML div element with an id attribute to serve as the container for the form: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <div id="form"></div>
@endsection

Next, include a JavaScript block within the view. This script block will be used to configure and define the form: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <div id="form"></div>
    <script>
    </script>
@endsection

To initialize the form, use the Z.Forms.create method from the framework's JavaScript API. The dom property specifies the container's ID: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <div id="form"></div>
    <script>
        var form = Z.Forms.create({
            dom: "form",
        });
    </script>
@endsection

Fields can now be added to the form. For example, to include a text input field for a task description, use the createField method. Define attributes such as name, type, text, and required to specify the field's behavior: 

@extends($layout)

@section("content")
    <div id="form"></div>
    <script>
        var form = Z.Forms.create({
            dom: "form",
        });

        form.createField({
            name: "description",
            type: "text",
            text: "Todo",
            required: true,
        });
    </script>
@endsection

What does the attributes mean?

Each field's attributes serve specific purposes:

  • name: Identifies the field for backend processing.
  • type: Determines the input type (e.g., text, number, password, or date).
  • text: Displays a label for the field above the input.
  • required: Marks the field with a red asterisk in its label. It performs no client-side validation, so enforce it on the server with ->required().

There are additional attributes available to customize your fields. You can find the full list here

docs.title: Handle Form in the backend
docs.text:
To handle submitted form data, go to your controller which send you the view of the form. Begin by checking for the presence of form data with $req->hasFormData(). This function ensures the backend processes only valid form submissions: 

<?php
    class TodoController extends z_controller {

        // function action_list

        public function action_add(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("todo.add");

            if($req->hasFormData()) {

            }

            return $res->render("todo/add");
        }
    }
?>

$req->hasFormData() is similar to req->isAction(). Both methods are used to check if the frontend is requesting the backend to process a specific action.

Once it is determined that a form needs to be handled, the next step is to validate the form. In this example, we ensure that the description field is mandatory and that the user input is between 5 and 15 characters long.

<?php
    class TodoController extends z_controller {

        // function action_list

        public function action_add(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("todo.add");

            if($req->hasFormData()) {
                $formResult = $req->validateForm([
                    (new FormField("description"))
                        ->required()->length(5, 15),
                ]);
            }

            return $res->render("todo/add");
        }
    }
?>

If validation fails, return errors to the frontend using $res->formErrors(): 

<?php
    class TodoController extends z_controller {

        // function action_list

        public function action_add(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("todo.add");

            if($req->hasFormData()) {
                $formResult = $req->validateForm([
                    (new FormField("description"))
                        ->required()->length(5, 15),
                ]);

                if($formResult->hasErrors) {
                    return $res->formErrors($formResult->errors);
                }
            }

            return $res->render("todo/add");
        }
    }
?>

$formResult->hasErrors tells if there is any invalid input. If errors are present, the method return $res->formErrors($formResult->errors); sends the errors to the frontend, allowing them to be displayed to the user for correction.

Upon successful validation, use $res->insertDatabase to save the data to a database. Ensure field names in the frontend match database column names: 

<?php
    class TodoController extends z_controller {

        // function action_list

        public function action_add(Request $req, Response $res) {
            $req->checkPermission("todo.add");

            if($req->hasFormData()) {
                $formResult = $req->validateForm([
                    (new FormField("description"))
                        ->required()->length(5, 15),
                ]);

                if($formResult->hasErrors) {
                    return $res->formErrors($formResult->errors);
                }

                $res->insertDatabase("todo", $formResult);
                return $res->success();
            }

            return $res->render("todo/add");
        }
    }
?>
By following these steps, the form can be created, validated, and handled efficiently, ensuring both the frontend and backend work seamlessly together.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Z.Forms.create: Initializes a form within a view. It requires a dom attribute to specify the container where the form will be rendered.
  • createField: Creates individual fields with various attributes to customize their behavior and appearance.
  • hasFormData(): Similar to req->isAction(), it checks if the frontend is requesting the backend to handle form data.
  • validateForm: Validates form fields based on predefined rules to ensure data meets the intended criteria.
  • formErrors: Sends validation errors back to the frontend if any fields contain invalid input, allowing for user correction.
  • insertDatabase: Inserts validated form data directly into the database.

docs.title: Updating to the newest version of the framework
docs.text:
This page assumes the framework is a Composer dependency, as in a project built by the install script.

  1. Run composer update zubzet/framework. The package has no version key, Composer takes versions from the git tags (e.g. v1.2.0).
  2. Follow the upgrade guide for every version you skip.
  3. Check the result with php index.php info:startup, which prints the installed version (unknown if Composer cannot tell).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: ZubZet projects are set up with an install script. It builds the project and bundles a Docker development stack: Apache + PHP, MariaDB, phpMyAdmin, and a mail catcher.

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text: Docker is required. Nothing else needs to be installed on your host.

docs.title: Database server
docs.text:
ZubZet requires MariaDB 11.7 or newer and does not support MySQL: the bundled migrations use MariaDB-only syntax (ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, ADD INDEX IF NOT EXISTS, DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS) and the native UUID column type. The Docker stack of a new project runs mariadb:11.8, and the framework's e2e suite runs MariaDB 11.8 as a three-node Galera cluster.

No other SQL dialect is wired up: the runtime connection is mysqli, the migration tooling is hard-coded to the DBAL mysqli driver with MySQL80Platform, and the query builder uses the Cake\Database\Driver\Mysql driver.

docs.title: PHP extensions
docs.text:
The Docker image provides every extension the framework needs. On your own PHP build, composer.json only requires ext-openssl, but you also need:

  • ext-mysqli built against mysqlnd: every query calls mysqli_stmt::get_result(), which the libmysqlclient build of mysqli does not offer.
  • ext-mbstring and ext-fileinfo: the framework calls mb_* functions (e.g. in Helpers), and the asset proxy detects MIME types through league/mime-type-detection, which needs fileinfo.
  • ext-ctype, ext-filter and ext-hash: required by PHPMailer, which sends the mails of Response::sendEmail().
  • Argon2id support: new password hashes use password_hash() with PASSWORD_ARGON2ID, so PHP must be compiled with Argon2 (--with-password-argon2, or the PASSWORD_ARGON2ID constant is undefined).

docs.title: Install script
docs.text:
One command creates a project in a new folder (replace my-project):

bash <(curl -fsSL https://zubzet.com/install.sh) my-project

Without the folder argument the script asks for it. https://zubzet.com/install.sh redirects to the script inside this documentation for the latest stable release, https://zubzet.com/docs/latest/setup/install.sh. The script is versioned with the framework, so for another version fetch it from that version's docs, https://zubzet.com/docs/<version>/setup/install.sh. It is printed in full below so you can read what it does before running it, or save it as install.sh and run it with bash install.sh my-project.

The script asks which framework version to install; pass it as second argument to skip the question: latest for the newest stable release, a Composer constraint such as ^1.3, or a branch such as dev-develop. It writes the project's composer.json, runs composer require zubzet/framework in the project folder and then bin/install from the new vendor, which copies the project template (Docker stack, app/ skeleton, zubzet console entry point and the project script) around it and never overwrites an existing file. All of it runs inside the PHP image the project uses; the container exits when it is done. The script then runs ./project start in the new project, see below.

#!/usr/bin/env bash


# ----------------
# Check Bash
# ----------------

# Before anything else and in plain POSIX syntax, since `sh install.sh` would choke on the Bash-only parts below
if [ -z "${BASH_VERSION:-}" ]; then
    echo "Error: This installer needs Bash, but it was started with another shell." >&2
    echo "Run it with: bash install.sh" >&2
    exit 1
fi


# ----------------
# Output
# ----------------

bold=""; dim=""; red=""; green=""; reset=""

# Colors only on a terminal and not when NO_COLOR is set (https://no-color.org)
if [ -t 1 ] && [ -z "${NO_COLOR:-}" ]; then
    bold=$'\033[1m';
    dim=$'\033[2m';
    red=$'\033[31m';
    green=$'\033[32m';
    reset=$'\033[0m'
fi

# Start on a clean screen so the banner is at the top
if [ -t 1 ]; then
    printf '\033[H\033[2J'
fi

printf '%s' "$green"
cat <<'EOF'
 _____     _    _____    _
|__  /   _| |__|__  /___| |_
  / / | | | '_ \ / // _ \ __|
 / /| |_| | |_) / /|  __/ |_
/____\__,_|_.__/____\___|\__|
EOF
printf '%s\n' "$reset"
echo "${green}ℹ ${bold}Welcome to ZubZet!${reset}"
echo


# ----------------
# Spinner
# ----------------

# The installation output is hidden in a log. The spinner shows its last line below itself and
# the whole log only if something fails.
# Only on a terminal, in logs and pipes the installer prints a plain line instead.
log="$(mktemp)"
spinner_pid=""
tty_state=""

# Seconds as MM:SS
clock() {
    printf '%02d:%02d' "$(($1 / 60))" "$(($1 % 60))"
}

spinner_start() {
    if [ ! -t 1 ]; then
        echo "Installing dependencies..."
        return 0
    fi
    cols="$(tput cols 2>/dev/null || echo 80)"

    # Hide the cursor and reserve the line below the spinner for the log
    printf '\033[?25l\n\033[1A'

    # Keys pressed meanwhile (e.g. Enter) must not be echoed, they would move the spinner down
    if [ -t 0 ]; then
        tty_state="$(stty -g)"
        stty -echo
    fi

    (
        frames=('⠋' '⠙' '⠹' '⠸' '⠼' '⠴' '⠦' '⠧' '⠇' '⠏')
        start=$SECONDS
        i=0
        while true; do
            # Last line of the log, progress bars rewrite their line with \r
            last="$(tail -n 1 "$log" 2>/dev/null)"
            last="${last##*$'\r'}"
            last="${last//[^[:print:]]/}"
            last="${last#"${last%%[![:space:]]*}"}"

            printf '\r\033[K%s%s%s Installing dependencies... %s[%s]%s\n\033[K  %s%s%s\033[1A' \
                "$green" "${frames[i]}" "$reset" "$green" "$(clock "$((SECONDS - start))")" "$reset" \
                "$dim" "${last:0:$((cols - 4))}" "$reset"
            i=$(( (i + 1) % ${#frames[@]} ))
            sleep 0.08
        done
    ) &
    spinner_pid=$!
}

spinner_stop() {
    if [ -z "$spinner_pid" ]; then
        return 0
    fi
    kill "$spinner_pid" 2>/dev/null
    wait "$spinner_pid" 2>/dev/null
    spinner_pid=""

    # Drop what was typed meanwhile and restore the terminal
    if [ -n "$tty_state" ]; then
        while read -r -t 0.01 _; do :; done
        stty "$tty_state"
        tty_state=""
    fi

    # Clear both lines and show the cursor again
    printf '\r\033[K\n\033[K\033[1A\r\033[?25h'
}

# Also clean up when aborted with Ctrl+C or when a step fails
cleanup() {
    spinner_stop
    rm -f "$log"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT TERM


# ----------------
# Check Environment
# ----------------

if ! command -v docker >/dev/null; then
    echo "${red}${bold}Error:${reset} Docker is required but was not found in your PATH." >&2
    echo "Install Docker: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/" >&2
    echo "Then run this installer again." >&2
    exit 1
fi


# ----------------
# Project Directory
# ----------------

# Given as first argument (./install.sh my-project), otherwise asked for
if [ $# -ge 1 ]; then
    directory="$1"
else
    question="${bold}Where would you like to create your project?${reset}"
    echo "${green}?${reset} $question ${dim}(leave empty for current directory)${reset}"
    read -r -p "> " directory

    # Replace the question with its answer once it is given
    if [ -t 0 ] && [ -t 1 ]; then
        printf '\033[2A\r\033[J'
        echo "${green}✔${reset} $question"
        echo "${directory:-.}"
    fi
fi
directory="${directory:-.}"

# ----------------
# Framework Version
# ----------------

# Given as second argument (./install.sh my-project 1.3.0), otherwise asked for. A release number,
# any Composer constraint or branch (dev-develop), or "latest" for the newest stable release.
# The docs deploy replaces the default with the version these docs belong to, so the script of a
# release installs that release.
default_version="1.3.0-RC1"
if [ $# -ge 2 ]; then
    version="$2"
else
    question="${bold}Which version would you like to install?${reset}"
    echo "${green}?${reset} $question ${dim}(leave empty for $default_version, or enter a constraint like ^1.3 or dev-develop)${reset}"
    read -r -p "> " version

    if [ -t 0 ] && [ -t 1 ]; then
        printf '\033[2A\r\033[J'
        echo "${green}✔${reset} $question"
        echo "${version:-$default_version}"
    fi
fi
version="${version:-$default_version}"

mkdir -p "$directory"
directory="$(cd "$directory" && pwd)"
echo "${green}ℹ${reset} Creating a new project in ${green}$directory${reset} with zubzet/framework ${green}$version${reset}."

# The project belongs to the user running the installer.
# Apache refuses to run as root, so for root the project goes to uid 1000 instead, the uid of the application container.
owner="$(id -u):$(id -g)"
if [ "$(id -u)" = 0 ]; then
    owner="1000:1000"
    chown "$owner" "$directory"
fi

# ----------------
# Install
# ----------------

# Everything runs inside the PHP image the project uses, so the host needs nothing but Docker.
# The project's composer.json comes first, then one `composer require` builds the vendor in place
# (latest: without a constraint, so Composer picks the newest stable release and writes the ^
# constraint itself), then bin/install from that vendor adds the rest of the project template.
constraint="$version"
if [ "$version" = latest ]; then
    constraint=""
fi

install_start=$SECONDS
spinner_start
if [ ! -f "$directory/composer.json" ]; then
    cat > "$directory/composer.json" <<'JSON'
{
    "type": "project",
    "config": {
        "audit": {
            "ignore": {
                "GHSA-2jx3-65f3-xr8r": {
                    "apply": "block",
                    "reason": "otphp 11 requires PHP 8.1+, PHP 8.0 stays on 10.x"
                },
                "GHSA-g7m4-839x-ch6v": {
                    "apply": "block",
                    "reason": "otphp 11 requires PHP 8.1+, PHP 8.0 stays on 10.x"
                },
                "PKSA-g499-cm4q-v35y": {
                    "apply": "block",
                    "reason": "symfony/filesystem 6.4.50+ requires PHP 8.1+, PHP 8.0 stays on 6.0"
                }
            }
        }
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "app/"
        }
    }
}
JSON
fi
# Written by root -> the container (uid 1000) must be able to update it
if [ "$(id -u)" = 0 ]; then
    chown "$owner" "$directory/composer.json"
fi
if ! docker run --rm -u "$owner" -e HOME=/tmp -e "ZUBZET_CONSTRAINT=$constraint" -v "$directory":/app -w /app --entrypoint sh ghcr.io/zubzet/php:8.5-apache -c '
    composer require --no-ansi "zubzet/framework${ZUBZET_CONSTRAINT:+:$ZUBZET_CONSTRAINT}" &&
    php vendor/zubzet/framework/bin/install /app
' > "$log" 2>&1; then
    spinner_stop
    echo "${red}${bold}Error:${reset} The installation failed:" >&2
    cat "$log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
spinner_stop

echo "${green}✔${reset} Done! ZubZet installed in ${bold}$directory.${reset} ${green}[$(clock "$((SECONDS - install_start))")]${reset}"


# ----------------
# Start
# ----------------

# The installer container is gone by now, the project starts on the host through its own script
echo
echo "${green}ℹ${reset} Starting the project..."
if ! (cd "$directory" && ./project start); then
    echo "${red}${bold}Error:${reset} The project was installed but could not be started. Run ${bold}./project start${reset} in ${bold}$directory${reset} again." >&2
    exit 1
fi


# ----------------
# Next Steps
# ----------------

# Laid out like the output of `info:startup` in the framework
rule="  ${dim}─────────────────────────────────────────────${reset}"

# Label in the muted color, value in bold
info_row() {
    printf '  %s%-8s%s %s\n' "$dim" "$1" "$reset" "$2"
}

echo
echo "$rule"
# Only when the project is not in the current directory
if [ "$directory" != "$PWD" ]; then
    info_row "Enter" "${bold}cd $(printf '%q' "$directory")${reset}"
fi
info_row "Stop" "${bold}./project stop${reset}"
echo
info_row "Docs" "${green}https://zubzet.com/docs${reset}"
info_row "Issues" "${green}https://github.com/zubzet/framework/issues${reset}"
echo "$rule"
echo

docs.title: Install with an agent
docs.text:
If an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ...) does the setup or the work on an existing project, give it this one line first:

Fetch https://zubzet.com/agent.md and follow it before working on this ZubZet project. If you cannot fetch it, do nothing and tell me.

The page is a short signpost for agents. It tells them to run the install script above for a new project, where the documentation and the agent skill live inside vendor/zubzet/framework/ (docs/ and skills/zubzet/), how the project script drives the Docker stack, and that a project's own AGENTS.md wins over the skill. Two things to know before you paste it:

  • Docker must be installed and the agent must be allowed to run it. The install script, the application and the tests all run in containers; an agent in a sandbox without Docker can read the sources but cannot install, start or test the project.
  • The agent reads the skill. The skill is a directory in the framework package, vendor/zubzet/framework/skills/zubzet, that holds the architecture, design and style rules for ZubZet projects. Every agent can read it right there. A tool that loads project skills from a folder of its own gets a link to that directory, which the agent offers to create; the framework itself creates no tool specific folder in a project.

The same prompt works on an existing project at any time; it is the fastest way to give a new agent session the full context.

docs.title: Start the project
docs.text:
The install script starts the project itself. Later, or after a ./project stop, run inside your project folder:

./project start

Every start resets the database on purpose

./project start drops and recreates the database, so all local data is lost each time.

This single command:

  1. Builds the application image and starts the Docker stack (detached),
  2. Runs composer install inside the application container,
  3. Seeds the database with db:seed, which drops and recreates the database, runs all migrations and loads the seed data (local data is lost on every start),
  4. Prints the startup info with info:startup.

To stop and remove the stack (and its volumes), run ./project stop. ./project shell opens a shell inside the application container. See console commands for all project commands.

docs.title: Access your application
docs.text:
Service URL Application http://localhost:8080 Database UI (phpMyAdmin) http://localhost:8081 Mail catcher (smtp4dev) http://localhost:3300

The seed creates no user accounts. app/Database/seed/accounts/0_permissions.sql adds the roles Admin (permission *.*) and User (permission dashboard); create a user and assign it a role, see Z-Admin permissions. Adjust or remove the seed before going to production.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
tests/e2e/ in the framework repository is a complete reference project. The framework resolves every default path relative to the process working directory, so an entry script has to chdir() to the project root before booting (the stub index.php does chdir(realpath(__DIR__)), webroot/index.php changes to its parent folder). This matters for cron jobs and other CLI calls started from elsewhere.

  • index.php: entry script in the project root that boots the framework, for HTTP requests (via webroot/index.php, which requires the first existing of index.php, zubzet.php and zubzet) and for CLI use (php index.php <command>). It calls chdir(realpath(__DIR__)), requires autoload.php from $COMPOSER_VENDOR_DIR (default ./vendor), then runs new z_framework() (an alias of ZubZet) and ->execute(). Web and CLI share this script: for php index.php <command>, execute() hands over to the console when no route matches.
  • app/Controllers/: default z_controllers directory with the <Name>Controller.php files. A controller in a sub-folder is found by its plain name, see controllers.
  • app/Models/: default z_models directory with the <Name>Model.php files. A sub-folder is addressed in lower case through dot notation, getModel("reports.GuestbookStats") loads reports/GuestbookStatsModel.php.
  • app/Views/: default z_views directory with views, mail templates and the layout/ folder. Further sub-folders are allowed and addressed in the view name (employee/index).
  • app/Routes/: default routes directory. Every top-level *.php file in it is require_onced when the route dispatcher is built on the first request, sub-folders are not read.
  • app/Database/migrations/: migration files read by db:migrate and db:sync. A missing folder is created with mode 0755.
  • app/Database/seed/: seed files read by db:seed. Sub-folders can be used as selectors for -i and -e. A missing folder is created with mode 0755.
  • z_config/z_settings.ini: settings file at the default config_file path. It is read without an existence check, so a project without it does not boot.

docs.title: Web root
docs.text:
Apache serves only webroot/ (DocumentRoot /var/www/html/webroot, see packaging/docker/site-000-default.conf). Everything above it is outside the web root and cannot be requested, so /app/Controllers/AdminController.php, /composer.json, /vendor/autoload.php and /z_config/z_settings.ini answer 404 and never expose source code or settings. The .htaccess in webroot/ (RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f with RewriteRule . index.php [L,QSA]) sends every request that is not an existing file to webroot/index.php and keeps the query string, so such a request reaches the framework router, which has no route for it, and the response is the framework's 404 page. Existing files in webroot/ (assets, uploads/) are served by Apache directly, and PHP files there are executed directly, bypassing the framework. Keep secrets and application code out of webroot/.

The rewrite rule is an Apache .htaccess, so it needs mod_rewrite and AllowOverride All for the document root (set in packaging/docker/site-000-default.conf of the Docker stack). Any other web server needs an equivalent rule that sends requests for non-existing files to webroot/index.php.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings live in z_config/z_settings.ini. When allow_env_config = true, any setting can be overridden by a CONFIG_* environment variable. The Docker stack uses this to inject the database and mailer credentials (see packaging/docker/docker-compose-base.yml). Keep secrets out of the committed INI file and provide them via the environment, but declare a placeholder such as dbpassword = env in the INI for each of them: a variable is ignored unless its key already exists (see environment variable overrides).

Three keys must exist in the INI, otherwise the framework does not boot: host (the base URL, e.g. http://localhost:8080), rootDirectory (the sub-path the app is served from; the key must be present, but its value may be empty; write it without leading or trailing slash, although surrounding slashes and backslashes are trimmed before use) and showErrors (0, 1 or 2, see error handling). A missing key throws an InvalidArgumentException ("The attribute '...' does not exist in the attribute store (yet)") during startup. CONFIG_* environment variables and constructor parameters only override keys that already exist, so they cannot supply a missing one. The project stub in stubs/project/z_config/z_settings.ini already defines all three.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Migrations — schema management and the migration CLI.
  • Configuration — every available setting.
  • MVC and Routing — build your first pages.

docs.title: Upgrade Steps
docs.text:
1. Remove Submodule from Git 

    git submodule deinit -f z_framework
git rm -rf z_framework

    Then delete the leftover directory:

    .git/modules/z_framework

    This unregisters the submodule from Git so it won’t be tracked anymore.

  2. Remove from .gitmodules Delete the entry for z_framework, e.g.:

    [submodule "z_framework"]
    path = z_framework
    url = https://github.com/zubzet/framework.git

    This removes the last configuration reference to the submodule.

  3. Add via Composer 

    composer require zubzet/framework

    The framework is now managed via Composer, making version upgrades and dependency handling much easier.

  4. Clean up index.php Remove this line:

    require_once "z_framework/main.php";

    The main.php is now loaded automatically through Composer’s autoloader, so you no longer need to include it manually.

Upgrade script for Linux 
[ -d z_framework ] && rm -rf z_framework

git config --file .gitmodules --get-regexp 'submodule\.z_framework\.path' >/dev/null 2>&1 && \
    git submodule deinit -f z_framework && \
    git rm -f -r z_framework

[ -d .git/modules/z_framework ] && rm -rf .git/modules/z_framework
[ -f .gitmodules ] && sed -i '/\[submodule "z_framework"\]/,/^$/d' .gitmodules

composer require zubzet/framework

[ -f index.php ] && sed -i '/require_once\s\+"z_framework\/main.php";/d' index.php

After this, your project will automatically use the Composer autoloader and the framework will be ready to run.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• New Features
  • Deprecated Features
  • Other Changes
